en: The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground in the Original Life Stories, Scroll One. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Prajñā of Kapiśī during the Great Tang Dynasty, by Imperial Decree. Chapter One: The Introduction. **Chapter One: The Introduction** Thus have I heard. At one time the Bhagavat was dwelling in the city of Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandakanivāpa, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred great bhikṣus and a great assembly of bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, all of whom were great beings who had attained the stage of non-retrogression. Among them were the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Akṣayamati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajramati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gaganagañja, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and others such as these, numbering eight thousand. At that time, the World-Honored One was seated upon a lion throne made of various precious jewels, adorned with a multitude of banners and canopies, draped with various celestial garments, and spread with a layer of celestial *karpāsa* cotton. He sat cross-legged, his body upright, and established himself in mindfulness before him. His countenance was serene and majestic, like the full moon emerging from behind a cloud; he was surrounded by a retinue of gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, as well as kings, ministers, brahmins, householders, and other laypeople, all of whom were gazing at the Buddha with single-minded devotion. Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Bhagavat:

"World-Honored One, today this great assembly is pure and free from defilement. All the great bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, and the fourfold assembly have gathered here. World-Honored One, what is the name of this dharma-gate? What is its profound meaning? For what reason has the Bhagavat manifested such a wondrous sign? Having spoken thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya prostrated himself at the feet of the Buddha and withdrew to one side. At that moment, the entire great earth shook in six ways: it moved, trembled, and quaked; it surged, subsided, and rolled. It shook from the east and rose in the west; it shook from the west and rose in the east; it shook from the south and rose in the north; it shook from the north and rose in the south. It shook from the four quarters and rose in the intermediate directions; it shook from the intermediate directions and rose in the four quarters. It shook from above and rose from below; it shook from below and rose from above. The entire great trichiliocosm was filled with a vast radiance, surpassing the light of the sun and moon. All the heavens rained down celestial flowers, incense, and perfumes, while celestial music played spontaneously. Then the Bhagavat addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya: "Excellent, excellent, Maitreya! You have asked the Tathāgata about this matter out of a desire to benefit and bring peace to all sentient beings. Listen attentively and reflect well upon what I shall now explain. Maitreya replied, "I am eager to hear, World-Honored One; may the Bhagavat speak. The Buddha said to Maitreya: "This dharma-gate is called 'The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground in the Original Life Stories. Its meaning is profound and subtle, difficult to understand and difficult to enter. It is not something that śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas can know. Why is this? Because it reveals the true nature of the mind-ground, which is the source of all dharmas. [The rest of the text follows the narrative of the Buddha’s teaching on the contemplation of the mind-ground.]
Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of thirty-two thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats—whose minds were well-liberated, whose wisdom was well-liberated, who had accomplished what was to be done, laid down their heavy burdens, attained their own benefit, exhausted the fetters of existence, gained great mastery, dwelt in pure precepts, were adorned with skillful means and wisdom, and had realized the eight liberations, reaching the further shore. Their names were as follows:

The Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya, Aśvajit, Mahānāman, Bhadrika, Mahākāśyapa, Gavāmpati, Revata, Uruvilvākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākātyāyana, Mahākapphiṇa, Cunda, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Aniruddha, Subāhu, Subhūti, Bakula, Nanda, Sundarananda, and Rāhula.

In this manner, the venerable Arhats, as well as those still in training such as Ānanda, each accompanied by several hundred thousand followers, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

Furthermore, there were eighty-four thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all of whom were great Dharma-princes in their final birth before Buddhahood. Possessing great majestic power like that of great dragon kings, their bodies were replete with a hundred merits and radiated light that surpassed the brilliance of a thousand suns in dispelling all darkness. Their wisdom was as clear and transparent as the great ocean, and they had thoroughly realized the secret realms of all Buddhas.

He kindles the great torch of the Dharma to guide sentient beings, acting as a great captain upon the ocean of birth and death; he regards all beings with compassion as if they were his own infants, constantly bestowing peace and happiness at all times; his fame is heard throughout the worlds of the ten directions, and he sports with mastery in subtle supernatural powers.

Having already attained mastery over all doors of dhāraṇī, they possess the sovereign power of the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence; having already attained the perfection of the sovereign power of great vows, they have skillfully accomplished the sovereign power of enlightened activities; having already attained skillful entry into the sovereign power of samādhi, they are fully endowed with the sovereign power of merit and virtue, and constantly act as unsolicited friends to all sentient beings.

Having diligently cultivated the six perfections for immeasurable kalpas and served successive Buddhas, they do not abide in nirvana; having severed all afflictions and eliminated both seeds and habitual tendencies, they manifest birth within the six realms of existence yet remain free from fault.

Manifesting bodies throughout the ten directions to preach the wondrous Dharma, they transform and benefit sentient beings across immeasurable worlds; they subdue all non-Buddhists and crush perverse minds, leading them away from the causes of nihilism and eternalism so that right view may arise, all while remaining free from any sign of coming, going, or movement.

Without being adorned, he adorns the Buddha-lands of the ten directions; without speaking, he proclaims the wondrous principle of profound stillness. Dwelling in non-dwelling, he delivers the multitudes of humans and devas; experiencing the vast joy of the Dharma without receiving anything, he dons the armor of diligence and grasps the sword of wisdom. He shatters the hosts of Māra and beats the Dharma drum; his body constantly and universally occupies all sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Blowing the great Dharma conch, he awakens all classes of beings, so that every sentient being receives benefit; none who hear his name or see his body pass away in vain.

Possessing the three types of penetrating wisdom, they have awakened to the phenomena of the three periods of time; they skillfully know the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of sentient beings, administering medicine according to their ailments without further doubt.

They spread the great cloud of Dharma and pour down the rain of ambrosia, turning the wheel of the Dharma of non-retrogressive wisdom-seal; they close the prison of birth and death and open the gate of Nirvana, giving rise to great vows to deliver all living beings until the end of the future.
These bodhisattvas shall before long attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; their names are:
Vimalakīrti Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva, Siṃhanāda Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Vimalakīrti Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva.
Vajragarbha-rāja Bodhisattva, Kṣitigarbha-rāja Bodhisattva, Gaganagarbha-rāja Bodhisattva,
Dhāraṇīśvararāja Bodhisattva, Samādhiśvararāja Bodhisattva, Sumeru-rāja Bodhisattva,
Mahāsāgara-gambhīra-rāja Bodhisattva, Prabhūtavyūharāja Bodhisattva, and Nandana Bodhisattva.
Bodhisattva King of Height, Bodhisattva King of Great Supernatural Transformations, Bodhisattva Sovereign King of Dharma,
Bodhisattva King of Pure Rain, Bodhisattva Medicine King, Bodhisattva Superior Medicine, Bodhisattva Healer of the Disease of Afflictions, Bodhisattva Jewel Mountain,
Bodhisattva Jewel Wealth, Bodhisattva Supreme Jewel, and Bodhisattva Jewel Virtue.
The Bodhisattvas: Ratnagarbha, Ratnakūṭa, Ratnapāṇi, Ratnamudrāhasta, Ratnaprabha, Ratnadatta, Ratnaketu,
Mahāratnaketu, Ratnavarṣa, Ratnasaṃprāpta, and Ratnadaṇḍa.
Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin, Bodhisattva Ratnaśrī, Bodhisattva Ratneśvara, Bodhisattva Candanagandha, Bodhisattva Mahāratnolkā,
Bodhisattva Mahāratnavyūha, Bodhisattva Sūryaprabha, Bodhisattva Candraprabha,
Bodhisattva Tārakāprabha, Bodhisattva Tejaprabha, and Bodhisattva Vidyutprabha.
The Bodhisattva Capable of Bestowing Mindfulness and Wisdom, the Bodhisattva Destroyer of Māra, the Bodhisattva Victor over Māra,
the Bodhisattva Constantly Diligent, the Bodhisattva Unceasing, the Bodhisattva Who Never Ceases Great Vows,
the Bodhisattva of Great Renown, the Bodhisattva of Unimpeded Eloquence, and the Bodhisattva of Unimpeded Turning of the Wheel of Dharma— thus [there were] none...
The Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas such as Vimala, each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues;
and further, there were billions of devaputras of the six heavens of the desire realm, whose names were:

Devaputra Susthita, Devaputra Tejodhipati, Devaputra Samantaprabha, Devaputra Viśuddhamati, Devaputra Śrī, Devaputra Mahāśrī, Devaputra Īśvara, Devaputra Maheśvara, Devaputra Sūryaprabha, and Devaputra Candraprabha.

These and other such devaputras, with Śakra Devānām Indra as their leader, all cherished and delighted in the sublime Dharma of the Mahāyāna; they vowed to serve and attend upon the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, enter the inconceivable secret realm, and adorn the bodhimaṇḍas of the assemblies of all Buddhas, each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
Furthermore, there were as many sons of the gods from the realm of form (rūpadhātu) as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, whose names were:

the Son of the God Great Light Shining Universally; the Son of the God Stainless Adornment; the Son of the God Sporting in Supernatural Powers; the Son of the God Sovereign in Samādhi; the Son of the God Sovereign in Dhāraṇī; the Son of the God Great Nārāyaṇa; the Son of the God Fulfilling Supreme Vows; the Son of the God Unobstructed Eloquence; the Son of the God Auspicious Merit and Wisdom; and the Son of the God Constantly Making Great Vows.

These and other such devaputras, with the Great Brahmā King of Radiance as their leader, were all fully endowed with samādhi, supernatural powers, and the eloquence of joyful exposition. Having served the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, they arrived at the assemblies whenever a Bodhisattva sat upon the Vajra-seat beneath the Bodhi tree, defeated the armies of Māra, and realized enlightenment. At that time, they were always among the first to entreat the Tathāgata to turn the wondrous Wheel of Dharma and open the gate of ambrosia to deliver the multitudes of devas and humans. They had skillfully awakened to the secret intentions of all Buddhas and never again regressed from great bodhi;
each was accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
Furthermore, there were forty-eight thousand great dragon kings:

the Dragon King Manasvin, the Dragon King Takṣaka, the Dragon King Nanda, the Dragon King Upananda, the Dragon King of Lake Anavatapta, the Dragon King Mahāmukha, the Dragon King Maṇiratna, the Dragon King Varṣavararatna, the Dragon King Nityavarṣa, the Dragon King Mahātejas, and the Dragon King Balavaśavartin.
These dragon kings, with the Dragon King Sāgara as their leader, all cherished and delighted in the sublime Dharma of the Mahāyāna;
they gave rise to great vows to reverently protect and uphold it, each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
Furthermore, there were fifty-eight thousand yakṣa deities:

the yakṣa deity Great Lion King, the yakṣa deity Sun-Disc Radiance, the yakṣa deity Sublime Nārāyaṇa, the yakṣa deity Most Terrifying, the yakṣa deity Lotus Radiance Color, the yakṣa deity Exquisite Faculties, the yakṣa deity Protector of the True Dharma, the yakṣa deity Offering to the Triple Gem, the yakṣa deity Raining Down Various Precious Jewels, and the yakṣa deity Maṇiprabha.

Such yakṣas as these, with the yakṣa Saṃjñeya as their leader, are all fully endowed with inconceivable light of wisdom, inconceivable torches of wisdom, inconceivable practices of wisdom, and inconceivable accumulations of wisdom; for the sake of sentient beings, they subdue malevolent spirits, enabling them to attain peace and happiness, extending their merit and wisdom, and protecting the Mahāyāna so that it shall never be interrupted;
each is accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
Furthermore, there were eighty-nine thousand gandharva kings:

the Gandharva King Jewel-Crown on the Summit, the Gandharva King Universally Radiating Light, the Gandharva King Vajra-Jewel Banner, the Gandharva King Pure Exquisite Sound, the Gandharva King Pervading All Assemblies, the Gandharva King Manifesting Everywhere in All Directions, the Gandharva King Delighting in the Mahāyāna, and the Gandharva King Turning the Non-Retrogressive Wheel.

These Gandharva kings, headed by the Gandharva King Viśuddhendriya, all conceived deep love and reverence for the Mahāyāna; they constantly sought to benefit and bring happiness to sentient beings without ever becoming weary, each accompanied by several hundred thousand retinues.
Furthermore, there were ten billion asura kings:

the asura king Rāhula, the asura king Vemacitrin, the asura king Prabhāva-udgata, the asura king Mahā-dṛḍhabala, the asura king Manojña-svara, the asura king Samanta-prabhāsa, the asura king Nitya-jaya-yuddha, and the asura king Kuśala-māyā-nirmāṇa.
These Āsura kings, headed by the Āsura king Vast and Sublime Eloquence, were all well-practiced in abandoning all forms of pride;
they upheld the Mahāyāna and revered the Triple Gem, each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
Furthermore, there were five hundred million *garuḍa* kings:

the *garuḍa* king Ratnaśikhin, the *garuḍa* king Vajraviśuddhaprabha, the *garuḍa* king Vāyuvegavat, the *garuḍa* king Gaganaviśuddhamati, the *garuḍa* king Viśālaviśuddhakāya, the *garuḍa* king Avivartyacitta, the *garuḍa* king Viśālanetra-viśuddha, the *garuḍa* king Mahodara-paripūrṇa, the *garuḍa* king Mahātejas, and the *garuḍa* king Jñānaprabhāsa.
These Garuḍa kings, headed by the Garuḍa King Manojñaprabha, had all attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and skillfully benefited all sentient beings;
each was accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of followers.
Furthermore, there were nine hundred million kinnara kings:

the Kinnara King Earth-Shaker, the Kinnara King Wondrous Jewel Flower Banner, the Kinnara King Radiance of Jewel Trees, the Kinnara King Radiance of the Good Dharma, the Kinnara King Supreme Adornment, the Kinnara King Radiance of the Great Dharma, the Kinnara King Upholder of the Sublime Dharma, the Kinnara King Adorned with Wondrous Jewels, and the Kinnara King Accomplished in Sublime Contemplation.
These and other kings of the kinnaras, headed by the Kinnara King Manojñaghoṣa, were all endowed with pure and wondrous wisdom;
they dwelt in physical and mental bliss, sporting with sovereign ease, each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
Furthermore, there were ninety-eight thousand mahoraga kings:

the mahoraga king Citracūḍa, the mahoraga king Mahātejas, the mahoraga king Ratnacitracūḍa, the mahoraga king Śuddhanetra-sūkṣma, the mahoraga king Prabhā-ratnadhvaja, the mahoraga king Siṃhavakṣas, the mahoraga king Merukalpa-acala, and the mahoraga king Priyaprabha.

These and other such Mahoraga kings, with the Mahoraga King Youxi (Amusement) as their leader, have already cultivated skillful means to cause all sentient beings to forever leave behind the entanglements of craving;
each is accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.

Furthermore, there were wheel-turning sage-kings from ten billion lands in other directions—wheel-turning sage-kings of the golden wheel, silver wheel, copper wheel, and iron wheel—along with their retinues of seven treasures and a thousand sons.

They were adorned with immeasurable elephants, horses, and chariots; they displayed countless jeweled banners and suspended great precious pennants; they carried flower garlands, jeweled canopies, silken streamers, and white whisks; and they possessed various rare and wonderful jewels, necklaces, ointments, powdered incense, and ten thousand kinds of blended, subtle, and exquisite fragrances. Each held a priceless, precious incense burner and burned great precious incense as an offering to the World-Honored One. With sublime words, they praised the Tathāgata’s profound ocean of wisdom and addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One!..."
I now do not seek the tainted fruits of existence within the three realms—those of humans or devas—but seek only the supramundane *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this?

Within the three realms, although the bliss and fortune of humans and devas place one in a position of honor, once the merit of previous lives is exhausted, one will again be born in the evil destinies and undergo immeasurable suffering.
What wise person would take pleasure in worldly delights?
Having spoken these words, they joined their palms with single-minded devotion, each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of followers.
Furthermore, there were sixteen great kings:

the Great King Śuddhodana of the kingdom of Kapilavastu; King Bimbisāra of the kingdom of Magadha; the Great King Kasi of the kingdom of Vārāṇasī; the Great King Udayana of the kingdom of Avanti; and King Kapphiṇa, the lord of the kingdom of Sālā.

These sixteen great kings and various minor kings, with King Prasenajit of Śrāvastī—named Candraprabha—as their leader, were all fully endowed with merit, wisdom, and supernormal powers. Possessing great majesty and virtue like a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*), all their enemies naturally submitted to them. Their populations flourished and their lands were prosperous and joyful; having planted roots of goodness under immeasurable Buddhas, they were constantly protected and remembered by all the Buddhas.
During the Kalpa of Adornment (*Vibhūṣaṇakalpa*), when one thousand Buddhas appear, these kings shall constantly serve as their patrons;
during the Fortunate Kalpa (*Bhadrakalpa*), when one thousand Buddhas appear, these kings shall likewise serve as their patrons;
and in the future Starry Kalpa (*Tārakakalpa*), when one thousand Buddhas appear, they shall likewise serve as their patrons.

Until all Buddhas appear in the world in the future, these kings, by the power of their original vows, shall constantly practice the giving of alms to benefit sentient beings; they shall skillfully enter various gates of expedient means as appropriate, and though acting as kings, they shall not crave worldly pleasures. Disgusted with and detached from birth and death, they shall cultivate the causes of liberation, diligently seeking the Buddha-way and delighting in the Mahāyāna. They shall transform and benefit all living beings without clinging to any signs, thereby continuing the lineage of the Triple Gem so that it never ceases.

To hear the Dharma, they made offerings to the Tathāgata, extensively preparing exquisite foods and solemnly presenting incense and flowers; they came to the Buddha’s dwelling, each accompanied by twelve thousand, twenty thousand, or even ten million followers.
Furthermore, there were the consorts of sixteen great kings:
Queen Vaidehī, Queen Subhāsumanā, Queen Atiramaṇīyā, Queen Trilokānupamā, Queen Puṇyavipākābhā, Queen Maniratnaprabhā, Queen Mallikā, and Queen Guṇavatī.

Among these ladies, the Lady of Exquisite and Wondrous Countenance was the foremost; she had already attained skillful entry into immeasurable right concentrations and manifested a female body for the sake of delivering sentient beings. Having cultivated her mind through the three gates of liberation, she possessed great wisdom and perfect merit, as well as unconditional great kindness and unimpeded great compassion. She cherished all sentient beings like her own infant, and by the power of her original vows, she encountered the World-Honored One.

Desiring to hear the Dharma, they came to the presence of the Buddha; gazing upon his venerable countenance without averting their eyes for even a moment, they presented the World-Honored One with immeasurable kinds of supreme human offerings, as well as countless exquisite jewel necklaces, making offerings to the Tathāgata together with their respective retinues of several hundred thousand followers.

Furthermore, there were hundreds of thousands of immeasurable people—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen; brahmins, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and śūdras; as well as elders and householders from all the various kingdoms and all the common folk.

This great assembly, having conceived pure faith and a heart of profound reverence, and having planted roots of goodness in past lives, were born into an age when the Buddha-dharma exists. Seeking transcendence from the world, they gave rise to the thought that such an encounter is difficult to find; thus they came to where the Buddha was, with single-minded palms joined, each accompanied by several hundred thousand followers.
Furthermore, there were countless followers of various non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika):

non-Buddhists of ascetic practices, non-Buddhists of extensive learning, non-Buddhists of worldly wisdom, non-Buddhists who delight in seclusion, and non-Buddhists of the Lokāyata school; among them, the non-Buddhists of the Lokāyatika-Ṛddhi were the leaders. Having attained the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā) and mastery over flight, they conceived a rare and marvelous resolve and came to the Buddha’s dwelling to hear the Dharma, each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of attendants.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable and innumerable non-human beings and hungry ghosts, namely:

the wealthless ghosts (*akiṃcana*), the ghosts who eat human vomit, the ghosts who afflict sentient beings, the ghosts who eat mucus and saliva, the ghosts who are never satiated, the piśāca ghosts, the extremely foul-smelling ghosts, the ghosts who eat filth and excrement, the ghosts who eat human fetuses, the ghosts who eat newborn children, the ghosts who eat impurities, and the ghosts who bring auspiciousness.

These various spirits, with the great spirit king Virūḍhaka as their leader, abandoned their poisonous minds and took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha. They all vowed to protect the True Dharma of the Tathāgata and came to the place where the Buddha was for the sake of hearing the Dharma. Prostrating themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, they gazed up thirstily at the World-Honored One, each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable and innumerable kings of birds and beasts:
the king of jīvaṃjīvaka birds, the king of parrots, as well as the lion king, the elephant king, and the deer king.

All these kings of birds and beasts, with the golden lion king as their leader, took refuge in the Tathāgata, the Great Teacher. Desiring to hear the Dharma, they came to the Buddha’s presence and, each according to the power of their vows, made offerings to the World-Honored One, saying to the Buddha:
“We pray only that the Tathāgata...”

We beseech you to accept our humble offerings, so that we may forever sever the seeds of evil karma in the three miserable realms and obtain the retributive fruits of happiness and fortune among humans and devas. May you open and expound the ambrosial Dharma-gate of the Mahāyāna, swiftly severing ignorance so that we may attain liberation.

When the various bird kings had finished speaking these words, they joined their palms with single-minded devotion and gazed up at the Tathāgata, each accompanied by several hundred thousand retinues.

Furthermore, there were hundreds of thousands of Yamarāja kings, together with countless great rākṣasas of various forms, various evil kings, and the officials and subordinates of the netherworld—the jailers and judicial officers who calculate merit and demerit—who, through the Buddha’s awesome power, abandoned their malevolent intentions. Accompanying the Yamarāja kings, they came to listen to the Dharma and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Because of ignorance, all sentient beings crave the pleasures of the five desires and commit the five heinous crimes. They enter the various hells and transmigrate without end; due to the causes of their own karma, they undergo great suffering and affliction, like silkworms in cocoons entangling themselves.”
“May the Tathāgata, we pray, rain down the great Dharma-rain to extinguish the fires of hell, bestow the cool breeze of liberation, open the gate of deliverance, and close the three evil realms.

When King Yama had spoken these words, he made offerings of various precious jewels to the Tathāgata; with single-minded reverence, he circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, together with several hundred thousand attendants, each prostrating at the Buddha’s feet and withdrawing to sit to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One sat upon a lion throne of precious lotus flowers. That lion throne was the color of deep blue lapis lazuli, magnificently adorned with various rare and exquisite jewels. A crystal gem formed its stem, and purple-golden *suvarṇa* made its lotus petals; the pericarp of the lotus was composed of *maṇi* gems as its filaments. Eighty-four thousand great precious lotus flowers of Jambūnada gold served as its retinue. He was surrounded before and behind by the great assembly, who paid him homage, venerated him, honored him, and praised him.

At that time, the Bhagavān sat cross-legged upon the lion throne, his majestic demeanor exceptionally sublime. He was like Mount Sumeru, composed of the four jewels, naturally towering above the great ocean; like hundreds of thousands of suns illuminating the void, emitting immeasurable light to shatter all darkness; and like ten million full moons standing alone among the stars, radiating cool brilliance to clarify the world.

At that time, the Tathāgata entered the supreme samādhi of the Peak of Existence called the King of the Heart-Necklace Jewel Adornment; having dwelt in this concentration, his body and mind remained unmoving.
At that time, all the devaputras of the formless realm rained down immeasurable varieties of exquisite flowers and incense, descending from the void like clouds.

The various devas of the form realm and the eighteen Brahmā kings rained down countless celestial flowers of many colors—hundreds of thousands of millions of kinds—and the sublime incense of the Brahma heavens filled the void, descending like clouds.

The devas of the six heavens of desire and their hosts of sons, by the power of their celestial merit, rained down various flowers—*utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, *puṇḍarīka*, *campaka*, *atimuktaka*, *pāriyātraka*, *sumana*, *māndārava*, *mahāmāndārava*, *mañjūṣaka*, and *mahāmañjūṣaka*—which fell in profusion and in disarray through the air as an offering to the Buddha and the multitude of Dharma jewels.

Furthermore, priceless celestial incense rained down; like clouds, this incense manifested the colors of a hundred jewels, and through the power of the devas, its fragrance filled these worlds, making offerings to the great assembly.

At that time, the World-Honored One arose from samādhi and, remaining on his original seat, again entered the Lion’s Display Samādhi. Manifesting great supernormal powers, he caused this trichiliocosm to shake in six ways: namely, shaking, intense shaking, and universal intense shaking; surging, intense surging, and universal intense surging; trembling, intense trembling, and universal intense trembling; clashing, intense clashing, and universal intense clashing; roaring, intense roaring, and universal intense roaring; and bursting, intense bursting, and universal intense bursting.

Furthermore, this world surged in the east and subsided in the west; it surged in the west and subsided in the east; it surged in the south and subsided in the north; it surged in the north and subsided in the south; it surged in the center and subsided at the edges; it surged at the edges and subsided in the center. The ground became majestic and pure, entirely supple, causing the flora and vegetation to flourish and benefiting all living beings. It caused the three thousandfold world-system to be free of hells, hungry ghosts, animals, and other sentient beings in the unfavorable states of existence, so that they all attained liberation from suffering. After casting off these bodies, they were reborn among human beings and the six heavens of the desire realm. All of them, possessing the knowledge of past lives, leaped for joy and together proceeded to the Buddha’s dwelling. With profound and sincere hearts, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and offered various rare jewels and countless necklaces; realizing the emptiness of the three spheres, they repaid the Buddha’s kindness.

At that time, the Tathāgata emitted a great radiance from the region of his chest and from all his pores, named "The Play of the Supernatural Powers of All Bodhisattvas Causing Non-retrogression from Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
The color of its radiance was like Jāmbūnada gold; this golden light shone universally throughout the trichiliocosm and other realms,
reaching even unto the hundred billion Sumeru Kings of Mountains, as well as all the Snowy Mountains,
Fragrant Mountains, Black Mountains, Golden Mountains, Jewel Mountains, and Mount Meru and Great Meru.
Mount Lūśan, Mount Mucilinda, Mount Mahāmucilinda, the Lesser Iron Ring Mountains, and the Great Iron Ring Mountains;

the rivers, great oceans, flowing springs, and bathing pools; as well as the ten billion sets of four great continents, the sun, moon, and stars, and the palaces of the devas, the nāgas, and all the various honored deities—along with these.
The various kingdoms, cities, royal palaces, and villages; the realm of Yama;
all the various hells of the eight cold and eight hot types where sentient beings with karmic offenses undergo suffering;

and even the states of suffering experienced by animals and hungry ghosts throughout the ten directions—the signs of suffering and happiness experienced by all sentient beings within the five destinies of every world.
All these were manifested within this great golden radiance.

Furthermore, within this light, there appeared the various manifestations of the Bodhisattva’s practice of the Buddha-way: from when Śākyamuni Bodhisattva was King Prabhāsa in the past and first gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, until his attainment of the Buddha-way beneath the Bodhi tree and his entry into *nirvāṇa* within the Śāla grove.

During the interval of three hundred thousand million *kalpas*, all his practices of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, as well as the eighty-four thousand gates of the *pāramitās*, were realized. Furthermore, in the past, he served as a Golden Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*) over the four continents, extending to the limits of the great oceans. His subjects were flourishing and his realm was abundant and joyful; he transformed the world through the True Dharma for immeasurable *kalpas, and all manner of rare treasures filled his kingdom.

At that time, that wheel-turning monarch observed that all worlds are entirely impermanent; weary of the pleasures of the five desires, he renounced his position as a wheel-turning monarch to leave the household life and study the Way.
Or, as the beloved son of a king in a great kingdom, he cast away his own life to throw himself before a starving tiger;
or, becoming King Śibi, he cut his own body to save a dove.
At times he saved a pregnant deer by sacrificing his own body as a deer king;
at other times, on the Snowy Mountains, he sacrificed his entire body to seek half a verse of the Dharma;

or he manifested birth into the house of King Śuddhodana, where he renounced sixty thousand ladies of the inner palace and various exquisite musical entertainments, scaled the city walls to leave the household, practiced austerities for six years, subsisted daily on hemp and wheat to subdue the non-Buddhists, and having sat beneath the Bodhi tree and defeated the armies of Māra, attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
All such inconceivable marks of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Ganges-sands of practices and vows were simultaneously manifested within this great golden light.
Furthermore, within this light, there appeared the inconceivable eight great precious stupas of the Tathāgata:
the precious stupa of his birth at the palace of King Śuddhodana in the kingdom of Kauśala;
and the precious stupa of his attainment of Buddhahood beneath the Bodhi tree near the city of Gayā in the kingdom of Magadha; [and so forth].
The precious stupa of the initial turning of the Wheel of Dharma to deliver sentient beings at the Deer Park in Vārāṇasī;
the precious stupa of the fame of attaining all-knowledge after debating with various non-Buddhists for six months at the Jetavana Grove in Śrāvastī;

and the miraculous precious stupa that appeared when descending from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Jambudvīpa via three jeweled stairways, having ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to preach the Dharma for his mother near the city of Kuśinagara in the land of Andhra, accompanied by a multitude of one hundred and twenty thousand, including the Brahma King and Śakra Devendra.

The precious stūpa of the Mahāyāna scriptures, such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and the *Ekayānacittabhūmi-sūtra*, at Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain near Rājagṛha in the kingdom of Magadha;
the precious stūpa of the inconceivable manifestation of illness by the elder Vimalakīrti in the Āmrapālī Grove in the kingdom of Vaiśālī;
and the precious stūpa of the parinirvāṇa in the Śāla grove on the banks of the Hiranyavatī River in Kuśinagara.

Thus, these eight stupas represent the transformative manifestations of the Great Sage, the refuge for sentient beings among humans and devas; making offerings and paying them reverence serves as the cause for attaining Buddhahood.
Such sounds and the reflections of the various stupas all manifest within the great radiance as inconceivable events throughout the three periods of time.

Furthermore, the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, as well as the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment of the great Bodhisattvas, their miraculous transformations and rare feats, and the sublime Dharma taught by all the Tathāgatas—all these were like echoes, heard and seen within this great golden radiance.
All sentient beings who encounter this light and behold those auspicious signs will all resolve to attain the peerless, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the great assembly, beholding the inconceivable spiritual power of the Buddha, marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and said to one another:

"Today the Tathāgata has entered into samādhi and emitted a great radiance that illuminates the worlds of the ten directions. We are thus able to see all the inconceivable deeds of the Tathāgata in the past—how he tamed sentient beings with wrong views in this degenerate age, causing them to give rise to right understanding and incline toward Bodhi."
How rare is the Tathāgata!

You are the father of all the world, difficult to encounter even in immeasurable kalpas. Having cultivated various practices and vows over successive eons, we have now met the Great Teacher of gods and humans within the triple world.
"May the Compassionate Honored One, out of pity for the world, arise from meditative concentration and preach the profound Dharma to instruct, benefit, and gladden all sentient beings.
Having spoken these words, they gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance and remained silent.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Siṃhanāda—having cultivated merit and wisdom for three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, destined to succeed to the rank of a Buddha within the Bhadrakalpa, and having received the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) to become a Great Dharma King—who surveyed the vast ocean-like assembly in the four directions and, raising a great voice, spoke these words:

“In the past, throughout immeasurable kalpas, I have already resolved my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and have served all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. In the foremost assemblies at the sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), I have witnessed inconceivable supernatural transformations; yet I have never before beheld such golden radiance, which manifests the practices and vows of all bodhisattvas, displays the various marks and signs of the Tathāgata, and causes one to see the inconceivable matters of the three periods of time.”

I only pray that you, O Benevolent One, will with single-minded devotion join your palms and gaze upon the Honored Countenance; arise from samādhi, bestow the medicine of nectar to eliminate the disease of feverish affliction, and cause us to realize the Dharma-body of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
These Tathāgatas possess two dharmas by which they do not remain long within samādhi:
first, great loving-kindness (maitrī), and second, great compassion (karuṇā).

Relying on great loving-kindness, they bestow happiness upon sentient beings; relying on great compassion, they extract the suffering of sentient beings. By means of these two dharmas, they have cultivated their minds throughout incalculable eons and attained perfect enlightenment.

The sentient beings of the world endure manifold sufferings and afflictions; for this reason, the Tathāgata will soon arise from samādhi and shall expound for them the sublime Dharma of the Mahāyāna, the gateway to the contemplation of the mind-ground.
He addressed the great assembly:
"Do not seek the blessings and pleasures of all humans and devas; rather, quickly seek the supramundane *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

Why is this? Today the World-Honored One has emitted golden light from his breast; wherever it shines, everything becomes like gold. The intent revealed by the Buddha is profoundly deep, such that all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas in the world, though they exhaust their thoughts and measurements, cannot know it.
You ordinary beings do not observe your own minds; therefore, you drift in the ocean of birth and death.
Because the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are able to observe the mind, they cross the ocean of birth and death and reach the other shore.
“The Dharma of all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time is exactly like this; the emission of this radiance is not without cause or condition.
When the entire assembly heard these words of the Great Being, their hearts leaped with joy at such an unprecedented experience.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Siṃhanāda, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"I pay homage to the Great Awakened Honored One of gods and men, Whose merit and wisdom are as complete as the sands of the Ganges;
Whose golden light and hundredfold auspicious marks adorn his form, Arousing in sentient beings hearts of love and joy."
Surpassing the three realms, you alone are the Honored One; Your merit is most supreme, without peer.
Universally employing the sovereign power of supernormal faculties, You manifest before each according to their own karma.
With my divine eye I survey the world, And find no one at all who equals the Buddha;
Your rare golden countenance is like the full moon, Rarer even than the udumbara flower.
Boundless merit and wisdom benefit all living beings; Great radiance shines everywhere like a thousand suns.
The ignorant masses suffer through the long night, But once touched by this light, it is entirely dispelled.

I observe the Tathāgata’s past conduct: having approached and made offerings to countless Buddhas throughout immeasurable kalpas of asaṃkhyeya, he strove for bodhi for the sake of all sentient beings.
Ever within the bitter sea of birth and death, you act as a great captain to ferry across all beings;
you proclaim the nectar-like, true, and pure Dharma, causing them to enter the gate of unconditioned liberation.

For three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, you delivered sentient beings; Diligently cultivating the eighty thousand *pāramitās*, With causes perfected and fruits fulfilled, you attained Perfect Enlightenment; Your lifespan remains steadfast and unchanging, free from coming or going.
Each and every mark and excellence pervades the Dharma-realm; The marks of all Buddhas of the ten directions are likewise so.
This profound realm is difficult to conceive; No humans or devas can fathom it.
The essence and function of all Buddhas are without distinction, Like a thousand lamps illuminating one another to increase their brilliance;
Their wisdom is like space, without limit, Appearing in forms according to objects, like the moon reflected in water.
The boundless realm of phenomena is eternally tranquil; Suchness is unmoving, equal to empty space.
The Tathāgata’s pure and wondrous Dharma-body Naturally possesses virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Pervading the entire Dharma-realm without end, Neither born nor extinguished, without coming or going, The Dharma King eternally dwells in the palace of the wondrous Dharma; The radiance of his Dharma-body shines everywhere.
The Tathāgata’s dharma-nature is without obstruction; In accordance with conditions, he universally responds to benefit all beings.
Each sentient being perceives him before them, Proclaiming for their sake the nectar-like Dharma.
Following the mind, one can extinguish all afflictions; The manifold sufferings of humans and devas are all removed.
The Dharma King who shatters existence is most extraordinary; His radiance shines forth like a mountain of gold.
Appearing in the world to deliver sentient beings, you are able to light the torch of Dharma to shatter the darkness;
sentient beings are submerged in the ocean of birth and death, cycling through the five destinies with no time of escape.
The Sugata is ever the wondrous vessel of Dharma, Able to cut through the flow of craving and transcend to the other shore;
His great wisdom and skillful means are immeasurable, Constantly bestowing inexhaustible bliss upon all sentient beings.
He is the Great Compassionate Father of the world, Pitifully regarding all sentient beings;
The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is extremely rare, Manifesting but once in countless billions of kalpas.
Just as the wondrous and auspicious udumbara flower, Is rare for all humans and devas,
appearing but once in immeasurable eons, So too is it when one beholds the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
These sentient beings lack merit and wisdom; They dwell forever in the sunken and swirling sea of birth and death.
For billions of kalpas they do not see the Tathāgatas, And following their various evil karmas, they constantly suffer.
For countless hundreds of thousands of kalpas, we have cultivated the four immeasurables and the three doors of liberation;
now that we behold the Great Sage, the Honored Muni, it is as if a blind turtle has encountered a floating log.
May I, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in future lives, never abandon the Teacher of Gods and Humans in every thought-moment;
may I follow him like a shadow follows a form without even a moment’s separation, diligently cultivating the knowledge of all modes day and night.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will have compassion for me, Always allowing me to behold the Greatly Compassionate Honored One;
With my three karmas free from weariness, may I constantly uphold [the teachings], And together with all sentient beings, may we realize perfect enlightenment.
Now the Great Guide of the Three Realms, Sits cross-legged upon his seat, entering samādhi;
Abiding alone in the stillness of the empty and silent chamber, Body and mind unmoving like Mount Sumeru.
None among all the Brahmās and Māras in the world can disturb the Tathāgata’s meditative concentration;
all beings—ordinary or noble—in this realm and other directions know that the Tamer dwells in dhyāna.
Extensively arranging boundless and subtle offerings, they were presented to the Most Victorious Virtue, the Able One;
the devas of the six desire realms came to make offerings, as celestial flowers fell in profusion throughout the void.
The retribution for the ten wholesome actions is priceless incense;

it transforms into clouds of fragrance in a hundred jewel-colored hues, completely covering the immeasurable multitudes of humans and devas, raining down various wondrous jewels as offerings to the Tathāgata.
Fragrant incense billows before the Triple Gem;
hundreds of thousands of musical instruments hover in the realm of space, playing exquisite melodies without being struck, making offerings to the Honored One among Men, the Two-Legged Sovereign.
The eighteen Brahmā assemblies rained down celestial flowers, And rained down myriad kinds of diverse jewels;
Brahmā-maṇi pearls and exquisite necklaces, With various precious ornaments and sublime celestial robes.
Great jewel-flower banners with suspended victory-flags were held as offerings to the Honored Muni;
the gods of the Formless Realm rained down precious flowers, each as vast and wide as a chariot wheel.
A fine rain of subtle fragrance fills the world, An inconceivable offering for this samādhi;
Dragon kings, asuras, humans, and non-humans Present rare and wondrous jewels in response to its inspiration.
Each made offerings to the God among Gods, desiring to hear the most supreme path to enlightenment;
at that time, the Bhagavat, the Great King of Physicians, skillfully heals the suffering of afflictions in the world.
By the power of the Lion’s Stretch Samādhi, the six kinds of earth tremors pervade the three thousandfold world system;
by this, those with karmic affinity are awakened, while those without such affinity remain entirely unaware.
According to the needs of those humans and devas who were ready for deliverance, they beheld the Buddha’s various supernormal powers;
gazing up at the moon-like face of the Honored Muni, they gathered like clouds, having purified their three karmic actions.
The Tathāgata, through his unconditioned compassion, Benefits all sentient beings and brings them to supreme virtue;
From his breast he emits this great radiance, Named "Non-retrogression of All Bodhisattvas."
Just as when the kalpa comes to an end and the seven suns appear, blazing and radiating a thousand rays of light,
all the lights existing in the world cannot equal the light from a single pore of a Buddha.
Immeasurable and unimpeded divine radiance Shines everywhere throughout the Buddha-fields of the ten directions;
The Tathāgata’s merit and wisdom are both perfected, And the divine light he emits is likewise peerless.
That light is brilliant and radiant like the color of gold, Pervasively illuminating all lands throughout the ten directions;
Within the manifestation of the Great Sage’s golden light, All the various forms and images of the world are clearly seen.
In all the worlds of the three thousandfold great chiliocosm, All the kings of mountains that exist—
The wondrous Mount Sumeru composed of the four jewels, The Snowy Mountains, the Fragrant Mountains, and the seven golden mountains,
Mount Mucilinda, Mount Meru, The Great Iron Ring Mountains, the Lesser Mountains, and so forth—
The great oceans, rivers, and bathing pools; The countless billions of four-continent worlds;
The suns, moons, stars, and palaces of various jewels; The palaces of devas, nagas, and all the spirits;
The kingdoms, cities, royal palaces, and all the villages— All these are clearly manifested within this light.
Furthermore, he manifests the Tathāgata’s past causes: how he accumulated merit and virtue seeking the Buddha-way.
In the past, when the Tathāgata was in the kingdom of Śibi, he once occupied a position of honor as a king of men.
The realm of the kingdom is filled with rare treasures; He constantly transforms the world through the True Dharma.
With compassion, joy, and equanimity, he is ever tireless; Able to relinquish what is difficult to relinquish, he proceeds toward Bodhi.
He cut his own flesh to save a dove, never once feeling regret; with a profound heart of compassion, he sought to rescue all sentient beings.
Long ago, when the Buddha was still an ordinary man, he entered the Snowy Mountains to seek the Way of the Buddha.
Gathering the mind with courageous and diligent effort, he sacrificed his entire body to seek even half a verse;
because of this cause and condition for seeking the True Dharma, he transcended the suffering of birth and death for twelve kalpas.
In the past, when he was the sage Māṇava, he offered his hair as an act of devotion to Dīpaṃkara Buddha;
by virtue of the causal conditions of such diligence, he transcended the ocean of birth and death for eight kalpas.
In the past, when he was Prince Sattva, he cast his beloved body to a starving tigress;
through the causes and conditions of benefiting both himself and others, he transcended the causes of birth and death for eleven kalpas.
The Elder Śrotodāra, a great king of physicians, Equally rescued and protected all sentient beings;
Having delivered the fish so they each attained rebirth in the heavens, The gods rained down necklaces to repay his kindness.
Standing on one foot for seven days, he praised the Tathāgata; through such diligence, he transcended nine kalpas.
Formerly, as a king of six-tusked white elephants, his tusks were exquisite and beyond compare;
sacrificing his own body and life to a hunter, he sought the unsurpassed Great Bodhi of the Buddha.
Sometimes he was the King of Perfect Merit and Wisdom, Who gave his eyes and sought the Buddha-way with diligence;
Again, he was the Great Deer King of Golden Hue, Who sacrificed his body and sought the Buddha-way with diligence.
As King Maitrībala of the kingdom of Kāśī, he gave his entire body to five yakṣas;
again, as King Alaṃkāra of a great nation, he gave away his wife and children without any stinginess.
Some become Bodhisattvas of the supreme body, giving their heads, eyes, marrow, and brains to sentient beings;
such Bodhisattvas practice compassion, all vowing to seek realization of the path to Bodhi.
In the past, the Buddha was once a Wheel-Turning King;
The four continents were filled with rare treasures, He possessed a thousand sons and a vast retinue, And for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, he transformed people through the ten wholesome paths.
The land is peaceful and secure like a celestial palace, where the enjoyment of the five desires is inexhaustible;
yet at that time, the Wheel-Turning King realizes that both himself and the world are not solid or enduring.
The gods of the Heaven of No-Thought live for eighty thousand years; when their merit is exhausted, they return once more to the various evil realms.
They are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows, and are also like morning dew or flashes of lightning.
Fully realizing that the three realms are like a burning house, filled with the eight sufferings and difficult to escape;
until one has attained liberation and crossed to the other shore, what wise person would delight in saṃsāra?
Only the supramundane body of the Tathāgata is neither born nor extinguished, eternally peaceful and blissful;
such difficult-to-practice bodhisattva deeds are all fully manifested within this golden light.
Furthermore, within this light appear eight stupas, all of which are excellent fields of merit for sentient beings:
the stupa of the birthplace in King Śuddhodana’s palace, the stupa of attaining Buddhahood beneath the Bodhi tree,
the stupa of turning the Wheel of Dharma in the Deer Park, and the stupa of renowned fame in the Jetavana Grove.
The Jewel Staircase Stūpa by the city of Kanyākubja; The Prajñāpāramitā Stūpa on Vulture Peak Mountain;
The Vimalakīrti Stūpa in the Āmrapālī Grove; And the Parinirvāṇa Stūpa within the Śāla Forest.
Thus, this World-Honored One’s stupa of the eight treasures is constantly venerated by devas, nāgas, and spirits;
Vajrapāṇi, Guhyapada, and the Four Heavenly Kings protect and uphold it day and night, never departing.
If one constructs eight stupas and makes offerings to them, In this very life, merit and longevity will naturally extend;
Wisdom will increase and one will be honored by all, With all mundane and supramundane aspirations fully fulfilled.
If a person prostrates and pays homage with the mind to these eight inconceivable stupas,
both individuals will obtain equal merit without distinction, and swiftly realize the path of unsurpassed bodhi.
Thus, all deeds of benefit throughout the three periods of time are seen within this light;
the bodhisattvas of the Buddha-lands in the ten directions, the various rishis who sport with supernatural powers,
and the wheel-turning kings of billions of lands— all seek out this radiance and gather like a vast cloud.
Each, by means of their supernormal powers, came to make offerings, raining down wish-fulfilling jewels to honor the Compassionate Honored One.
Hundreds of thousands of kinds of celestial music, without being struck, spontaneously produced wondrous sounds;
celestial flowers fell in profusion, filling the void, while various fragrances universally perfumed the great assembly.
With countless jeweled banners and various necklaces, They offer them to the Honored One among Men.
With subtle and wondrous verses they praise the Tathāgata: "Excellent!
You are able to enter samādhi, Manifesting inconceivable and great supernormal powers, To subdue all sentient beings who are difficult to transform."
May they abide in a firm and non-retrogressive mind; I deeply rejoice in this before the Buddha.

I only pray that the World-Honored One will arise from samādhi and turn the wheel of Dharma for all sentient beings, forever severing all afflictions and causing them to abide in the great nirvāṇa of non-abiding.
With minds as pure as ours, we have come from ten billion lands to hear the Dharma;
through the power of samādhi, we constantly observe with clarity—out of compassion, please accept our humble offering.
The giver, the recipient, and the gift— In the three periods of time, none of these are apprehended.
Abiding in this most supreme mind, We make offerings to all Buddhas of the ten directions.
In life after life, may I draw near to the Lord of Great Compassion, And constantly serve the Honored One of Great Benevolence;
By means of these wondrous roots of goodness born of non-attainment, May I realize the perfect fusion with the Dharma-realm and proceed toward true awakening.
The Tathāgatas of the past entered into tranquil meditative concentration, Manifesting great supernormal powers and turning the wheel of Dharma;
Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is likewise so, Entering concentration and emitting light just as those Buddhas did.
Therefore, I reflect that the Lion of the Śākyas intends to definitively expound the gateway of the mind-ground;
if one wishes to distance oneself from the causes of birth and death, one will surely attain the fruit of the true and eternal throughout the three periods of time.
"All you people, with palms joined and single-minded, wait; He shall now enter the Tathāgata’s palace of peace and bliss.
*The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground in the Jātaka Tales*, Fascicle One.
*The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground in the Jātaka Tales*, Fascicle Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā of Kapiśa during the Great Tang Dynasty, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Two: Repaying Kindness (Part One of Two).
At that time, the World-Honored One arose calmly from samādhi and addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
You great beings,
you sons of good family!”

Desiring to draw near to the Father of the World, desiring to hear the supramundane Dharma, desiring to contemplate the principle of suchness, and desiring to cultivate the wisdom of suchness, they have come to the Buddha’s presence to make offerings and pay him homage.
I now expound this wondrous Dharma of the Mind-ground to guide sentient beings and lead them into the Buddha-wisdom.
Such a wondrous Dharma is spoken by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, only after the passing of immeasurable kalpas.

The appearance of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, in the world is extremely rare to encounter, like the udumbara flower; even if a Tathāgata should appear in the world, it is likewise difficult for him to preach this sublime Dharma.

Why is this? Because all sentient beings have distanced themselves from the bodhisattva practices and vows of the Mahāyāna, turning instead toward the enlightenment of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; they weary of and seek to escape saṃsāra, entering permanently into nirvāṇa, and take no delight in the Mahāyāna’s fruit of eternal bliss and wondrous excellence.
However, when the Tathāgatas turn the wheel of Dharma, they do so by remaining free from four errors, teaching the Dharma in accordance with reality:
first, there is no inappropriate place; second, there is no inappropriate time; third, there is no inappropriate recipient; and fourth, there is no incorrect teaching.

Administering medicine according to the illness to bring about recovery is the unique virtue of the Tathāgata; it is a state not yet attained by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, and it is a realm not shared with the assembly of Bodhisattvas. For these reasons, the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground, which is the right path to Bodhi, is difficult to see and difficult to hear.

If there are good sons or good daughters who hear this sublime Dharma but once with their ears, and for even a brief moment collect their thoughts and contemplate the mind, they will perfume themselves with the seed of unsurpassed, great Bodhi; before long, they shall sit upon the Vajra-jewel throne under the Bodhi tree and attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, in the great city of Rājagṛha, there were five hundred elders, whose names were:

the elder Sudhana, the elder Śūra, the elder Dharmika, the elder Buddhanusmṛti, the elder Sumati, the elder Bodhi, the elder Subhāṣita, the elder Dharmacakṣu, the elder Prabhāsa, and the elder Pūrṇamanoratha.
These great wealthy householders had attained right view and made offerings to the Tathāgata and the assembly of noble ones.
When these householders heard the World-Honored One praise this Dharma-gate of the Mahāyāna Mind-Ground, they thought to themselves:

"I see the Tathāgata emitting golden light that manifests the difficult and painful practices of the bodhisattvas. I have no desire for the mind that practices such austerities; who could dwell in birth and death for eternal kalpas to undergo all manner of suffering and affliction for the sake of sentient beings?"

Having formed this thought, he immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, spoke to the Buddha in a single voice:
"World-Honored One!
We do not delight in the practices of the Mahāyāna bodhisattvas, nor do we rejoice in hearing the sound of their ascetic labors. Why is this?
Because all the vows and practices cultivated by bodhisattvas are entirely devoid of gratitude and the repayment of kindness.

Why is this? Having distanced themselves from their parents to enter the homeless life, they gave away their own wives and children to those who desired them; they bestowed their heads, eyes, marrow, and brains according to whatever was requested, enduring all manner of afflictions through giving. Throughout three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they fully cultivated the various perfections and the eighty-four thousand practices of the *pāramitās*, thereby crossing the stream of birth and death to finally reach the state of great peace and bliss that is *bodhi*.

It is better to advance toward the fruits of the paths of the Two Vehicles, accumulating the necessary provisions for three lifetimes or a hundred kalpas, severing the causes of birth and death to realize the fruit of nirvana, and swiftly attaining peace and happiness; only then can it be called repaying kindness.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the five hundred elders:
"Excellent, excellent!

Having heard this praise of the Mahāyāna, you have given rise to a mind of renunciation and have initiated this sublime teaching to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings in future ages who are unaware of the debt of gratitude they owe."
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well. I shall now, for your sake, analyze and explain the places where there is gratitude, both mundane and supramundane.
Noble son!
What you have said is not in accord with correct principle. Why is this?
There are four kinds of worldly and world-transcending kindness:
First is the debt of gratitude to one's parents; second, the debt of gratitude to sentient beings; third, the debt of gratitude to kings; and fourth, the debt of gratitude to the Triple Gem.
These four debts of gratitude are to be borne equally by all sentient beings.
"Good son! Regarding the kindness of parents, the father possesses the kindness of compassion, while the mother possesses the kindness of pity.
As for the mother's kindness of pity, even if I were to remain in the world for an entire kalpa, I could not exhaustively describe it; I shall now proclaim a small portion of it for you."

Suppose there were someone who, for the sake of merit, reverently made offerings to one hundred pure-practicing great Brahmins, one hundred great immortals possessing the five supernatural powers, and one hundred virtuous friends; placing them within a magnificent hall adorned with the seven treasures, providing them with hundreds of thousands of kinds of exquisite delicacies, hanging jeweled necklaces and various precious garments, furnishing dwellings with *candana* and aloeswood incense, providing beds and bedding embellished with a hundred jewels, and supplying a hundred kinds of medicinal decoctions to treat their various ailments—serving them with single-minded devotion for a full hundred thousand kalpas.

This would not equal the merit of a single thought of filial piety, using even a small amount of material goods to nourish and care for one’s compassionate mother; compared to the former merit, it cannot be measured by even a hundred-thousand-millionth part.

"The compassionate mother of the world has no peer in her thoughts for her child; her kindness extends even to that which is not yet formed. From the moment of conception until the end of the tenth month, she undergoes various sufferings in walking, standing, sitting, and reclining that cannot be fully described by words. Though she obtains sensual pleasures, food, drink, and clothing, she feels no attachment to them. Her mind of anxious concern never rests, as she thinks only of the impending birth. As the time of delivery approaches, she gradually undergoes all manner of suffering, with grief and distress day and night.
When the birth is difficult, it is as if hundreds of thousands of blades come together to butcher and carve her, perhaps even leading to her death."
If there is no suffering or affliction, one's kinsmen and relatives will experience inexhaustible joy.

It is like a poor woman who obtains a wish-fulfilling jewel; her child’s cries are like the hearing of music, he uses his mother’s breast as a place for sleep and rest, and he constantly walks upon her left and right knees. From within her breast flows a spring of nectar, and the kindness of her nurturing extends beyond the heavens, while the virtue of her compassion is vast and peerless.
Among all that is lofty in the world, nothing surpasses the mountain peaks; yet the grace of a compassionate mother exceeds Mount Sumeru.
Among all that is weighty in the world, the great earth comes first; yet the grace of a compassionate mother likewise surpasses it.

"If there are sons or daughters who turn their backs on kindness and are disobedient, causing their parents to give rise to thoughts of resentment, and if the mother utters evil words, the child will immediately fall accordingly—either into hell, as a hungry ghost, or as an animal."
Among the maladies of the world, none surpasses the violent wind; yet the signs of resentment are even swifter than that.
Neither all the Tathāgatas, Vajras, and devas, nor the ṛṣis possessing the five supernatural powers, can provide protection.

If a son or daughter of good family, relying on the instructions of their compassionate mother, follows them with obedience and without contravention, they shall be protected by the devas and enjoy inexhaustible merit and happiness.

Such sons and daughters are called of the noble lineage of devas and humans; or perhaps they are bodhisattvas who, in order to deliver sentient beings, manifest as sons or daughters to benefit their parents.

"If a good man or a good woman, in order to repay their mother's kindness, were to spend an entire kalpa daily cutting flesh from their own bodies three times a day to nourish their parents, they would still not have repaid even one day's debt of gratitude."

Why is this so? All sons and daughters, while dwelling within the womb, suckle at the breast and drink their mother’s blood; and from the time they emerge from the womb until they reach childhood, they consume one hundred and eighty *hu* of their mother’s milk. When the mother obtains superior flavors, she first gives them to her child; with regard to precious and exquisite clothing, it is likewise so. Though the child may be foolish or base, the mother’s affection remains no different.

In the past, there was a woman who traveled far to another country; while carrying her newborn son, she attempted to cross the Ganges River, but as the waters surged violently, she could not advance. Out of love and unable to let him go, both mother and son drowned together.
By the power of these roots of goodness from his mind of loving-kindness, he immediately attained rebirth in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven as a Great Brahmā King.
For this reason, the mother possesses ten virtues:
first, she is named "Great Earth," because within her womb he takes it as his support.
The second is named "Able to Give Birth," because she is able to give birth after undergoing manifold sufferings.
The third is named "Able to Correctly [Tend]," because she constantly uses her own hands to attend to the five sense organs.
The fourth is named "Nurturer," because she is able to foster growth in accordance with the requirements of the four seasons.
The fifth is named "Wisdom," because it is able to give rise to wisdom through skillful means.
The sixth is named "Adornment," because it is beautifully decorated with exquisite necklaces.
The seventh is named "Peace and Security," because it provides rest within the mother’s embrace.
Eighth is called "instruction," because through skillful means one guides the child.
Ninth is called "admonition," because by means of excellent speech one causes them to abandon all evils.
Tenth is called "entrusting with affairs," because one is able to hand over the family business to the child.
“Good son! Among all those in the world, who is the wealthiest?
Who is the poorest?”
When the compassionate mother is present in the hall, it is called wealth; when the compassionate mother is not there, it is called poverty.
When the compassionate mother is present, it is called midday; when the compassionate mother dies, it is called sunset.
When the compassionate mother is present, it is called a bright moonlit night; when the compassionate mother passes away, it is called a dark night.
Therefore, you all should diligently cultivate the practice of filial piety and support for your parents; the merit of one who makes offerings to the Buddha is no different from this.
You should repay the kindness of your parents in this manner.

“Good son! As for the debt of gratitude owed to sentient beings, since beginningless time, all sentient beings have transmigrated through the five realms for hundreds of thousands of kalpas; throughout many lifetimes, they have alternately served as one another’s fathers and mothers.

Because they have alternately been one another’s parents, every man is a compassionate father and every woman is a merciful mother. Since there was great kindness toward them in life after life, it is no different from the kindness of one’s present parents.”

Thus, even though past kindnesses have not yet been repaid, one may encounter various conditions of adversity or favor due to deluded karma; because of such attachment, one instead becomes their enemy. Why is this?

Ignorance obscures the clear knowledge of past lives, such that one does not realize that in previous births they were one's own parents; thus, failing to repay their kindness by mutually benefiting one another—and failing to provide such benefit—is called filial impiety.
For these reasons,
all classes of sentient beings also possess great kindness toward us at all times, and this is truly difficult to repay.
Such matters are called the "kindness of sentient beings."

"The king’s grace is the most supreme in merit; for although he is born among humans, he attains sovereignty, and because the sons of the gods in the Heaven of the Thirty-three constantly bestow their power upon him and perpetually protect him, the mountains, rivers, earth, and everything within his realm as far as the great ocean belong to the king. This is because the merit of a single person surpasses the merit of all sentient beings."
This Great Sage-King transforms through the True Dharma and is able to bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
Just as in the world, pillars are the foundation of all halls and palaces;
so too, the King is the foundation for the abundance and joy of the people, for they exist in dependence upon him.
Furthermore, just as the Brahma King can give birth to all things, so too can the Sage King give birth to the laws for governing the state to benefit sentient beings.
Just as the Sun Deity is able to illuminate the world, so too can the Sage King observe the people of the world to ensure their peace and happiness.
When a king loses the way of righteous governance, the people have no refuge.

If he governs with righteousness, the eight great terrors will not enter his kingdom; namely: invasion and oppression by foreign states, rebellion within one's own realm, afflictions from evil spirits and diseases, famine within the land, unseasonable winds and rains, excessive winds and rains, eclipses of the sun and moon, and the portents of anomalous stars.
When a king of men governs with righteousness for the benefit of his people, the eight difficulties cannot invade them.

It is like an elder who has but one son; his love and care are incomparable, and out of compassion he seeks to benefit him, constantly bestowing peace and happiness upon him without ceasing day or night.
The great sage-king of the land is likewise thus: he treats all living beings equally as if they were his only son, and his heart of protection never ceases day or night.
Such a king of men who causes others to cultivate the ten wholesome actions is called a Lord of Merit;
if he does not cause them to cultivate them, he is called a Lord of Non-Merit.

Why is this so? If a single person within the kingdom cultivates goodness, the merit they produce is divided into seven parts: the person who performed the good deed receives five parts, while the king of that country constantly obtains two parts. This is because the king’s cultivation serves as a cause for the good, and thus the benefit and merit are shared;
the same applies to the commission of the ten unwholesome deeds, as the matter is shared in common.
All things produced within the kingdom’s fields, gardens, and groves shall likewise be divided into seven portions.
If there is a king who achieves right view and transforms the world according to the Dharma, he is called a Lord of Heaven.
Because he transforms the world through celestial wholesome dharmas, the various celestial deities and the World-Protecting Kings constantly come to provide protection and guard the royal palace.
Although he dwells among humans, he practices the deeds of the heavens; his mind regarding rewards and punishments is free from partiality.
The laws of all noble kings are thus; such a sovereign lord is called a King of Righteous Dharma (*saddharmarāja*).
By these causes and conditions, he accomplishes ten virtues:
first, he is "able to illuminate," because he illuminates the world with the eye of wisdom.
The second is named Adornment, because it adorns the kingdom with great merit and wisdom.
The third is named Bestowing Joy, because it bestows great peace and happiness upon the people.
The fourth is named Subduing Enemies, because all hostile adversaries are naturally subdued.
The fifth is named "Free from Fear," because it can ward off the eight difficulties and eliminate all terror.
The sixth is named "Entrusting to the Worthy," because it assembles various sages to deliberate on the affairs of the state.
The seventh is named "Root of Dharma," because the myriad subjects dwell in peace by relying upon the king.
Eighth is named Upholder of the World (*Lokadhara*), because he upholds the world through the dharma of the celestial kings.
Ninth is named Master of Karma (*Karmapati*), because all wholesome and unwholesome karmas belong to the king.
Tenth is named Lord of Men (*Puruṣapati*), because the king is the sovereign over all the people.
All kings, by virtue of the merit accumulated in previous lives, achieve these ten kinds of supreme virtues.

Mahābrahmā and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven constantly assist the king of men in experiencing supreme and wondrous bliss; and although the rākṣasa kings and various deities do not manifest their forms, they secretly come to protect the king and his retinue.
When the King sees that the people commit various unwholesome deeds and he is unable to restrain them, all the devas and other celestial beings distance themselves from him.
However, if they see him practicing virtue, they rejoice and praise him, all exclaiming:
"This is our Holy King!"
The dragons and devas will rejoice and pour down rain of ambrosia, causing the five grains to ripen and the people to enjoy abundance and happiness.

If one does not associate with evil persons, universally benefiting the world so that all follow the transformation of the Right Dharma, the wish-fulfilling jewel will surely appear in the king’s realm; neighboring kingdoms will all come to submit and serve, and both humans and non-humans will offer praise without exception.

"If there is an evil person within the king's realm who gives rise to a rebellious mind for even a moment, such a person's merit will naturally decline and perish; at the end of their life, they shall fall into hell and pass through the animal realm, undergoing all manner of suffering."
Why is this so? It is because the noble king failed to recognize kindness and gave rise to various acts of malice and rebellion, thereby receiving such retribution.

If there are people who can cultivate a virtuous mind, respectfully assisting and honoring the benevolent king as they would the Buddha, those people will enjoy peace, security, abundance, and joy in their present lives; whatever they seek or desire shall be fulfilled according to their wishes.
Why is this so? Because in the past, all kings received the pure precepts of the Tathāgata and have always served as peaceful and happy rulers for their people.
By these causes and conditions, the retributions for both opposition and compliance are like echoes responding to sounds.
The benevolence and virtue of the Sage King are as vast as this.
"Good son!..."

The grace of the Three Jewels is called inconceivable benefit and happiness for sentient beings without cessation. This body of the Buddhas is truly wholesome and untainted, realized through causes cultivated over countless great eons; the karmic fruits of the three realms of existence are forever exhausted without remainder, and this mountain of jewel-like merit is towering and peerless, such that all sentient beings cannot know it.

His merit is profoundly deep like the great ocean; his wisdom is unimpeded and equal to space; his supernormal powers and transformations fill the world; and his radiance shines universally throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Yet all sentient beings remain entirely unaware of their own afflictions and karmic obstructions.

Sunk in the ocean of suffering, birth and death are without end; the Triple Gem appears in the world as a great captain, able to cut through the stream of craving and transcend to the other shore, so that all who possess wisdom gaze up in reverence.
“Sons of good family!
The single Jewel of the Buddha possesses three bodies:
first, the svabhāvakāya (body of intrinsic nature); second, the sambhogakāya (enjoyment body); and third, the nirmāṇakāya (emanation body).”
The first Buddha-body possesses the virtue of great severance, manifested through the two kinds of emptiness; all Buddhas are entirely equal in this regard.
The second Buddha-body possesses the virtue of great wisdom, which is true, eternal, and untainted; all Buddhas are entirely of one mind in this regard.
The third Buddha-body possesses great merit and virtue; through its meditative concentration, supernormal powers, and transformations, all Buddhas perform their activities in concert. "Good son!

Its self-nature body (svabhāvakāya) is without beginning and without end, free from all marks, transcending all conceptual proliferation (prapañca), all-pervasive and boundless, eternally abiding in unchanging stillness."
The Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) has two aspects: first, the self-enjoyment body; second, the other-enjoyment body. Regarding the self-enjoyment body:
