having cultivated the myriad practices for three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings, and having reached the fulfillment of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), one proceeds directly to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven. Transcending the triple world, one sits upon a vast, immeasurable great jewel lotus in a pure and wondrous land, surrounded before and behind by an unspeakably vast ocean-like assembly of bodhisattvas. With stainless silk ribbons bound upon their heads, these bodhisattvas offer worship, respect, reverence, and praise. This is called the benefit of the subsequent retribution.

At that time, the Bodhisattva entered the Vajra-samādhi, severed all subtle cognitive afflictive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), and realized *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; such a wondrous fruit is called the benefit of present retribution.

This is the true Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya), which has a beginning but no end; its lifespan and number of kalpas are without limit. From the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment until the furthest reaches of the future, its faculties and marks of excellence pervade the entire Dharma-realm, and its four wisdoms are fully perfected.
This is the true retributive body that experiences the enjoyment of the Dharma.

First is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*): by transforming the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), one attains this wisdom, which is like a great perfect mirror manifesting all forms and images.

In this way, within the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) of the Tathāgata, the various wholesome and unwholesome karmas of sentient beings can be manifested; for this reason, this wisdom is called the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*mahā-ādarśa-jñāna*).

Relying on great compassion, it constantly takes sentient beings as its object; relying on great wisdom, it is always in accordance with the dharma-nature. It simultaneously contemplates the ultimate and conventional truths without interruption, and is constantly able to sustain the untainted faculties and body, serving as the basis for all meritorious qualities.

2. The Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*): By transforming the consciousness of self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi-vijñāna*), one attains this wisdom. Because it is able to realize the two kinds of selflessness—the equality of self and other—it is called the Wisdom of Equality.

Third, the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*): by transforming the discriminating consciousness (*vikalpa-vijñāna*), one attains this wisdom. It is able to observe the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena and to preach various sublime teachings before assemblies, enabling sentient beings to attain non-retrogression; for these reasons, it is called the wisdom of wondrous observation.

Fourth, the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*): by transforming the five kinds of consciousness, one attains this wisdom, which can manifest all manner of transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) to bring sentient beings to maturity in their wholesome karma. For these reasons, it is called the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done.

With these four wisdoms as the foremost, they are fully endowed with eighty-four thousand gateways of wisdom; all such meritorious qualities and dharmas are called the Tathāgata’s body of self-enjoyment.
"O sons of good family!

Second is the Tathāgata’s Body of Enjoyment for Others, which is fully endowed with eighty-four thousand marks and signs of excellence. Residing in the truly pure land, it teaches the Dharma of the One Vehicle, causing all bodhisattvas to enjoy the subtle and wondrous Dharma-bliss of the Mahāyāna."
All Tathāgatas, in order to transform the assembly of Bodhisattvas of the ten stages, manifest ten kinds of *parasaṃbhoga-kāyas*.

The first Buddha-body sits upon a hundred-petaled lotus flower and expounds the "Illumination-Gate of the Hundred Dharmas" for the Bodhisattvas of the first stage. Having attained realization, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), manifesting transformations that fill a hundred Buddha-worlds, bringing benefit, peace, and happiness to countless sentient beings.

The second Buddha-body sits upon a thousand-petaled lotus flower and expounds the "Dharma-Gate of the Thousand Illuminations" for the sake of Bodhisattvas of the Second Stage. Having attained realization, these Bodhisattvas give rise to great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), manifesting transformations that fill a thousand Buddha-worlds, thereby bringing benefit, peace, and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings.

The third Buddha-body sits upon a ten-thousand-petaled lotus flower and expounds the "Gate of Illumination of the Ten Thousand Dharmas" for Bodhisattvas of the third stage. Having attained awakening, these Bodhisattvas manifest great supernormal powers, transforming themselves to fill ten thousand Buddha-lands, thereby benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to countless sentient beings.

In this manner, the Tathāgata gradually increases [in stature] until, as the Enjoyment Body for Others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*) at the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), he sits upon an ineffable, wondrous jewel lotus and expounds ineffable gateways to the illumination of all dharmas for the bodhisattvas of the tenth stage. Having realized these, the bodhisattvas give rise to great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and manifest transformations that fill ineffable, subtle Buddha-lands, benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to immeasurable and boundless multitudes of sentient beings whose varieties are beyond description.
Thus, these ten bodies all sat beneath the king of bodhi trees made of the seven treasures and realized anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
O sons of good family!

Each individual flower petal constitutes a separate trichiliocosm, each complete with ten billion Sumeru Kings, the four great continents, the sun, moon, and stars, and all the heavens of the three realms, none lacking anything.

Upon each and every leaf, within all the Jambudvīpas, there is a Vajrāsana and a king of Bodhi trees; beneath each tree, hundreds of thousands of myriads—indeed, unspeakably many—great and small transformation Buddhas, having each defeated the armies of Māra, simultaneously realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

In this way, these various emanated Buddha-bodies, both great and small, each fully endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, preach the wondrous Dharma of the Three Vehicles according to the needs of all bodhisattvas—whether they possess the various provisions or the four roots of goodness—as well as those of the two vehicles and ordinary beings.
For the sake of the bodhisattvas, he teaches the six pāramitās, enabling them to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the ultimate wisdom of a Buddha.
For those seeking the state of a pratyekabuddha, he teaches the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination;
for those seeking the state of a śrāvaka, he teaches the dharma of the four noble truths, leading them across birth, old age, sickness, and death to ultimate nirvāṇa.
For other sentient beings, he teaches the instructions for humans and devas, causing them to attain the wondrous fruits of peace and happiness as humans and devas.
All such emanation buddhas, whether great or small, are collectively termed the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body) of the Buddha.
"Good sons!
Although these two kinds of Transformation and Response Buddhas manifest parinirvāṇa, their Buddha-bodies continue to abide eternally. O good sons!"

Just as with the Jewel of the Buddha, there are such immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable vast merits of benefit and happiness for sentient beings; for these reasons, he is named Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, and World-Honored One.
Good son! Within the single Jewel of the Buddha, six kinds of subtle and wondrous merits are fully present:

first, he is the unsurpassed field of great merit; second, he possesses unsurpassed great benevolence and virtue; third, he is the most honored among beings with no feet, two feet, or many feet; fourth, he is extremely difficult to encounter, like the udumbara flower; fifth, he appears alone within a trichiliocosm; sixth, his mundane and supramundane merits are perfected, and he is the refuge for all purposes.
"Endowed with these six kinds of merit, he is constantly able to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings; this is called the inconceivable grace of the Buddha Jewel.
At that time, five hundred elders addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
As the Buddha has taught, within a single Jewel of the Buddha, immeasurable transformation Buddhas fill the worlds to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings.
For what reason and by what causes do the sentient beings of the world mostly fail to see the Buddha and instead undergo various sufferings and afflictions?
The Buddha told the five hundred elders:
"It is like the celestial son Sūryaprabha, who emits hundreds of thousands of rays of light to illuminate the world, yet there are those who are blind and do not see the radiance."
"O son of good family!
What do you think?
Does the Sun Deity, the Son of Heaven, have any fault?"
Then the householder said:
“No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said, “Good son!

The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, constantly expound the True Dharma to benefit and bring joy to sentient beings; yet these sentient beings constantly create evil karma, remaining entirely unaware of it, lacking a sense of shame or remorse, and taking no pleasure in drawing near to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.”

Thus, these sentient beings have deeply rooted and heavy karmic offenses; for immeasurable kalpas they have been unable to see or hear even the names of the Triple Gem, just as that blind man cannot behold the light of the sun.

If there are sentient beings who revere the Tathāgata, delight in the Mahāyāna, and honor the Triple Gem, you should know that such persons will have their karmic obstructions eliminated, their merit and wisdom increased, and their roots of goodness perfected; they shall swiftly behold the Buddha, forever leave birth and death behind, and realize Bodhi.
“O sons of good family!
Just as there are immeasurable Buddhas within a single Buddha-jewel, so too is the Dharma-jewel taught by the Tathāgata; within a single Dharma-jewel, there are immeasurable meanings.”
Good son! Within the Dharma Jewel there are four kinds:
first, the Dharma of teaching; second, the Dharma of principle; third, the Dharma of practice; and fourth, the Dharma of fruition.
All untainted [dharmas] that can destroy ignorance, afflictions, and karmic obstructions—namely sounds, names, phrases, and syllables—are called the Dharma of Teaching;
the existence and non-existence of all phenomena are called the Dharma of Principle;
and the practices of precept, concentration, and wisdom are called the Dharma of Practice.
That which is the fruit of the unconditioned is called the "Dharma-fruit.
These four kinds are termed the Jewel of the Dharma; they guide sentient beings out of the ocean of birth and death to reach the other shore.
Good son! That which all Buddhas take as their teacher is the Jewel of the Dharma. Why is this so?

The Buddhas of the three periods of time practice according to the Dharma, severing all obstacles to attain Bodhi, and benefiting sentient beings until the end of the future; for this reason, the Tathāgatas of the three periods constantly make offerings to the subtle and wondrous Dharma-jewel of the various pāramitās—how much more so should all sentient beings within the triple world, who have not yet attained liberation, revere this subtle and wondrous Dharma-jewel?

"Good son! In the past, for the sake of seeking the Dharma, I entered a great pit of fire as a Dharma-seeking king to seek the True Dharma, thereby forever severing birth and death and attaining Great Bodhi."
Therefore, the Jewel of the Dharma can shatter the prison of all birth and death, just as a vajra can destroy all things;
the Jewel of the Dharma can illuminate sentient beings in the darkness of ignorance, just as the Sun Deity can illuminate the world;
the Jewel of the Dharma can rescue impoverished sentient beings, just as a maṇi jewel rains down various treasures.
The Dharma Jewel can bestow joy and happiness upon sentient beings, just as the celestial drum delights the devas;
the Dharma Jewel serves as a precious staircase for the devas, for by hearing the True Dharma one attains birth in the heavens;
the Dharma Jewel serves as a sturdy great ship, for it carries one across the ocean of birth and death to the other shore.
The Dharma Jewel is like a wheel-turning sage king, for it can eliminate the thieves of the three poisons and afflictions;
the Dharma Jewel can serve as exquisite clothing, covering those sentient beings who lack a sense of shame;
the Dharma Jewel is like adamantine armor, for it can shatter the four māras and realize bodhi.
The Dharma-treasure is like the sharp sword of wisdom, for it severs birth and death and brings liberation from bondage;
the Dharma-treasure is precisely the precious chariot of the Three Vehicles, for it carries sentient beings out of the burning house;
the Dharma-treasure is like all-encompassing bright lamps, for it can illuminate the dark places of the three miserable realms.
The Dharma Jewel is like a bow, arrow, spear, and halberd, for it can pacify the national borders and crush enemies;
the Dharma Jewel is like a guide on a perilous path, for it skillfully leads sentient beings to reach the place of jewels.
Good son! The wondrous Dharma taught by the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time contains such inconceivable matters as these; this is called the inconceivable grace of the Jewel of the Dharma.
“Good son! There are three kinds of Saṃgha in the mundane and supramundane realms:
first, the Bodhisattva Saṃgha; second, the Śrāvaka Saṃgha; and third, the Saṃgha of ordinary beings.”
Mañjuśrī, Maitreya, and others constitute the bodhisattva saṃgha;
Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others constitute the śrāvaka saṃgha;

and those ordinary persons who have accomplished the prātimokṣa precepts, up to those who are fully endowed with all right views and are able to extensively expound and reveal for others the dharmas of the noble path to benefit and bring joy to sentient beings, are called the ordinary-person saṃgha.
Although they have not yet attained the untainted (anāsrava) precepts, meditative concentration, wisdom, and liberation, those who make offerings to them obtain immeasurable merit.
These three types are called the Sangha of the True Field of Merit.

Furthermore, there is another class known as the Field of Merit (puṇyakṣetra) monks. They conceive deep reverence and faith toward the Buddha’s relics, the Buddha’s images, and the various teachings and precepts established by the Noble Ones. Being themselves free from false views, they cause others to be likewise; they can proclaim the True Dharma and praise the One Vehicle. With profound faith in cause and effect, they constantly make virtuous vows and repent for their transgressions to eliminate karmic obstructions.

You should know that the power of this person’s faith in the Triple Gem surpasses that of all non-Buddhists by hundreds of thousands of millions of times, and also surpasses that of the four kinds of wheel-turning sage kings; how much more so does it surpass that of all other classes of sentient beings?
Just as the saffron flower, though withered and faded, still surpasses all other varieties of flowers, so too is a bhikṣu of right view:

he excels all other sentient beings by hundreds of thousands of millions of times. Although he may have violated the prohibitions and precepts, he does not destroy his right view; for this reason, he is called a "field of merit" monk.

If good sons and good daughters and others make offerings to such a field of merit—the Sangha—they shall obtain inexhaustible merit; this is exactly equal and no different from the merit obtained by making offerings to the aforementioned three types of the true Sangha Jewel.

"These four classes of the Sangha Jewel—both noble and ordinary—constantly provide benefit and happiness to sentient beings without ever ceasing for a moment; this is called the inconceivable grace of the Sangha Jewel.
At that time, five hundred elders addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Today we have heard the sound of the Buddha’s Dharma and attained realization, understanding how the Triple Gem benefits the world.
Yet, we do not yet know by what meaning the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are called "gems."

I pray that the Buddha will explain this, manifesting it for the assembled multitude and all sentient beings of future ages who revere and have faith in the Triple Gem, so that they may forever sever the net of doubt, attain indestructible faith, and enter the inconceivable ocean of the Triple Gem.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the elders, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
You, sons of good family!"
You have been able to inquire about the profound and wondrous Dharma of the Tathāgata, which will benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings in future ages.
Just as the world’s foremost precious jewel, endowed with ten qualities, adorns the realm and benefits sentient beings, so too are the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha.

First is steadfastness: just as a mani jewel cannot be destroyed by anyone, so too are the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; for neither non-Buddhists nor celestial Māras can destroy them.

Second is being stainless: just as the supreme jewels of the world are pure, radiant, and untainted by dust or filth, so too are the Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; they are all entirely able to remain far removed from the dust and defilement of afflictions.

Third is the bestowing of happiness: just as the celestial vase (*devakalaśa*) is able to grant peace and joy, so too are the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; they are able to bestow upon sentient beings both worldly and supramundane happiness.

Fourth is the difficulty of encountering them: just as auspicious jewels are rare and difficult to obtain, so too are the Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; for sentient beings obscured by karmic hindrances, they are difficult to encounter even in hundreds of millions of eons.

Fifth is the ability to destroy: just as a wish-fulfilling gem can destroy poverty, so too are the Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; for they can destroy all the poverty and suffering of the world.

Sixth is majestic power (*tejas*): just as the wheel-treasure (*cakraratna*) possessed by a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) can subdue all enemies, so too are the Treasures of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; endowed with the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), they subjugate the four māras.

Seventh is the fulfillment of vows: just as a maṇi jewel can rain down various treasures according to whatever the mind desires, so too are the Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; they can fulfill the virtuous vows cultivated by sentient beings.
Eighth is adornment: just as worldly treasures adorn a royal palace, so too do the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha adorn the Bodhi-jewel palace of the Dharma King.

Ninth is the most exquisite: just as the wondrous jewels of the heavens are the most subtle and refined, so too are the Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; they transcend all worlds as the most supreme and exquisite of jewels.
Tenth is immutability: just as pure gold does not change when placed in fire, so too are the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; they cannot be shaken by the eight winds of the world.

The Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha is endowed with immeasurable supernormal powers and transformations, benefiting and bringing happiness to sentient beings without even a moment’s rest.
For this reason, the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are called "gems."
"Good sons!

For your sake, I have briefly explained these four types of objects of gratitude, both mundane and supramundane. You should know that in practicing the bodhisattva path, you ought to repay these four kinds of kindness."
At that time, five hundred elders addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
These four debts of gratitude are extremely difficult to repay. What practices should one cultivate to repay such kindness?"
The Buddha addressed the elders, saying: "Good sons,
for the sake of seeking Bodhi, there are three kinds of ten pāramitās:
First, the ten kinds of *dāna-pāramitā*; second, the ten kinds of *upaniṣad-pāramitā*; third, the ten kinds of *tattva-pāramitā*.

If there are good sons or good daughters who resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and are able to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures to bestow as alms upon immeasurable impoverished sentient beings, such giving is merely called the *dāna-pāramitā*, but it is not called the true *pāramitā*.

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, having generated the mind of great compassion to seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, give away their own wives and children to others with a heart free from stinginess, and even give their own flesh, hands, feet, head, eyes, marrow, and brain, as well as their very life, to those who come seeking them—such giving is merely called "approximating" the *pāramitā*, but is not yet called the "true" *pāramitā*.

If a son or daughter of good family generates the unsurpassed mind of great enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi-citta*), abides in non-apprehension, and exhorts all sentient beings to likewise generate this mind, bestowing upon even a single sentient being a single four-line verse of the true Dharma so that they may be directed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—this is called the true *pāramitā*.

The first two types of giving are not yet called "repaying kindness"; if a son or daughter of good family can practice this third, true *pāramitā*, they are then said to truly be able to repay the four debts of gratitude.
Why is this so? Because the first two types of giving involve a mind that grasps at attainment, whereas the third type of giving involves a mind of non-attainment.

By bestowing the gift of the true Dharma upon even a single sentient being, causing them to resolve upon the unsurpassed, great Bodhicitta, that person shall, when they realize enlightenment, extensively deliver sentient beings without end, continuing the lineage of the Triple Gem so that it is never severed. For these reasons, it is called "repaying kindness."

At that time, the five hundred elders, having heard from the Buddha this teaching on repaying kindness never before heard, were filled with leaping joy at such an unprecedented experience. They resolved their minds to seek supreme enlightenment, attained the samādhi of patience, entered inconceivable wisdom, and became forever non-retrogressive.

At that time, eighty-four thousand sentient beings within the assembly gave rise to the bodhicitta and attained firm faith; furthermore, the great multitude gathered for this ocean-like assembly of samādhis all attained the Vajra-Forbearance Samādhi, realized the forbearance of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and the forbearance of compliance (*ānulomikī-kṣānti*), or some realized the first stage (*bhūmi*) and attained the forbearance of non-arising. Immeasurable sentient beings gave rise to the bodhicitta and dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the five hundred elders:

"In future ages, if any sentient beings hear this 'Chapter on Repaying the Four Enquiries' from the *Cittabhūmi-parivarta*, and receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, copy, and widely disseminate it, such persons shall increase in merit and wisdom; they shall be protected by the devas, remain free from illness in their present bodies, and enjoy extended lifespans.

At the time of their death, they shall immediately attain rebirth in the inner palace of Maitreya; beholding the mark of the white tuft between his brows, they shall transcend birth and death. At the three assemblies under the Dragon Flower tree, they shall attain liberation, be reborn at will in the pure lands of the ten directions, see the Buddhas and hear the Dharma, enter the stage of the right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), and swiftly achieve the Tathāgata’s wisdom of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
