The Second Chapter on Repaying Kindness, Part Two.
At that time, eighty yojanas to the northeast of the great city of Rājagṛha, there was a small kingdom named Puṇyavardhana.

In that country, there was an elder named Jñānaprabha; he was advanced in years and had only one son, who was of a wicked disposition and would not obey his parents, refusing to follow any of their instructions.

From afar, they heard that the Tathāgata Śākyamuni was at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, proclaiming for the sake of immeasurable sentient beings in this defiled and evil age the Mahāyāna Dharma of Repaying Kindness. Their parents, their son, and all their kinsmen, in order to hear the Dharma, brought offerings and came to where the Buddha was; having made their offerings and paid their respects, they addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I have a son whose nature is wicked and who does not accept any of our parental instructions. Now, having heard the Buddha preach on the four kinds of kindness to be repaid, he has come to where the Buddha is in order to hear the Dharma."
We only pray that the World-Honored One will,

for our sake and that of all our kinsmen, proclaim the profound and wondrous meaning of the four debts of gratitude, so that those wicked children may give rise to hearts of filial piety and obedience, attaining peace and happiness in this life and the next.
At that time, the Buddha said to Jñānaprabha:
“Excellent, excellent!
For the sake of the Dharma, you have come to my presence to make offerings and pay respect, and you delight in hearing this Dharma.”
Listen attentively, all of you, and reflect upon this well.

If there are sons or daughters of good family who resolve their minds on Bodhicitta in order to hear the essential Dharma, then for every single atom of dust upon the ground they tread as they lift and set down their feet, regardless of distance, by virtue of these causes and conditions, they shall attain the status of a Cakravartin King of the Golden Wheel.

When the retribution of that king’s life is exhausted, he becomes a King of the Desire Realm Heavens; when the retribution of his life in the Desire Heavens is exhausted, he becomes a Brahmā King. Thereupon, seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, he will swiftly realize the wondrous fruit.

"You, Great Householder, and the rest of this assembly, have come to me for the sake of the Dharma; having traveled eighty yojanas, you have accumulated as many merits as there are atoms of dust upon the great earth, each of which is capable of bringing about the karmic fruition of rebirth among devas and humans or as a Wheel-Turning King."
Having heard the Dharma, you shall in the future realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Although I have previously explained the profound and subtle meaning of the four debts of gratitude, I now proclaim this same meaning for you once again.
And he spoke in verse:
"The Most Victorious Dharma-King, the Great Holy Lord, To whom no human or deva is equal;
Adorned with all the marks and signs upon his body, His ocean of wisdom is like space—immeasurable."
The practices for the benefit of self and others are all perfected; Your fame is heard throughout all lands;
Having forever severed the afflictions and their residual habitual tendencies, You skillfully maintain secret conduct and guard the sense faculties.
With the one hundred and forty kinds of unique qualities, the vast ocean of merit is entirely fulfilled;
endowed with all samādhis and supernormal powers, he constantly sports in the palace of the eight masteries.
Among the humans, devas, and non-Buddhists of the ten directions, there is none who can challenge the Teacher, the Tamer;
with his golden mouth he proclaims unimpeded eloquence, speaking of his own accord even though there is no one to question him.
Just as the ocean tide never misses its time, and just as the celestial drum proclaims according to the will of the gods,
such mastery belongs only to the Buddha, and not to those with the five supernatural powers, nor to the *asuras*, *brahmās*, or others.
Through vows cultivated over inconceivable oceans of kalpas, I have realized such great supernormal powers;
Entering the chamber of great tranquility in samādhi, I observe all faculties, as well as their medicines and ailments.
Emerging from meditative concentration, he praised the gateway to the mind-ground of the Buddhadharma of the three periods of time;
at that moment, the elder householders retreated from the Mahāyāna resolve, taking pleasure instead in dwelling in the self-benefiting practices of the two vehicles.
I have opened the teachings of great wisdom and skillful means, leading others into the three gates of liberation of emptiness;
the Tathāgata’s underlying intent is immeasurable, known only by a Buddha as the true secret.
Even if sharp-witted śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, along with bodhisattvas who diligently seek non-retrogression,
were to measure it together for twelve kalpas, none could know even a small fraction of it.
Even if the wisdom of all ordinary and holy beings throughout the ten directions were bestowed upon a single person to make him a wise one,
such wise ones would be like a grove of bamboo, unable to fathom even a small fraction of it.
Ordinary worldlings lack the eye of wisdom; Deluded regarding the source of kindness, they lose the wondrous fruit.
The sentient beings of this degenerate age of five turbidities Fail to realize profound gratitude and constantly turn their backs on virtue.
I shall reveal the four debts of gratitude To lead them onto the path of right view and Bodhi.
The kindness of the compassionate father and the grieving mother in nurturing us—may all sons and daughters find peace and happiness.
The kindness of the compassionate father is as lofty as the king of mountains; the kindness of the grieving mother is as deep as the great ocean.
If I were to remain in the world for an eon, I could not exhaustively describe the kindness of my compassionate mother;
what I have now briefly stated is but a small fraction, like a mosquito or a gnat drinking from the great ocean.
Suppose there were someone who, for the sake of merit, made offerings to pure-practicing brahmins,
to seers possessing the five supernatural powers and self-mastery, to great wise teachers and virtuous friends;
providing them with halls and palaces fashioned from the seven treasures, as well as chambers of ox-head sandalwood.
Hundred-jeweled couches are each spread out; Worldly delicacies like ambrosia, And medicinal decoctions that cure ten thousand ailments, Are filled within vessels of gold and silver.
To make such offerings three times each day, even for as many as a hundred kalpas,
is not equal to offering even a small portion for a single moment to one’s compassionate mother, that field of great kindness;
the resulting merit is boundless and immeasurable, beyond comparison by any calculation or analogy.
The compassionate mother of the world conceived her child; for ten months she carried the fetus and endured long suffering.
She had no attachment to the pleasures of the five senses, and likewise remained moderate in her eating and drinking at all times.
Day and night she constantly harbored a heart of compassion, undergoing various hardships whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
When the child within the womb is about to be born, it is as if one’s limbs and joints were being severed by a mass of sharpened blades;
bewildered as to east or west, unable to distinguish direction, the entire body is racked with pain beyond endurance.
Or perhaps they meet their end because of this hardship, leaving their six types of kinsmen and relatives all in grief and distress;
such manifold sufferings all stem from having a son, and the intensity of this sorrowful lamentation cannot be fully expressed in words.
If you should recover and your body find peace and joy, your happiness will be immeasurable, like a pauper finding treasure;
gazing upon your countenance, I shall never tire of it, and my heart of compassion shall not forsake you for even a moment.
The affection between mother and child is always thus; In going out and coming in, it never leaves the breast.
A mother’s milk is like a spring of nectar; It nourishes and sustains in due time, never failing.
The grace of her compassionate thoughts is truly difficult to compare; The virtue of her nurturing care is likewise immeasurable.
The great earth of the world is called heavy, yet the compassionate mother’s kindness is heavier than that;
Mount Sumeru of the world is called high, yet the compassionate mother’s kindness is higher than that;
In the world, only the fierce wind is swift, yet the mother’s mind in a single thought is swifter than that.
If there are sentient beings who practice filial impiety,

causing their mothers to give rise even for a moment to a heart of resentment or to utter even a small portion of words of grievance, the child shall then encounter suffering and hardship in accordance with those words;
neither all the Buddhas nor the Vajra-devas, nor the secret dharmas of the immortals, can save them.
If there are sons or daughters who follow their mother’s instructions, honoring her countenance and never disobeying her,
all calamities and misfortunes will be completely eliminated, and they shall be constantly protected by the devas in peace and happiness.
If one can follow and obey their compassionate mother, such sons and daughters are by no means ordinary;
they are Great Compassionate Bodhisattvas manifesting among humans, demonstrating various skillful means for repaying kindness.
If there were a man or a woman who, to repay their mother’s kindness,
practiced filial piety by cutting flesh and drawing blood to provide for her constantly, doing so for a full kalpa and diligently cultivating every form of filiality—
even then, they would still not have repaid even a moment’s worth of her kindness.
For ten months dwelling within the womb, constantly holding the root of the breast to drink milk and blood;
from being an infant until childhood, the mother's breast milk consumed amounts to more than a hundred *hu*.
As for food, drink, medicinal decoctions, and exquisite clothing, it is the constant rule that the child comes first and the mother later.
Even if a child is foolish and loathed by others, the mother still cherishes him with compassion and does not abandon him.
Long ago, there was a woman who carried her son while crossing the torrential waters of the Ganges;
because the water surged so violently that she could hardly move forward, she perished together with her son, unable to leave him behind.
By the power of these roots of goodness from practicing loving-kindness, at the end of his life he was reborn above in the Brahma Heaven;
there he long enjoyed the bliss of Brahma-samādhi and encountered the Tathāgata to receive the Buddha’s prediction.
Therefore, the compassionate mother possesses ten virtues, each established as a name according to its corresponding benefit:
first, the Great Earth; second, the Ability to Give Birth; third, the Ability to Correctly Guide; fourth, Nurturing;
fifth, Bestowing Wisdom; sixth, Adornment; seventh, named Tranquility; eighth, Instruction; ninth, Protection; and tenth, Deliverance.
The nine instructions and ten karmas; no kindness exceeds that of a mother’s.
What dharma is most wealthy in the world?
What dharma is most impoverished in the world?
When the mother was present in the hall, one was most wealthy; when the mother was not present, one was most poor.
When the mother was alive, it was midday; when one grieves for the mother’s passing, it is sunset.
When the mother was alive, all was complete and perfect; when one grieves for the mother’s passing, all is utterly empty and void.

All good men and women in the world, Whose debt of gratitude toward their parents is as vast as a mountain, Should maintain filial piety and reverence ever in their hearts; To know this debt and repay it is the path of the sages.
They spared neither body nor life to serve their parents with delicious food, never for a single thought-moment failing in the care of their physical needs;
yet when their parents suddenly passed away, they found that even their sincere desire to repay such kindness could not reach them.
In the past, the Buddha practiced for the sake of his compassionate mother, Thereby attaining a body of golden hue adorned with the marks and signs;
His fame is vast and wide, pervading the ten directions, And all humans and devas bow their heads in reverence.
Both humans and non-humans alike pay him homage, As he himself repays the kindness of his mother through his former causes.
I ascended to the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where for three months I preached the True Dharma to my mother;
causing her to hear it and return to the Right Path, she awakened to the Patience of Non-arising and shall never again fall back.
All these acts are performed to repay the kindness of compassion; yet though such repayment is profound, it remains insufficient.

Maudgalyāyana, foremost in supernatural powers, having severed all afflictions of the three realms, used his supernormal powers to observe his compassionate mother and saw her suffering among the hungry ghosts.
Maudgalyāyana went in person to repay his mother’s kindness, rescuing his compassionate parent from her suffering;
she was reborn among the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others’ Transformations, where they together enjoy their pastimes in the celestial palace.
One should know that the kindness of parents is the deepest; all Buddhas and sages repay this virtue.

If a person makes offerings to the Buddha with a sincere heart, and another diligently practices filial piety and support—there is no difference in the merit of these two individuals, and their rewards shall endure inexhaustibly throughout the three periods of time.
When worldly people commit various transgressions on behalf of their children, they fall into the three miserable realms and suffer for a long time.
Since men and women who are not sages lack supernormal powers, they do not see the cycle of rebirth and thus find it difficult to repay [their parents].
Alas! Worldly beings lack the power of the sages; they cannot rescue their compassionate mothers.
For this reason, you should know: diligently cultivate all meritorious virtues that bring benefit and fortune.
Because their sons and daughters pursued supreme merit, a great golden light shone upon the hells;
within that light, profound and wondrous sounds were proclaimed, awakening their parents and causing them to resolve their minds [upon enlightenment].
Recalling that throughout my past lives I constantly committed transgressions, I now repent with a single thought, extinguishing them all.
Reciting "Namo to the Buddhas of the Three Times," I shall escape this body of suffering and hardship in the states of no-leisure;
reborn among humans and devas, I shall long enjoy happiness, behold the Buddhas, hear the Dharma, and attain Buddhahood.
Or one may be born within the pure lands of the ten directions, with the seven-jeweled lotus as one’s parents;
when the flower opens, one beholds the Buddha and awakens to non-arising.
With non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas as fellow students, one attains the sovereign power of the six supernatural faculties and enters the subtle and wondrous palace of Bodhi.
All these Bodhisattvas manifest as sons and daughters, transforming the human realm through the power of their great vows;
this is called truly repaying the kindness of one's parents—may you, all sentient beings, cultivate and learn this together.
Sentient beings transmigrate through the six realms, like the wheel of a cart without beginning or end;
as fathers, mothers, sons, or daughters, they have been mutually kind to one another in birth after birth and life after life.
Just as one views parents and others without distinction, there is no way to recognize them without realizing noble wisdom;
all men are fathers, and all women are mothers.
How can one fail to repay the kindness of past lives, Yet give rise to divergent thoughts that breed resentment and jealousy?
One must always repay kindness and mutually benefit one another; One should not strike or scold others to cause resentment and aversion.
If you wish to cultivate further the gates of merit and wisdom, you should make vows during the six periods of day and night:
"May I, throughout immeasurable kalpas of birth after birth, attain the great supernormal power of the knowledge of past lives."
Able to know hundreds of thousands of past lives, Mutually recognizing one another as fathers and mothers,
Cycling through the six destinies and four modes of birth— May I, in a single thought-moment, always reach them.
I preach the sublime Dharma to eliminate the causes of suffering, So that beings in the human and celestial realms may long enjoy happiness.
I exhort them to resolve upon the firm vow of Bodhi, And to practice the gateway of the Bodhisattva’s six perfections,
Forever severing the two kinds of causes for birth and death, To swiftly realize the unsurpassed path of Nirvana.
All the kings throughout the ten directions, who transform people through the True Dharma as sagely sovereigns—
whose merit and virtue are most supreme, and whose actions are autonomous, are called devas.
The gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three and other deities constantly employ the power of their merit to assist the King’s governance;
all the heavens protect him as if he were an only son, and for this reason he is entitled to the name "Son of Heaven."
The world takes the king as its foundation; all the people rely upon him, just as all dwellings in the world are established with pillars as their foundation.
When a king transforms the people through the True Dharma, he is like the Great Brahmā King bringing forth the myriad things;
when a king practices unrighteousness and lacks governance, he is like King Yama destroying the world.
When a king harbors wicked and deceitful people, it is no different from an elephant trampling a lotus pond;
do not say that this is merely the encounter with a degenerate age—know that good and evil are the result of the king’s own cultivation.
Just as the Sun Deity illuminates the world, so too does a king transform the world;
though the sun’s light does not shine during the night, it enables sentient beings to obtain peace and happiness.
If a king transforms the world through unrighteousness, all the people will have no refuge.
Whatever terrors exist in the world cannot arise through the power of the king’s merit;
that the people enjoy peace and happiness should be known as the reach of the king’s merit.
All the most excellent and wondrous flowers in the world bloom by the power of the king’s merit;
All the exquisite gardens in the world flourish by the power of the king’s merit;
All the medicinal herbs in the world cure various ailments by the power of the king’s merit.
The hundred grains and the crops of the world, Through the power of the king’s merit, all reach fruition;
The people of the world enjoy abundance and joy, Through the power of the king’s merit, always spontaneously.
Suppose an elder has an only son, Wise, dignified, and peerless in the world;
His parents’ affection for him is like that for their own eyes, Constantly giving rise to a mind of protective mindfulness day and night.
The Great Sage-King of the land is likewise: he cherishes all sentient beings as his only son;
he nurtures the elderly and rescues the orphaned and solitary, his mind regarding reward and punishment always remaining impartial.
Thus, this Benevolent King is a holy sovereign, revered by all living beings as if he were a Tathāgata.
Under the transformational governance of the Benevolent King, the land is free from calamity, and the myriad subjects are respectful, diligent, and ever at peace.
When a king lacks the Dharma to transform the world, pestilence spreads and sentient beings suffer disaster.
Thus, for all humans and non-humans alike, merit and fault are manifest and cannot be concealed;
within the laws of good and evil, the distribution is sevenfold: the creator receives five parts, while the king obtains two.
This applies equally to gardens, groves, fields, and houses, as well as to taxes and other such divisions.
When a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears, the realm is divided into six parts;
the King receives one part, while all the people receive five parts. The same applies to the retribution for good and evil karma.
If there is a king who cultivates right view and transforms the world according to the Dharma, he is named a Lord of Devas;
because he transforms the world by relying on the celestial laws, King Vaiśravaṇa will constantly protect him,
as will the other three devas and the hosts of rākṣasas— all shall guard the palace of this noble king.
When the Holy King appears in the world to govern the nation, he benefits all sentient beings and accomplishes ten virtues:
first, the ability to illuminate the realm; second, the adornment of the land;
third, the ability to bestow all forms of peace and happiness; fourth, the ability to subdue all enemies.
The fifth is named Able to Ward Off All Terrors; The sixth is named Cultivating and Accumulating All Noble Sages;
The seventh is named The Fundamental Source of All Dharmas; The eighth is named Protecting and Sustaining the World;
The ninth is named Able to Perform the Work of Creation; The tenth is named Sovereign of the Realm and Its People.
If a king accomplishes these ten supreme virtues, The Brahma kings, Śakra, and all the devas, The yakṣas, rākṣasas,
and the lords of the bhūtas, Will conceal their forms and constantly come to protect the realm;
The dragon kings will rejoice and send down sweet rain, The five grains will ripen, and the myriad people will be at peace.
Precious jewels sprang up everywhere within the kingdom; men and horses possessed great strength, and there were no enemies.
The wish-fulfilling jewel appeared before the king, and all kings beyond his borders submitted as guests.
If one gives rise to unwholesome thoughts within the kingdom, and with a single moment of mental arousal commits manifold evils,
that person will fall into hell at the end of life, suffering for eternal kalpas with no time of release.
If there are those who serve the king with diligence and sincerity, the devas will protect them and increase their honor and prosperity.
O Elder Jñānaprabha, you should know that all kings are moved by karma;
no phenomena arise except through causes and conditions—if there were no causes and conditions, no phenomena would exist.
To say that there are no rebirths in heaven or in the evil realms is for such a person not to understand causes;
this causeless and effectless view is a great perversion, through which one fails to know of sin and merit and gives rise to false conceptualizations.
The various blessings and joys you now enjoy, O King, were once attained by upholding the three pure precepts;
drawn forth by the cultivation of the virtue of these precepts, you have obtained this royal body as a wondrous fruit among humans and devas.
If a person gives rise to the bodhicitta, The power of their vows brings about the unsurpassed fruit;
Firmly upholding the supreme, pure precepts, They dwell with sovereign ease as a Dharma King.
With supernormal powers and transformations filling the ten directions, They universally rescue all classes of beings according to conditions.
By upholding the Bodhisattva precepts in a middling degree, one attains the sovereign power of a Cakravartin King;
whatever the mind intends is entirely accomplished, and immeasurable humans and devas all pay him homage.
The Great Ghost King who maintains the lower-superior grade of precepts causes all non-human beings to submit;
though he may have committed violations in his observance of the code of discipline, it is by virtue of the excellence of that discipline that he has become king.
Those who maintain the lower and middle grades [of discipline] become kings of birds and beasts; all that flies and runs submits to them.
Even if they have committed transgressions against the pure precepts, they attain the status of king by virtue of the excellence of their discipline.
One of the lowest-of-the-low grade who upholds the precepts becomes King Yama, exercising constant sovereignty within the hells;
though he may have violated the prohibitions and been born into an evil realm, it is by virtue of the excellence of his discipline that he has attained the status of king.
For this reason, all sentient beings should receive the pure precepts of a bodhisattva;
by skillfully upholding them without deficiency or transgression, they shall become kings of men wherever they are born.
If one does not receive the precepts of the Tathāgata, one will ultimately never attain even the body of a jackal;
how much less could one experience the most supreme happiness among gods and humans or dwell upon a royal throne?
Therefore, a king is not without cause; through the diligent cultivation of the karma of precepts, he achieves this wondrous fruit.
As the sovereign of his people, the king protects them with compassion as a mother nourishes her infant.
Such a ruler of men possesses great kindness, and the heart of one nurtured by him can hardly repay it.
For this reason, all sentient beings who are able to cultivate and realize great bodhi,
and who give rise to great compassion for all living beings, should receive the Tathāgata’s threefold aggregate of precepts.
If one wishes to receive the precepts in accordance with the Dharma, one should repent of one's offenses so that they are extinguished.
There are ten conditions that give rise to offenses: the three of the body, the four of the mouth, and the three of the mind.
Birth and death are beginningless and offenses are endless; The great ocean of afflictions is deep and bottomless.
Karmic obstructions are as steep and lofty as Mount Sumeru; The creation of karma arises from two kinds of causes.
What are called active manifestations and seeds, the store-consciousness (ālayavijñāna) maintains as all-encompassing conditions;
like a shadow following a form, they do not leave the body, obstructing the Noble Path at all times.
It obstructs the sublime fruits of happiness for humans and devas nearby, and obstructs the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi afar;
while living at home can summon the causes of affliction, leaving the home life can likewise break the pure precepts.
If one can perform repentance according to the Dharma, all afflictions will be entirely eliminated;
just as the fire at the end of an eon destroys the world, it burns away Mount Sumeru and the vast oceans.
Repentance can burn away the fuel of afflictions; Repentance can lead one along the path to the heavens;
Repentance can attain the bliss of the four dhyānas; Repentance rains down precious maṇi jewels;
Repentance can extend the adamantine lifespan; Repentance can enter the palace of eternal bliss.
Repentance can deliver one from the prison of the triple world; Repentance can cause the flower of Bodhi to bloom;
Through repentance, one beholds the Buddha’s Great Perfect Mirror; Repentance can lead one to the place of jewels.
If one is able to perform repentance according to the Dharma, one should practice based on two types of contemplative gates:
first, the gate of contemplating phenomena to extinguish offenses; second, the gate of contemplating principle to extinguish offenses.
There are three ways to observe the cessation of offenses through contemplating phenomena, categorized into three grades according to the superior, middling, and inferior faculties.
If one of superior faculty seeks the pure precepts, they will give rise to great diligence with no retreat;
weeping with tears of blood, they remain ever sincere and earnest, their profound grief manifesting as blood appearing all over their body.
Fixing one's mindfulness upon the Triple Gem of the ten directions, as well as all sentient beings of the six realms,
one kneels long with palms joined and undisturbed, revealing one’s faults, purifying the mind, and seeking repentance.
"I only pray that the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, out of great compassion, will take pity on me.
Dwelling in saṃsāra with nothing to rely upon, I remain forever unawakened through the long night of birth and death."
I am an ordinary being bound by all fetters, my狂心 (mad mind) inverted and grasping at objects everywhere.
Dwelling within the burning house of the triple world, I am delusively defiled by the six sense-objects, without any protection.
I was born into a poor and lowly family, lacking autonomy and constantly suffering.
I was born into a family of parents with wrong views, committing sins and relying upon evil associates.
I only pray that the Buddhas, the Honored Ones of Great Compassion, will look upon me with pity and mindfulness as if I were their only child.
Having repented once, I shall never again commit any transgressions; may the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time bear witness to this.
"One who repents with such vigor is called one who seeks the pure precepts in the highest degree.
If there is one of middling capacity seeking the precepts, they repent of all their transgressions with single-minded vigor;
weeping profusely and unaware of themselves, sweat flows from their entire body as they entreat the Buddha in sorrow."
I confess all karmic deeds from beginningless birth and death; May the waters of great compassion wash away my afflictions.
Purifying the obstacles of sin and cleansing the six sense faculties, Grant me the Bodhisattva’s threefold aggregate of precepts.
I vow to uphold them firmly without regression, Diligently practicing to deliver suffering sentient beings.
Having not yet attained deliverance oneself, one first delivers others; Until the end of the future, this shall never cease.

One who thus exerts themselves with such diligence and valor, Seeking Bodhi without sparing body or life, Can evoke the wondrous and miraculous signs of the Triple Gem; This is called the Middle-grade Great Repentance.
If there are those of inferior capacity who seek pure precepts, And give rise to the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment,
With tears of sorrow and weeping, their body hairs standing on end, They feel deep shame and remorse for the transgressions they have committed.
Before the Triple Gem of the ten directions, And before all beings of the six realms,
I sincerely confess and reveal, from time immemorial, All instances of having disturbed and troubled sentient beings.
Arousing a mind of unimpeded great compassion, they disregard their own bodies and lives to repent for the three karmas;
they confess all transgressions already committed and resolve never again to create new evils.
Thus, these three grades of repentance for all transgressions are all called the foremost pure precepts;
by washing away the dust of affliction with the water of shame and remorse, both body and mind become vessels of purity.
"O sons of good family, you should know: I have already explained the various repentances of pure contemplation;
they are without distinction in their principle and phenomena, differing only according to the faculties and conditions [of practitioners]."
If you wish to cultivate the contemplation of correct principle, remain far removed from all forms of distraction.
Donning fresh, clean robes, sit in the full lotus posture; gather the mind with right mindfulness and detach from all external conditions.
Constantly contemplate the wondrous Dharma-body of all Buddhas, whose essential nature is like space and cannot be grasped.
The nature of all transgressions is like suchness; they arise from the deluded mind through inverted causes and conditions.
Such characteristics of transgression are empty from the beginning; throughout the three periods of time, nothing can be apprehended.
Neither internal, nor external, nor in between; its nature and characteristics are suchness, entirely unmoving.
The wondrous principle of true thusness transcends names and words; only the wisdom of the sages can penetrate it.
Neither existent nor non-existent, neither both existent and non-existent, Neither non-existent nor non-non-existent, transcending names and signs;
Pervading the entire dharma-realm without arising or ceasing— All Buddhas are fundamentally of one and the same essence.
I pray that all Buddhas will grant their protective grace, Able to extinguish all inverted minds;
May I swiftly awaken to the source of true nature, And quickly realize the unsurpassed path of the Tathāgata.
If there is a son of good family with pure faith who is able to contemplate the wondrous principle of emptiness day and night, all karmic obstacles will naturally be eliminated;
this is called the supreme upholding of the pure precepts.
If a person contemplates and realizes the emptiness of the true mark, they can extinguish all grave offenses;
just as a great wind blows upon a fierce fire, it can burn away immeasurable grasses and trees.
This true contemplation, O sons of good family, is called the secret and essential gateway of all Buddhas.
If you wish to analyze it extensively for others, do not proclaim it among those lacking wisdom;
for when ordinary, foolish sentient beings hear it, they will inevitably give rise to doubt and lack faith.
If there are those of wisdom who give rise to faith and understanding, observing and contemplating moment by moment to awaken to True Suchness,
all Buddhas of the ten directions will appear before them, and they will naturally realize the wondrous fruit of Bodhi.

"O sons of good family, after my parinirvāṇa, those of pure faith in future ages shall constantly perform repentance through the two gates of contemplation and shall receive the Bodhisattva’s threefold aggregate precepts."
If you wish to receive and uphold the superior grade of precepts, you should invite the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as your precept masters.
I, Śākyamuni Buddha, shall serve as your Upādhyāya for the Bodhisattva precepts;
the Honored King of Pure Wisdom of the Dragon Lineage shall serve as your Ācārya for the pure precepts.
The future teacher, Maitreya Buddha, shall be the pure preceptor;
The present Honored Ones among two-legged beings of the ten directions shall be the pure witnesses of the precepts;
All Bodhisattvas of the ten directions shall be companions in the training of the precepts.
Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and Vajrapāṇi— May you serve as the external protectors for those training in the precepts.
I respectfully invite these Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as the Precept-transmitting Master present here before me.
In order to universally repay the four debts of gratitude,
One should give rise to the pure bodhicitta And receive the threefold aggregate of Bodhisattva precepts: The precept of benefiting all sentient beings,
The precept of gathering all virtuous dharmas, And the precept of gathering all forms of discipline.
These three clusters of pure precepts are protected and remembered by the Tathāgatas of the three times;
sentient beings who have not heard the Dharma and follow what is not the Dharma have never heard of or seen them throughout immeasurable kalpas.
Only the Buddhas of the ten directions in the past, Having received the pure precepts, constantly maintained them,
Permanently severed the two obstacles and afflictions, And attained the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi.
All the World-Honored Ones of the future, Guarding the jewel of the three clusters of pure precepts,
Having severed the three obstacles along with their habitual tendencies, Shall realize the Great Perfect Enlightenment.
The Sugatas of the ten directions in the present, Having fully cultivated the causes of the three clusters of pure precepts,
Have forever severed the cycle of birth and death’s suffering, And attained the fruit of enlightenment as the three bodies.
The pure precepts of the bodhisattva serve as a boat and raft to cross the deep and vast ocean of birth and death;
The pure precepts of the bodhisattva serve as a sharp sword to forever sever the fetters of greed, hatred, and delusion;
The pure precepts of the bodhisattva serve as a dwelling place amidst all the terrors of the perilous paths of birth and death.
The pure precepts can serve as a wish-fulfilling jewel, extinguishing the causes of all suffering from poverty and low status;
for all diseases caused by possession by ghosts and demons, the pure precepts of a bodhisattva are the efficacious medicine.
As kings among humans and devas, they attain sovereignty; the three clusters of pure precepts serve as their excellent conditions.
Even for those with the bodies of kings among the other four realms of existence, it is through pure precepts as a condition that they obtain these superior fruits.
Therefore, by cultivating the causes of mastery, one shall become a king and receive noble honor.
One should first pay homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions, increasing the cultivation of pure precepts day and night;
protected and remembered by all Buddhas, one constantly upholds them, so that these precepts are indestructible like a vajra.
The devas and benevolent deities of the three realms protect the King’s person and his retinue;
all enemies submit and surrender, while the myriad people rejoice, moved by the King’s transformative influence.
Therefore, by upholding the Bodhisattva precepts, one attains mundane and supramundane unconditioned fruits.
The Three Jewels abide eternally, transforming the world; their benevolence and virtue are vast and inconceivable.
Through the oceans of kalpas—past, future, and present—they bring merit to benefit sentient beings without ceasing.
The Buddha-sun, with its thousand rays, constantly illuminates the world, Benefiting all sentient beings and delivering those with whom he has a karmic affinity.
Those without such affinity do not behold the Buddha’s compassionate light, Just as the blind see nothing at all.
The Dharma-treasure is of one flavor, without change; the Buddhas of the past and the Buddhas of the future all teach the same.
Like rain of one flavor that universally moistens all, the grasses and trees flourish according to their size and distinction;
sentient beings each attain understanding according to their faculties, just as the plants that receive the moisture also differ.
Bodhisattvas and śrāvakas transform sentient beings, like the flow of a great river that never exhausts;
yet if sentient beings lack faith, they cannot be transformed, just as the sun finds it difficult to shine upon those dwelling in deep darkness.
The moonlight of the Tathāgata is exceedingly cool and refreshing; it can dispel all darkness in just this way.
Just as the moon does not shine upon an overturned basin, so too are deluded sentient beings.
The Dharma-treasure is a wondrous and excellent medicine of ambrosia, capable of curing all diseases of affliction;
those with faith who take this medicine realize Bodhi, while those without faith fall into evil realms according to their conditions.
Bodhisattvas and śrāvakas always remain in the world, delivering sentient beings through countless skillful means;
if there are sentient beings with hearts of faith and joy, each shall enter the state of peace and bliss of the three vehicles.
If the Tathāgata did not appear in the world, all sentient beings would enter onto deviant paths;
forever deprived of the drink of ambrosia, they would consume poisonous medicine and remain long submerged in the sea of suffering with no time of escape.
The Buddha-sun appears in the trichiliocosm, emitting great radiance that illuminates the long night;
sentient beings, as if asleep and unaware, receive this light and enter the chamber of non-action.
As long as the Tathāgata has not yet proclaimed the Single Vehicle Dharma, the lands of the ten directions remain entirely empty and desolate;
but once he resolves his mind, practices, and attains perfect enlightenment, all Buddha-lands become adorned and purified.
The Dharma-jewel of the One Vehicle is the mother of all Buddhas; from it are born the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time.
By practicing wisdom and skillful means without interruption, the path of liberation is perfected and one ascends to wondrous enlightenment.
If Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not appear, The sentient beings of the world will have no guide;
With no means to pass through the perils of birth and death, How could they reach the place of treasure?
With the power of great vows, they act as virtuous friends, Constantly preaching the sublime Dharma for practice;
They advance toward the ten stages and realize Bodhi, Skillfully entering the blissful state of Nirvana.
The Bodhisattva of Great Compassion transforms the world, employing skillful means to guide sentient beings;
while inwardly he maintains the true practice of the One Vehicle, outwardly he manifests as Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas.
Those of dull faculties and small wisdom, upon hearing of the One Vehicle, give rise to fear and require many kalpas to resolve their minds;
unaware that their own bodies contain the Tathāgatagarbha, they rejoice only in nirvāṇa and loathe worldly toil.
Sentient beings inherently possess the seed of bodhi, All residing within the ālayavijñāna storehouse consciousness.
If they encounter virtuous friends and resolve upon the Great Mind, Refining themselves through the three types of practice and cultivating wondrous deeds,
They will forever sever the afflictive and cognitive hindrances, And realize the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding body.
The wondrous fruit of Bodhi is not difficult to achieve, But a true spiritual friend is truly difficult to meet.
All Bodhisattvas who cultivate the supreme path Should know these four essential dharmas:
To draw near to virtuous friends is the first; To listen to the True Dharma is the second.
Third is contemplation in accordance with reality; fourth is cultivation and realization in accordance with the Dharma.
All the Great Holy Lords of the ten directions cultivated these four dharmas and realized Bodhi.
You, great assembly of elders, and those of pure faith in future ages,
must practice these four dharmas of the bodhisattva stages in order to attain the path to buddhahood.
Sons of noble family, listen attentively: among the four debts of gratitude spoken of by the Tathāgata, the debt to the Buddha Jewel is the most supreme;
it is for the sake of delivering sentient beings that he has resolved upon the Great Mind.
Throughout three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, He fully practiced hundreds of thousands of ascetic deeds;
His merit perfected, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, He reached the ultimate stage of the ten grounds and realized the three bodies.
The Dharma-body pervades all sentient beings; Myriad virtues are quiescent, its nature eternally abiding.
Neither born nor extinguished, without coming or going, Neither identical nor different, neither permanent nor annihilated.
The dharma-realm is all-pervasive like space; All Tathāgatas together cultivate and realize it.
All conditioned and unconditioned merits Reside within the dharmakāya, eternally pure.
The nature of the Dharma-body is like empty space; Far removed from the six sense-objects, it is unstained.
The Dharma-body is formless and free from all characteristics; Both the characteristic and the characterized are entirely empty.
Such is the wondrous Dharma-body of all Buddhas: Conceptual proliferation and verbal designations are stilled;
It is far removed from all discrimination, Where the sphere of mental activity ceases, its essence is entirely suchness.
Desiring to realize the body of a Tathāgata, the Bodhisattva skillfully cultivates the myriad practices;
the essence of wisdom is the unconditioned true Dharma-nature, wherein all Buddhas are identical in both form and mind.
Just as when a flying bird reaches a mountain of gold, its body becomes the same color as that mountain;
all Bodhisattvas are like these flying birds, for the Dharma-body of the Buddha is like the golden mountain.
The various marks and embellishments of the self-enjoyment body each pervade the lands of the ten directions;
with the four wisdoms perfectly luminous, one experiences the bliss of the Dharma, for the essence of all Buddhas, past and future, is identical.
Though pervading the entire Dharma-realm without obstruction, such a wondrous realm is inconceivable;
this body eternally abides in the land of the Reward Buddha, experiencing the bliss of the Dharma without interruption.
The various marks and signs of the Enjoyment Body for others manifest in accordance with their capacities, neither increasing nor decreasing;
to transform the Bodhisattvas on the stages, a single Buddha manifests ten kinds of bodies,
each appearing differently according to what is required, multiplying progressively until they reach the infinite.
Teaching the essentials of all dharmas according to their faculties, causing them to receive the joy of the Dharma and enter the One Vehicle;
they obtain supernatural powers that gradually increase, and the Dharma-gates they realize are likewise so.
Bodhisattvas of the lower stages give rise to wisdom, yet they cannot fully comprehend the higher stages.
The capacity to transform and those who are transformed increase according to each stage; each belongs to its respective sphere according to their original conditions.
Sometimes a single bodhisattva transforms many Buddhas, and sometimes many bodhisattvas are transformed by a single Buddha.
Thus ten Buddhas attained perfect enlightenment, each sitting beneath a bodhi tree of the seven treasures;
as one Buddha entered nirvana, the next attained enlightenment, unlike the manifested Buddhas who appear throughout the kalpas.
The lotus pedestals upon which the ten Buddhas sit each have a hundred thousand petals surrounding them;
within each petal is a Buddha-field, which is itself a trichiliocosm.
Within each and every realm there are ten billion suns, moons, stars, and the four great continents;
the six heavens of the desire realm, the four dhyānas, the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and so forth.
Among the four continents, in Jambudvīpa of the south,
there is a vajrāsana and a great bodhi tree king in each;
simultaneously realizing the path of enlightenment, they turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma throughout the great trichiliocosm.
Bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and śrāvakas attain the fruits of sainthood according to their respective faculties and dispositions.
Thus, the Buddha described as the three bodies is supreme, peerless, and named "Jewel."
The teachings spoken by the two bodies of the Response and Transformation are the Dharma-Jewel, consisting of doctrine, principle, practice, and fruition;
the Buddhas take the Dharma as their Great Teacher, which is the path to Bodhi realized through the cultivation of the mind.
The Dharma Jewel is unchanging throughout the three periods of time; all Buddhas alike take refuge in and study it.
I now prostrate to omniscience (*sarvajñā*); therefore, I declare the Dharma Jewel to be the Teacher of the Buddhas.
Some enter raging fires that cannot burn them, attaining true liberation at that very moment.
The Dharma Jewel can shatter the prison of birth and death, just as a vajra crushes all things;
the Dharma Jewel can illuminate the minds of sentient beings, like the Sun God appearing in the realm of space.
The Dharma-treasure can serve as a sturdy ship, capable of ferrying one across the river of craving to the further shore;
the Dharma-treasure can bestow happiness upon sentient beings, like a celestial drum that accords with the hearts of the gods;
the Dharma-treasure can relieve the poverty of sentient beings, like a mani-jewel that rains down all manner of treasures.
The Dharma Jewel can serve as the stairway to the Three Jewels; by hearing the Dharma and cultivating its causes, one is born in the higher realms.
The Dharma Jewel is the Great Holy King with the Golden Wheel, who uses the great power of the Dharma to destroy the four Māras.
The Dharma Jewel can serve as a great precious chariot, capable of transporting sentient beings out of the burning house.
The Dharma Jewel can act as the Great Teacher, leading sentient beings to the place of treasures;
The Dharma Jewel can blow the great Dharma conch, awakening sentient beings to the path of Buddhahood;
The Dharma Jewel can serve as the great Dharma lamp, illuminating all the darkness of birth and death.
The Dharma Jewel can serve as a vajra arrow, Able to pacify the realm and subdue all enemies.
The teachings spoken by the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time Can benefit sentient beings and liberate them from the bonds of suffering, Leading them into the city of nirvana’s peace and bliss;
This is called the debt of gratitude for the Dharma Jewel that is difficult to repay.

Elder Jñānaprabha, listen attentively: there are three kinds of Sangha, both mundane and supramundane—the assembly of Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and noble or ordinary beings—who are able to benefit sentient beings and serve as fields of merit.
Mañjuśrī, the Great Holy Honored One, is the mother of all Buddhas of the three periods of time;
the initial resolve of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions is entirely due to the power of Mañjuśrī’s transformation and instruction.
All sentient beings throughout all worlds, Upon hearing his name, seeing his body and its radiant marks,
And beholding his various emanations according to their kind, Shall all attain the inconceivable path of Buddhahood.
The Dharma Prince Maitreya Bodhisattva, from the moment he first resolved upon enlightenment, has abstained from eating meat;
for this reason he is named Maitreya, desiring to bring all sentient beings to spiritual maturity.
Abiding in the fourth Tuṣita Heaven, within forty-nine tiers of palaces of wish-fulfilling gems,
he constantly expounds the practice of non-retrogression day and night, delivering humans and devas through countless skillful means.
In the wondrous lotus pond of water with eight virtues, all those who possess the karmic affinity shall be born together;
I now entrust my disciples to Maitreya, so that they may attain liberation within the assembly at the Dragon Flower.
In the age of the Final Dharma, O sons of good family, by giving even a single morsel of food to sentient beings,
one shall see Maitreya through these roots of goodness and attain the ultimate path of Bodhi.
Śāriputra and the other great śrāvakas, with their wisdom and supernormal powers, transform all living beings.
If one can achieve the precepts of liberation, they are truly a person who practices right view;
preaching the Dharma for others and transmitting the Mahāyāna, such a field of merit is foremost.
There may be a class of ordinary beings within the Saṃgha who, though their precepts are incomplete, have given rise to right view;
they praise and chant the subtle and wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle, and by repenting immediately upon committing an offense, their hindrances are eliminated.
Because they serve as the cause for all sentient beings to attain Buddhahood, even such ordinary persons are the Jewel of the Saṅgha.
Just as a saffron flower, though withered and faded, still surpasses all other exquisite flowers,
so too is a bhikṣu of right view beyond the reach of the four kinds of wheel-turning kings.
These four classes of noble and ordinary monks tirelessly bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings;
they are called the world’s excellent field of merit, and this is known as the great virtue and grace of the Sangha Jewel.
As I have explained the meaning of the four debts of gratitude, these are called the causes that create the world;
all things arise from them, for without the four debts of gratitude, nothing can be found.
Just as all material forms in the world arise from the four great elements that create them,
so too does the world of sentient beings find its establishment through those four kinds of kindness.

At that time, the elder Jñānaprabha and his sons, having heard the Buddha’s teaching on the four kinds of great kindness, attained what they had never experienced before; with joy and palms joined, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One!

For the sake of sentient beings in this turbid and evil world who do not believe in cause and effect, who are unfilial toward their parents, and who hold false views, please preach the true and wondrous Dharma to bring benefit and joy to the world.

We only pray that the World-Honored One will explain the meaning of repaying kindness! Having now realized the profound nature of the four debts of gratitude, we do not yet know what wholesome deeds we should cultivate to repay this kindness.
The Buddha told the elder:
"O sons of good family!
I have already explained this extensively for the five hundred elders; now I shall explain it to you in brief."

If a son or daughter of good family, for the sake of attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, diligently practices the ten *pāramitās* yet perceives something as being attained, it is not called repaying the debt of gratitude;
if a person can practice even a single act of goodness for a brief moment with a mind free from attainment, that is truly called repaying the debt of gratitude.
Why is this so? Because all Tathāgatas realize non-attainment (*anupalambha*) and thereby achieve the Buddha-way to transform all sentient beings.

If there are sons of good family with pure faith who, upon hearing this sutra, believe, understand, accept, uphold, explain, and transcribe it; and if, through the emptiness of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala-śūnyatā*) and non-attainment, they should privately expound even a single four-line verse for another person, causing them to eliminate views of perversion and turn toward Bodhi—this is what is called repaying the four debts of gratitude.

Why is this? Because such a person shall attain unsurpassed bodhi, and by teaching and transforming immeasurable sentient beings in succession, they will cause them to enter the Buddha-way, ensuring that the seeds of the Three Jewels are never severed.
At that time, having heard these verses, the elder Jñānaprabha attained the samādhi of patience, grew weary of and detached from the world, and reached the stage of non-retrogression.
Simultaneously, eight thousand of his sons and others all attained this samādhi and together gave rise to the mind set upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, which is peerless.
Forty-eight thousand people also realized this samādhi; being distanced from dust and free from defilement, they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.

Chapter Three: On Renunciation and Abandonment.

At that time, the Elder Jñānaprabha, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Having now heard from the Buddha this profound and wondrous Dharma of repaying kindness, my heart leaps with joy at having attained what I never had before, like a person suffering from hunger and thirst encountering ambrosial food.”

I now desire to repay the four debts of gratitude by entering the monastic life under the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha to cultivate the Way, constantly exerting diligent effort in the hope of realizing Bodhi.
Out of great compassion, at one time the Buddha was in the city of Vaiśālī, where he expounded the profound Dharma for Vimalakīrti, saying:
"O Vimalakīrti!..."

A pure mind is the root of wholesome karma, while an unwholesome mind is the root of unwholesome karma; because the mind is pure, the world is pure, and because the mind is defiled, the world is defiled.

In my Buddha-dharma, the mind is sovereign; there are no phenomena that do not arise from the mind. You now dwell as a householder with great merit and virtue, possessing every kind of jewel and necklace in abundance.

Your children and kin live in peace and happiness; you have perfected right view and do not slander the Triple Gem. With a heart of filial piety, you revere your elders and parents; you give rise to great compassion to provide for the solitary and the destitute, extending this even to ants and termites, never harming them. You take patience as your garment and compassion as your dwelling; you honor those of virtue with a mind free from pride. You cherish all beings as if they were your own infants; you do not crave wealth or profit but constantly practice joy and relinquishment. In making offerings to the Triple Gem, your mind knows no satiety; for the sake of the Dharma, you would sacrifice your body without any stinginess.
"In this way, although you are a layperson who has not left the household life, you have already perfected immeasurable and boundless merit.

In a future age, when your myriad practices are complete, you shall transcend the three realms and realize great bodhi. The mind you cultivate is that of a true śramaṇa and a true brāhmaṇa; you are a true bhikṣu and a true renunciant."
"Such a person as this is what is called both a householder and one who has gone forth.

On one occasion, the World-Honored One was at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery, where he spoke the Dharma of instruction for the ill-behaved group of six bhikṣus, addressing them thus: "O you bhikṣus!
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Entering the ocean of the Buddha-dharma takes faith as its root; crossing the river of birth and death takes the precepts as one's raft.

If a person leaves the household life but does not protect the prohibitive precepts, greedily clinging to worldly pleasures and destroying the jewel of the Buddha’s precepts, or losing right view and entering the forest of false views, they will lead immeasurable people to fall into a great, deep pit.

Such a bhikṣu is not called one who has gone forth; he is neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa. His form resembles that of a śramaṇa, but his mind always dwells at home; such a śramaṇa lacks the practice of detachment.
There are two kinds of practice for seclusion:
first, physical seclusion;
second, mental seclusion.
Physical seclusion refers to when a person has left the household life and dwells in a quiet, secluded place; not being defiled by objects of desire is called physical seclusion.
Mental seclusion refers to when one who has left the household life cultivates a pure mind and is not defiled by objects of desire; this is called mental seclusion.
Though one has left the household life in body, if the mind craves objects of desire, such a person is not said to be "distant.

If a faithful son or daughter of noble family, while dwelling in a village, gives rise to the unsurpassed resolve and benefits all beings with great compassion—such practice is called true distancing.
Thereupon, the six groups of monks of evil character, hearing this sound of the Dharma, attained the patience of compliance (*anulomikī kṣānti*).
"Nevertheless, although we now believe what the Buddha has spoken, each of us harbors doubts and our minds have not yet reached certainty."
Excellent, World-Honored One!

You are the one who can sever all doubts in the world, the one who has attained mastery over all dharmas, the speaker of truth, the speaker without duality, the knower of the path, and the opener of the path. We pray that the Tathāgata [will grant us this].

For the sake of those such as ourselves and all sentient beings of future ages, please set aside expedient means and preach the Dharma of ultimate truth, so that we may forever be free from doubt and regret and enter the Buddha-way.

In this assembly there are two bodhisattvas: one is a renunciant and the other is a householder. These two bodhisattvas are well able to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings without ceasing. As I contemplate it, the renunciant bodhisattva does not equal the householder in cultivating the bodhisattva practice.

Why is this so? In the past, there was a Cakravartin King of the Golden Wheel who resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Disgusted with and detached from the impermanence, suffering, and emptiness of the world, he renounced the rank of a wheel-turning king as if discarding snot or spittle, and left the household life in purity to enter the path of the Buddha.

At that time, eighty-four thousand ladies of the inner palace and court maids, seeing the king renounce the household life, each harbored feelings of longing and attachment; they beat their breasts and wailed in lamentation, giving rise to great distress, as the suffering of separation from those one loves is like the agony of hell.

When the Golden Wheel-turning Sage King first assumed the throne, the precious queen he had won, his thousand sons, and his ministers and retinue were all deeply grieved by their separation and his renunciation of the throne to leave the household life; the sound of their wailing filled the four continents.
These various attendants each spoke these words:
"Our King’s merit and wisdom are immeasurable and boundless; how can he abandon us and go forth into the homeless life?
Alas, what misery! The world is now empty and void; from this day forward, we shall have no refuge and no protector."

"If there are sons or daughters of good family with pure faith who take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha and resolve to attain Bodhicitta, they may renounce their parents to leave the household life and enter the Path. Their parents, out of deep compassion and profound affection, will suffer the sorrow of separation that moves both heaven and earth; like a fish in a dried-up rut struggling upon the ground, the suffering of parting from those one loves is likewise so intense, just as was the heart of the Universal Monarch’s retinue."
A renunciant bodhisattva benefits sentient beings; how could they inflict harm upon their parents, wives, and children, causing immeasurable people to undergo great suffering and distress?

For these reasons, a renunciant bodhisattva lacks compassion and pity and does not benefit sentient beings; therefore, they are not like a householder bodhisattva, who possesses great loving-kindness and compassion, pities sentient beings, and benefits all.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the elder Jñānaprabha:
"Excellent, excellent!
Out of great compassion, you have exhorted me to speak on the relative superiority and inferiority of the two paths: that of the renunciant and that of the householder."
Regarding what you have now asked, that a renunciant bodhisattva is not equal to one who remains at home— this is not so. Why is this?
The renunciant bodhisattva surpasses the householder; they are immeasurable, boundless, and beyond comparison. Why is this?

Because by the power of right wisdom, the renunciant bodhisattva minutely observes all the various faults inherent in the household life: namely, that all worldly dwellings are filled with accumulations of which one never knows satisfaction, just as the great ocean receives all rivers, large and small, yet is never satisfied.

"Good son! To the south of Mount Gandhamādana and to the north of the Snowy Mountains lies Lake Anavatapta. The four great dragon kings each dwell in one corner: the dragon king in the southeast has the head of a white elephant; the dragon king in the southwest has the head of a great ox; the dragon king in the northwest has the head of a lion; and the dragon king in the northeast has the head of a great horse.
From each of these four corners, a great river gushes forth: first is the Gaṅgā River, and wherever its waters flow, a white elephant emerges along with them."
Second is the Śraddhā River; wherever its waters reach, water buffaloes emerge following them.
Third is the Varku River; wherever its waters reach, lions emerge following them.
Fourth is the Sītā River; wherever its waters reach, great horses emerge following them.

In this way, each of these great rivers has five hundred medium-sized rivers, and each medium-sized river has immeasurable small rivers; all these waters—great, medium, and small—enter the great ocean, yet this great ocean is never filled to capacity.

All the dwellings and houses of sentient beings in the world are likewise thus: various treasures are gathered from the four directions and enter the house, yet one is never satisfied; through much seeking and accumulation, one commits all manner of evils. When impermanence suddenly arrives, one abandons that old house; at that time, the master of the house undergoes retribution according to his karma, wandering for immeasurable kalpas with no place of ultimate refuge.
"Good son! That which is called a 'house' is the body of the five aggregates; the master of that house is your fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
What wise person would delight in a conditioned house?"
Only the precious palace of the bliss of Bodhi is free from old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and affliction.

If there are sons of good family with sharp faculties and profound pure faith who wish to deliver their parents, wives, children, and kinsmen, leading them into the unconditioned nectar-abode, they must take refuge in the Triple Gem, leave the household life, and study the Path.
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke again in verse:
“The bodhisattva who has left the home life is superior to one who remains at home; no calculation, no fraction, nor any analogy can compare them.”
Living at home is as confining as a prison; seeking liberation from it is exceedingly difficult.
Leaving home is as vast and open as space; it is free, unconditioned, and detached from all bonds.
Contemplate with clarity that household life abounds in faults;
One commits boundless sinful karma, Seeking gain through livelihood, never satisfied, Just as the great ocean is difficult to fill.
From the four corners of Lake Anavatapta, the Dragon King and others cause the four great rivers to surge forth;
all the waters of the large, medium, and small rivers flow day and night without ceasing for even a moment,
yet that great ocean is never filled.
Living at home, one frequently gives rise to various evil karmas, Yet never washes them away through repentance to eliminate them;
In vain one knows how to cherish this fragile body, Failing to realize that life ends with the morning dew.
Urged on by the messengers of Yama, one can take nothing with them—not wife, nor children, nor home.
Into the long night of the dark and gloomy underworld, one goes alone to the gate of death to experience the fruits of one's karma.
The Buddhas appear in the world out of compassion, desiring to cause sentient beings to weary of the mundane world;
you have now obtained this body so difficult to find—therefore, you should apply yourself with diligent effort and never be negligent.
The household life and its dwellings are deeply loathsome; The precious abode of emptiness and stillness is inconceivable.
Forever free from the suffering of illness and the distress of grief, All those with wisdom observe this well.
In the future, those sons and daughters of good family with pure faith, who wish to deliver their parents and kinsmen,
leading them into the city of unconditioned nectar; who aspire to leave the household life to cultivate the wondrous Way,
gradually practicing until they achieve perfect enlightenment, shall turn the unsurpassed Great Dharma Wheel.
"Furthermore, noble son!
A renunciant bodhisattva contemplates worldly dwellings as being like sparks from a flint, giving rise to a profound sense of wearying aversion. Why is this?
Just as a tiny spark can burn all manner of grasses and trees, so too are the houses and dwellings of the world; likewise, the greedy mind runs hither and thither in its quest for things.
If one has something to gain, one’s enjoyment will be insufficient, and one will pursue it at all times without satiety;
if one has nothing to gain, the mind gives rise to feverish distress, and one pursues it day and night.
Therefore, all dwellings in the world can give rise to the fire of immeasurable afflictions, for they constantly incite greed and a lack of contentment.
Worldly wealth and treasures are like grass and wood, while the mind of greedy desire is like the worldly dwelling. For this reason, all Buddhas describe the three realms as a "burning house."
"Good son!
A renunciant bodhisattva who is able to perform this contemplation and feels weary of and detached from the world is called one who has truly renounced the world.
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke again in verse:
“The renunciant bodhisattva contemplates the worldly abode as being like a small fire in the human realm that gradually consumes all grasses and trees; know that the worldly abode is likewise.”
All the wealth and treasures possessed by sentient beings, though pursued one after another, are never sufficient;
the suffering of not finding what they seek constantly dwells in their hearts, and the fires of old age, sickness, and death are never extinguished.
For these reasons, the World-Honored Ones have described the three realms as a house on fire.
If you wish to transcend the suffering of the three realms, You should cultivate the holy life as a śramaṇa;
When samādhi and supernormal powers manifest before you, Your own benefit and the benefit of others will both be perfected.
"Furthermore, noble son,
one who delights in leaving the household life should contemplate their home as being like a great treasure trove within a mountain cave deep in the wilderness."
It is like a householder who has an only son; his family is immensely wealthy with immeasurable treasures and riches, and he possesses countless servants, attendants, elephants, and horses.
Later, the father suddenly contracts a grave illness that neither skilled physicians nor excellent medicines can cure.
Knowing that his death would soon be at hand, the elder summoned his son and addressed him, saying:
"All the wealth and treasures I possess are now entrusted to you; guard them diligently and ensure they do not diminish or go astray."
Having thus entrusted [his son] with these instructions, he passed away.

At that time, the elder’s son did not follow his father’s command; he indulged in dissipation until his family estate was ruined, his wealth and goods were lost, and his servants fled, leaving him with no one to rely upon.
At that time, the old woman’s heart was filled with grief and distress; she subsequently fell gravely ill and passed away.
Her son, impoverished and having no one to rely upon, went into the mountain valleys to gather firewood and collect fruits, selling them to provide for himself.

At that time, encountering snow, he entered a stone cave to rest for a while; however, this cave was a place where a former king had hidden the seven treasures, and no one knew of it, having been utterly devoid of human presence for several hundred thousand years.

At that time, due to the karmic conditions of his past deeds, that poor man happened to enter a cave and saw immeasurable gold. His heart was filled with great joy at this unprecedented occurrence; he then divided the gold into portions, using some to build a house, some as dowry for taking a wife, and likewise for servants and slaves, elephants and horses—everything according to his desires, exactly as he wished.

While he was making this plan, a band of thieves, having pursued a fleeing deer, arrived at the entrance of the cave; seeing this poor man distributing gold, they abandoned the deer, killed the man, and took the gold.

Ignorant worldlings are likewise thus: they are deeply attached to worldly pleasures and find no joy in renunciation. Deep mountains and stone caves are like their worldly dwellings; hidden treasures of gold and jewels are like their roots of goodness; the messengers of Yama are like a band of robbers. Following their karma, they receive retribution by falling into the three evil realms; failing to hear the names of their parents or the Triple Gem, they lose their roots of goodness. For these reasons, one should cultivate weary detachment, give rise to the unsurpassed mind of Great Bodhi, leave the household life to practice the Way, and aspire to achieve wondrous enlightenment.
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke again in verse:
“Bodhisattvas who delight in the household life Regard their homes as if they were treasuries of jewels.”

For example, a householder had an only son; his family was immensely wealthy, abounding in riches and treasures, with servants, attendants, elephants, and horses—there was nothing required that was not plentiful.
Later, when the elder fell ill, all the skilled physicians of the world stood by with hands folded.
As he approached his end, he addressed his kinsmen, entrusting his family wealth to his son;
he instructed him to maintain a heart of filial care and to diligently perform ancestral sacrifices without interruption.
At that time, the son disobeyed his father’s command; He indulged extensively in folly and was greatly heedless.
The old mother harbored grief and her body fell ill; Furthermore, because of her wicked son, she soon passed away.
Separated from his kin and having no one to rely upon, he made a habit of gathering firewood to sell for his livelihood.
Once, while traveling through the mountains, he encountered wind and snow; he entered a stone cave to rest for a short while.
Within this cave, wondrous treasures were hidden in the past, long forgotten and unknown to anyone;
now a woodcutter has encountered a treasury of pure gold, his heart leaping with joy at such a rare occurrence.
Immediately distributing the genuine gold and treasures, he used them all as he desired:
some to build houses, some for wives and wealth, and others for male and female servants, elephants, horses, and carriages.
Calculatedly considering the future, he was unable to relinquish it; then a band of thieves, following the deer's tracks, arrived before him.
When they encountered their enemy, they killed the poor man and took the gold away.
Ignorant sentient beings are just like this: the stone cave is like a worldly house, the hidden treasure of pure gold is like roots of goodness, and the minions of King Yama are like bandits.
For these reasons, O sons of the Buddha, hasten toward the life of renunciation and cultivate the factors of virtue.
One should contemplate that body and life are like floating bubbles; Diligently cultivate the perfections of ethical discipline and patience.

You shall go to the Bodhi tree of the seven treasures, And upon the adamantine seat realize Suchness— Eternally abiding, indestructible, and inconceivable— Turning the wheel of the True Dharma to transform all beings.
"Furthermore, good son!
All dwellings in the world are like sweet-tasting food mixed with poison.

It is like a householder who has an only son, who is intelligent, of keen faculties, and has mastered the secret gate of the Garuḍa’s contemplation; he is skilled in discerning poisonous drugs through his expedient means, and his parents love and cherish him beyond compare."
At that time, the elder’s son had gone to the marketplace on business and had not yet returned home.
Meanwhile, his parents and their kinsmen were feasting joyfully, having prepared a full array of sweet delicacies.
At that time, there was an enemy who secretly placed poison in the food and drink without anyone noticing it.
At that moment, the parents were unaware that the food contained mixed poisons, so they had both the elderly and the young consume the poisoned meal.
Later, when their son arrived, the parents were filled with joy and gave him the food and drink they had set aside for him.
At that time, before his son had yet required food or drink, he contemplated the secret meditative gate of the garuḍa and immediately knew that there was mixed poison within the meal.
Although the son knew his parents were consuming poison, he did not tell them that they had mistakenly taken the poisoned medicine.
Why is this? If he were to wake up and consume the poison, his distress would intensify further; the toxic vapors would manifest swiftly and surely cause his death.
He immediately devised a skillful means and said to his parents:
"I shall not eat such food for now; I will go briefly into the marketplace and return to eat.
Why is this? I previously purchased an invaluable jewel and left it inside a chest, forgetting to seal it shut."
Thereupon, having heard the account of the precious jewel, the parents felt great joy and allowed their son to go wherever he wished.
The son then hurried away to the house of a physician, seeking the wondrous *agada* medicine that neutralizes poison.

Having obtained this medicine, he ran home in haste; he combined the three ingredients of milk, ghee, and granulated sugar, boiling them together with *agada* to prepare the medicine. Having finished making it, he said to his parents:
"I pray only that my parents will take this nectar; this is the *agada* medicine from the Snowy Mountains."
Why is this? My parents have recently mistakenly taken poison;
my brief departure was originally for the sake of my parents and all these people, so that I might seek out such a wondrous medicine of immortality.

Thereupon, the parents and the multitude were filled with great joy at such an unprecedented occurrence; they immediately took the wondrous medicine, which expelled all the poisonous vapors, whereby they attained non-death and further extended their lifespans.

The renunciant bodhisattva is likewise in this regard: past parents have sunk into the cycle of birth and death; present parents cannot transcend it; future births and deaths are difficult to exhaust; and present afflictions are difficult to subdue and eliminate. For these reasons, in order to deliver their parents and all sentient beings, they rouse the great compassion of identical essence and seek great enlightenment by renouncing the world and entering the Path.
"Good son! This is called a house being like sweet food mixed with poisonous medicine.
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke again in verse:
"All the dwellings that exist in the world Are said to be like sweet foods mixed with poison.
Suppose there were an elder who had an only son, Intelligent, sharp-witted, and moreover highly talented;
Skilled in the secret methods of the *garuḍa*, He was able to discern poisons through clever expedients."
The son had business that led him to the marketplace; having engaged in trade for a short while, he had not yet returned home.
His parents were feasting and gathering their relatives, with every kind of delicacy and rare delicacy fully provided.
There was an evil person who, carrying a poisonous drug, secretly brought it to be placed in the food and drink.
At that time, his son was not at home; for the sake of their child, the parents set aside one portion, and the entire family mistakenly consumed the mixed poison.
The son, mindful of the gateway of contemplation and knowing there was poison, immediately fled to the physician’s abode. There he obtained the *gāthā* of the medicine of immortality;
having prepared the medicine by blending and boiling the three flavors, he then addressed his relatives, urging them to take it.
Thus, what they took was like nectar (*amṛta*), curing all various poisons and bringing them peace and happiness.
