All sons of noble family with faithful hearts who leave the home life to cultivate the Way do likewise;
for the sake of rescuing their parents and all sentient beings, they must overcome the various poisonous medicines of afflictions—
those deluded and inverted minds that commit all manner of transgressions and sink forever into the ocean of birth-and-death, sorrow, and lamentation.
Sacrificing what is dear and bidding farewell to kin, they enter the Buddha-way; Having approached the Great Physician, the Tamer of Men, They cultivate the untainted Agada medicine.

Returning to their parents within the dwelling of the triple world, They cause them to take the medicine of the Dharma to sever the three obstructions, So that they may realize the fruit of unsurpassed Bodhi.
Enduring until the end of the future, never ceasing, Able to deliver sentient beings as their refuge,
Ultimately abiding in Great Nirvāṇa, As well as the Buddha’s Bodhi and the Perfect Mirror Wisdom.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
A renunciant bodhisattva constantly contemplates all dwellings in the world as being like a great wind that cannot remain for even a moment."
Why is this? Good son!

The mind of one living at home constantly gives rise to false conceptions; clinging to external objects, it cannot realize the truth. Intoxicated by the darkness of ignorance, it encounters objects in a state of perversion, never remaining stable. Evil thoughts arise easily, while a virtuous mind is difficult to produce.

Due to the arising of various afflictions through false conceptualization, one creates wholesome and unwholesome karma on account of those afflictions; based on such wholesome and unwholesome karma, the fruits of the five destinies are experienced, and in this manner, birth and death continue without interruption.

Only by possessing right view and an undistorted mind, performing various wholesome deeds, and through the three roots of goodness as well as faith and so forth, does one increase the naturally existing seeds of untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharmatā-bīja*), thereby being able to give rise to untainted samādhis and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
"In this way, as one realizes the continuity of the noble state, if one subdues deluded thoughts and cultivates right contemplation, all afflictions will be forever exhausted without remainder.
At that time, the elder Jñānaprabha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"There are immeasurable gateways for the cultivation of right contemplation; what kind of contemplation must one cultivate to be able to subdue deluded thoughts?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the elder, saying: "Good son!
One should cultivate the correct contemplation of signlessness (*animitta-samyak-darśana*).
This contemplation of signlessness can subdue deluded thoughts; by contemplating only the true nature (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*), one does not perceive the ten signs.
The essence of all phenomena is fundamentally empty and quiescent; to be without seeing and without knowing is called correct contemplation.

If there is a son of the Buddha who dwells securely in right mindfulness and observes in this way, practicing for a long time the signless and the unconditioned, the fierce winds of conceptual construction will become still and motionless; through the direct realization of noble wisdom, he will realize the perfection of the principle.
Good son! These are called the worthy sages; these are called Bodhisattvas; these are called the Tathāgata’s Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

For this reason, all Bodhisattvas, in order to subdue delusive thoughts so that they never arise again, and to repay the four debts of gratitude and accomplish the four virtues, leave the household life to practice and study, quelling the mind of delusive thoughts, and through immeasurable kalpas, achieve the Buddha-way.
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke again in verse:
“The renunciant bodhisattva observes the householder As being like a violent wind that does not stay for a moment,
And like the deluded grasping at the moon in water, Discriminating and calculating it to be real.”
In water there is originally no moon-reflection; Due to the condition of clear water, one sees the original moon.
All phenomena born of conditions are merely provisional; Fools and the ignorant falsely reckon them as a self.
These very phenomena arising from conditions are not real; they are falsely conceptualized and imagined to exist through discursive thought.
If one can sever these two types of grasping, one shall realize the unsurpassed, great Bodhi.
Ordinary sentiments and deluded thoughts are like a black wind, blowing through the forest of birth and death, arising moment by moment;
the demons of the four inversions constantly pursue one, causing the creation of the five kinds of causes for the uninterrupted hells,
while the three unwholesome roots manifest as entanglements, so that the cycle of birth and death continues perpetually.
If a person hears this sutra with deep faith and understanding, right view can eliminate their inverted mind;
the seeds of bodhi will arise in every thought-moment, giving rise to great wisdom, supernormal powers, and samādhis.
If one can cultivate profound and wondrous contemplation, The fruits of afflictions, karma, and suffering have no cause to arise;
By contemplating only the true nature of reality as it is, Subject and object both vanish, and all views are transcended.
The male and female characteristics are originally empty; Through deluded attachment, they arise according to conditions as two forms.
The Tathāgata has forever severed the causes of delusive thought; In true nature, there are fundamentally no male or female characteristics.
The realization of the wondrous fruit of Bodhi is identical for all; it is only through false conceptualization that ordinary beings perceive divergent signs.
The thirty-two marks are fundamentally not marks; to understand that marks are non-marks is the true mark.

If a person leaves the household life to cultivate the holy life, Withdrawing the mind to dwell in tranquility within a secluded place, This is the truly pure mind of a bodhisattva; Before long, they shall realize the fruit of enlightenment.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
A renunciant bodhisattva constantly observes the dwellings of the world day and night, seeing that they are all places where afflictions arise."
Why is this? Suppose there were a person who built eight houses and adorned them with various precious objects.
Having completed these houses, he had this thought:
"This house is now my own possession and does not belong to others; my house alone is the most auspicious, surpassing what can be found in the houses of others."

"Such attachments give rise to afflictions; with afflictions as the root, the grasping at 'I' and 'mine' emerges, and eighty-four thousand gates of defilement arise in mutual competition, filling the house."

Why is this so? Because ordinary worldlings living at home are deeply attached to the five desires; they possess wives, children, kinsmen, slaves, and servants in full measure. Due to these causes and conditions, birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction; the meeting with the hated and the separation from the beloved; poverty and various misfortunes; and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks—these manifold sufferings follow them like a shadow follows a form or an echo responds to a sound, continuing from lifetime to lifetime without ever ceasing.
Thus, these manifold sufferings do not arise without cause; the various afflictions constitute their root.
All wealth and treasures are obtained through pursuit; yet if there were no prior causes, they could not be pursued, and even if one were to pursue them, nothing would be gained.
"Good son!
For this reason, all afflictions have seeking as their root; if one extinguishes seeking, immeasurable afflictions will all be completely severed."

However, this present body is the locus of manifold sufferings; therefore, those who possess wisdom should give rise to weary detachment. As the Tathāgata Kāśyapa did for various birds and beasts in a past age, he spoke this verse:
"This body is the root of suffering, And other sufferings are its branches and leaves.
If one can sever the root of suffering, All manifold sufferings will be eliminated."
Due to the karma of your past lives, you committed offenses without remorse;
consequently, you have obtained these unlovely bodies of various species that undergo suffering.
If you give rise to a heart of earnest devotion and seek repentance for even a single thought-moment, [you shall be liberated].
Just as fire consumes mountains and marshes, all transgressions are utterly extinguished.
This body is suffering and impure; it is without self and impermanent.
You all should, therefore, give rise to a profound sense of weary detachment.

"At that time, immeasurable birds and beasts, having heard these verses, repented with utmost sincerity in a single thought-moment. They immediately abandoned the evil realms and were reborn in the Fourth Dhyāna Heaven, where they paid homage to a Bodhisattva in his last birth before Buddhahood, heard the Dharma of non-retrogression, and attained ultimate Nirvāṇa."
"Good son!
For these reasons, this present body of suffering is like a house, and all afflictions are the masters of that house.

Therefore, good sons of pure faith who resolve to attain bodhicitta, leave the home life, and enter the Way will certainly achieve liberation from all sufferings and shall all realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke again in verse:
“The renunciant bodhisattva constantly observes That the household life gives rise to all manner of afflictions.”
Suppose there is a person who builds a dwelling, adorning it with various kinds of rare jewels;
he thinks to himself that its magnificence is beyond compare, belonging to no one else but himself alone,
crafted with such supreme skill that no dwelling in the world can equal it.
Thus, through such discrimination, attachment arises;
with "self" and "what belongs to self" as its root, the eighty-four thousand afflictions fill one's dwelling and become a calamity.
All men and women in the world, with their six kinds of kinsmen and relatives complete,
give rise to manifold sufferings through these very causes and conditions— namely, birth, old age, sickness, and death. Sorrow, lamentation, pain,
and affliction constantly pursue them, never departing for even a moment, just as a shadow follows a form.
All sufferings arise from craving; if one cuts off seeking, all sufferings will end.
This body is the root of all suffering; diligently cultivate detachment and proceed toward Bodhi.
The body and mind within the three realms are like a house, And the afflictions dwell therein as its master.
You all should give rise to the bodhicitta, Abandoning the state of ordinary beings to transcend the three realms.
"Furthermore, good son!

A renunciant bodhisattva constantly observes those in the household life as being like an elder in a great kingdom who possesses immeasurable wealth and treasures; for many kalpas, the ancestral lineage of father and son has been passed down without interruption, and through the cultivation of various virtuous deeds, his fame has spread far and wide."
All the wealth and treasures possessed by this great elder are divided into four parts:
one portion of his wealth is constantly sought for interest and profit to support his household affairs;
another portion of his wealth is used to provide daily necessities as required.
One portion of his wealth and treasures he bestowed as alms upon the solitary and the destitute to cultivate merit for the future;
one portion of his wealth and treasures he used to rescue and sustain his kinsmen and traveling guests.
Thus these four parts were never interrupted, being inherited from father to son as a family tradition.

Later, he had a son who was foolish and wicked, deeply attached to the five desires and indulging in unrestrained dissipation. He disobeyed his parents' instructions and did not follow the four proper occupations. He constructed various residences and seven-story towers that exceeded ordinary regulations and were adorned with every kind of jewel; the floors were made of lapis lazuli, with precious windows reflecting one another, complete with dragon-heads and fish-shaped ornaments. Sublime music played incessantly day and night, and he enjoyed the pleasures of the five desires like those in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Consequently, ghosts and spirits detested him, while humans and devas shunned him from afar.
Thereupon, a fire suddenly broke out in the neighboring house; its fierce flames blazed intensely, spreading with the wind and consuming the storehouses as well as the various pavilions and towers.

At that time, the elder’s son, seeing this raging fire, gave rise to a heart of great anger and quickly ordered his wife, children, servants, and kinsmen to enter the inner chambers and close the doors of the pavilions; due to their ignorance, they all died together at once.

It is the same for ordinary worldlings living at home: the foolish people of the world are like the sons of the elder, while the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are like the elder; by failing to follow the Buddha’s teachings and instead committing evil deeds, they fall into the three evil realms and undergo great suffering and distress.
For this reason, a renunciant bodhisattva should regard the householder as being like the son of an elder who, by disobeying his parents, was consumed by fire along with his wife and children.
"Sons of good family!
You should give rise to weary detachment from the worldly pleasures of humans and devas; cultivate pure conduct and you shall realize Bodhi.
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke again in verse:
“The renunciant bodhisattva views the householder as a wealthy elder who has fathered a foolish son.
Though his house is rich with various treasures, inherited for a long time without deficiency,
and the ancestral estate passed down from generation to generation, all his assets are divided into four parts.”
Constantly cultivating supreme practices free from fault or evil, His fame pervades all lands;
Gold, silver, and rare treasures are boundless in number, And his profits from trade extend to foreign countries.
With a heart of loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity, never wearying, He bestows gifts upon the orphaned and the poor without ever ceasing.
The elder finally fathered a son who was foolish, unfilial, and lacked wisdom;
though his years had advanced and his physical strength had declined, he entrusted all the family wealth, both internal and external, to this son.
The son disobeyed his father’s command and acted with heedlessness; failing to carry on the fourfold lineage, he brought ruin upon the family.
He constructed a seven-storied tower of precious jewels, with windows and casements made of deep-blue lapis lazuli;
the sounds of singing and stringed instruments never ceased, for he constantly took what is unwholesome as his teacher within his heart.
Enjoying the pleasures of the five desires as if in a celestial palace, all the nāgas and spirits have fled far away.
Suddenly, a calamitous fire breaks out in the neighboring house; its fierce flames, driven by the wind, are difficult to restrain.
The treasures and wealth in the storehouses, as well as wife and children, and the multi-storied towers and dwellings, are all consumed by the flames.
Accumulating evil invites calamity until the body is destroyed; wife, children, and kinsmen perish along with them.
The Buddhas of the three ages are like the elder, while all ordinary beings are like foolish sons;
failing to cultivate the Right Path and giving rise to deviant thoughts, they fall into the various evil realms at the end of their lives.
For long eons you shall alone endure the suffering of being burned, continuing thus in succession without end.
O sons of the Buddha dwelling at home, you should know this: do not crave worldly pleasures, but diligently practice for realization;
weary of the world, leave the household life to cultivate pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) in the tranquility of mountain forests, free from all external conditions.
To repay the four debts of gratitude, cultivate supreme virtue; You shall become a Dharma King within the triple world.
Throughout the limits of the future, deliver all sentient beings; Act as an uninvited friend, constantly preaching the Dharma.
Forever sever the flow of craving and transcend to the other shore, Dwelling in the city of pure nirvana.
"Furthermore, good son!
A renunciant bodhisattva contemplates all dwellings in the world as being like a great dream.
For example, suppose there were an elder who had a young daughter, fifteen years of age, beautiful and exquisite."

At that time, the parents were on a three-storied terrace, enjoying various pleasures with their beloved daughter; during the middle of the night, mother and daughter lay together, sleeping peacefully upon a single jeweled bed.

Thereupon, the young girl saw in a dream that her parents betrothed her to a husband’s family, and after many years had passed, she gave birth to a son who was handsome and extraordinary, possessing the marks of wisdom. As he grew day by day under their loving care, he was able to walk about himself; while standing upon a high tower, he fell because of its precariousness, yet before reaching the ground, he saw a starving tiger catch him and devour him.
At that time, the young girl was doubly terrified; she raised her voice and wailed, whereupon she suddenly awoke from her dream.
Then her parents asked their daughter, "By what cause and condition have you suddenly become so terrified?"
At that time, the girl was ashamed and refused to speak of it.
Her mother, with persistent earnestness, secretly questioned her about the reason.
Then, the girl privately told her mother the details of what she had dreamed as described above.
"Good son!

The conditioned dwelling of birth and death in the world is a place where one dwells long within saṃsāra without yet attaining true awakening; throughout all such stages, one constantly remains in a dream within the dwelling of the three realms of birth, old age, sickness, and death."
Just as that young girl was in her dream, so too is false conceptualization.
The messengers of the Lord of Death suddenly arrive, like a starving tiger seizing an infant from the midst of the sky and devouring it.
All sentient beings likewise experience the suffering of impermanence, aging, illness, and death in every thought-moment.
What wise person would cherish such a body?

For this reason, one should contemplate birth and death as a long night within a dream, resolve to attain Bodhicitta, and cultivate weary detachment from the world, so as to eventually realize the Tathāgata’s wondrous fruit of eternal abiding.
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke again in verse:
“O Son of the Buddha, seeking the unsurpassed path, You should regard your home as being like a dream.”
For example, there was a wealthy and noble elder who had a young daughter of exquisite beauty;
following her parents up to a high tower, she gazed upon the processions and enjoyed herself with great delight.
The woman had such a dream while in her chamber; clearly she dreamed that she had recently taken another as her husband.
Later, she gave birth to a son at her husband’s house, and his mother loved him with a heart full of compassion.
The son ascended the pavilion, indulging in joy and pleasure; Due to the peril, he fell into the jaws of a tiger.
Thereupon, losing his voice, he awoke from the dream; Only then did he realize that the dream-visions were fundamentally not real.
The obscuration of the darkness of ignorance is like a long night; before attaining perfect enlightenment, one is as if in a dream.
The world of birth and death is eternally unreal, and deluded conceptualization is likewise so.
Only the four wisdoms of great perfect luminosity can shatter this darkness and are thus called true, wondrous enlightenment.
Impermanence strikes moment by moment like a starving tiger; conditioned things are false and cannot endure long.
As birds nesting overnight fly apart at dawn, so too is our parting when life ends.
Coming and going, dwelling in karma and receiving its various retributions, we fail to recognize the kindness of our parents.
Alas! The ordinary person’s body of birth and death Revolves through the three miserable realms, suffering long.
If one knows that good and evil follow the retribution of karma, One should perform repentance so that they may be extinguished.
All the wondrous fruits of happiness for humans and devas have shame, remorse, and right view as their cause;
one should resolve upon the firm bodhicitta and don the armor of diligence to practice with vigor.
"Furthermore, good son!

A renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his house as being like the Mare’s Mouth Ocean, which emits fierce flames that swallow up the four great rivers; there are no streams from the hundred rivers that are not completely consumed by the fire.
For example, in the past, in the kingdom of Rādha, there was a bodhisattva named Suvratottīrṇa; this bodhisattva possessed a heart of compassion and constantly harbored the intent to benefit others.

There were merchants who went to sea to gather treasures; they took this Bodhisattva aboard their ship, and all reached the island of jewels, crossing over dangers and difficulties without hindrance, arriving at the further shore.
Later, as the Bodhisattva grew old and his years advanced until he was already a hundred years of age, he could no longer move forward when rising from a seat without the support of a staff.
A merchant leader came to the Bodhisattva’s dwelling to pay homage and make offerings, and addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"I wish to enter the sea to seek various precious gems, so that I may forever leave poverty behind and attain great wealth and nobility."
"I now request that you, O Bodhisattva, go with me.
At that time, the Bodhisattva said to the merchant leader, "I am now old and infirm;
my strength and vigor are diminished, and I cannot enter the sea."
The merchant leader spoke again:
"I pray only that you, Great Being, will not abandon your compassion but graciously accept my invitation; that you simply sit at ease within my ship is my heart's desire."
At that time, the Bodhisattva accepted the merchants' invitation and boarded a great ship to enter the vast ocean, heading toward the southeast to reach the place of jewels.

There he encountered a north wind that drove them adrift into the southern sea; the fierce winds blew so swiftly, ceasing neither by day nor night, for seven days. Then he saw the waters of the great ocean turn golden, like molten gold.
At that time, the merchants addressed the Bodhisattva, saying:
"By what causes and conditions has the water turned golden, manifesting such a sign?
The Bodhisattva replied:

"You should know this: I have now entered the great ocean of yellow gold. It is filled with immeasurable and boundless *cāmpeya* gold, and the intermingling radiance of these precious metals manifests such a phenomenon."
"Having strayed from the right path and fallen into this sea, each of you must diligently seek out various expedient means to return to the north.
After several more days had passed, they saw that the waters of the great ocean had turned white, like jade or snow. The Bodhisattva said to them:
"You should know that I have now entered the Great Sea of Pearls; white jade and pearls fill the sea, and the reflection of the jewels in the water produces such an appearance."
"You should exert all your strength and employ every skillful means to return to the north.
After several more days had passed, the waters of the great ocean turned the color of blue lapis lazuli. The Bodhisattva said:
"I and you have already entered the sea of blue crystal; immeasurable and boundless blue crystal jewels fill the great ocean, their crystalline colors reflecting one another in this manner."
After several more days had passed, the waters of the great ocean turned red, appearing like blood. The Bodhisattva said:
"I and you all have now entered the Sea of Red Beryl; immeasurable and boundless red beryl jewels fill the great ocean, their true color a deep crimson, reflecting one another in this manner."

After several more days had passed, the water turned black like ink. From afar, they heard the sound of fierce explosions, like a great fire burning a dry bamboo grove; the blazing smoke and flames were most terrifying, a sight such as this never having been seen or heard before.

Furthermore, I saw a great fire arise from the south, resembling a cluster of peaks rising over a hundred *zhang* in height; its flames surged into the air, sometimes merging and sometimes dispersing, with streaks of light flashing like lightning—such a phenomenon as this had never before been seen or heard of.
"Indeed, our own lives and bodies are difficult to preserve.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva addressed the multitude, saying:
"You all are now in a state of great terror."

Why is this? We have already entered the Sea of the Mare’s Mouth; all the four great oceans and the various large and small streams of the four continents that enter the Northern Mouth of the sea are completely consumed by fire.
Why is this so? It is due to the sovereign power of the karma of sentient beings that the natural fires of heaven are able to burn the waters of the ocean.
If these heavenly fires did not burn the ocean waters, within a single day and night all the dry land would turn into a great sea, and all sentient beings would be swept away and drowned.
"But now we have encountered a great black wind and are being swept away by this Mare’s Mouth Sea; the remaining lives of us all are but few.
At that time, more than a thousand people on the ship simultaneously raised their voices in lamentation and weeping; some tore out their own hair, while others threw themselves down, saying:
"We have entered the great ocean seeking precious treasures, yet we have met with this perilous calamity! Alas, what suffering! Alas, what misery!"
"By what skillful means can we escape this calamity?

At that time, the thousand men took refuge with utmost sincerity; some invoked the Compassionate Mother, some the Benevolent Father, some Brahmā, some the Heavenly King Maheśvara, and some the Greatly Powerful Nārāyaṇa. Others took refuge in the Bodhisattva Pāragata and paid homage to the Mahāsattva, saying:
"We pray only that the Bodhisattva will deliver us."
At that time, the Bodhisattva, in order to free these people from all fear, spoke these verses:
“The Great Man, supreme in the world, Though entering the gateway of death, feels no dread.”
If you lose wisdom through grief and sorrow, you should single-mindedly employ skillful means;
if you attain the gateway of skillful means, you will leave behind the eight difficulties and transcend to the other shore.
"Therefore, set your mind at ease and do not fear; you should earnestly contemplate the Great Compassionate Honored One.
Having spoken this verse, the Bodhisattva burned various famous incenses and paid homage to and made offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions, making this vow:

"Namo to the Buddhas of the ten directions! Namo to the Buddhas of the ten directions! To the assembly of all great Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, the four stages and four fruits of all worthy sages, those with the divine eye, those with the divine ear, those who know the minds of others, and those with mastery over the multitudes: for the sake of sentient beings, I mobilize the heart of great compassion, relinquishing my body and life to rescue them from all suffering and hardship."
"However, my present body possesses one root of goodness: I have upheld the Tathāgata’s precept against false speech, never failing or violating it throughout immeasurable lifetimes.
If I had uttered a single falsehood in even one lifetime, this evil wind would have intensified further;
since the virtue of such a precept is not in vain, I pray that by dedicating this merit to all beings, I and all sentient beings shall attain the Buddha-way."

If this is true and not false, may these evil winds subside immediately, and may favorable winds arrive according to my wish and thought; for all sentient beings are my own body, and there is no distinction between sentient beings and myself.

Once this Great Bodhisattva had thus aroused such a vow of non-obstructed great compassion based on the identity of self and others, within the space of a single thought-moment the adverse winds ceased; he immediately obtained a favorable wind, was liberated from all perils, reached the place of treasures, and acquired all manner of precious jewels.
At that time, the Bodhisattva said to the merchants:

"Such rare treasures are difficult to encounter and difficult to find. It is because you practiced the giving of alms extensively in previous lives that you have encountered these various wonderful treasures; yet, because your hearts were stingy at the time you formerly practiced giving, due to these causes and conditions, you have met with this malignant wind."
"You merchants must know the limit of the precious treasures you have obtained and not take too much, lest you indulge your greed and subsequently invite great calamity.
You should all know that among all treasures, the treasure of life is supreme; if one preserves their life, it is a treasure beyond price."
At that time, the merchants, having received the Bodhisattva’s instruction, gave rise to a mind of contentment and did not dare to take much.
Thereupon, the multitude escaped the calamity and obtained great treasures; they were distanced from poverty and reached the other shore.
“O sons of good family!

It is the same for a bodhisattva who has left the household life: by drawing near to the Buddhas and virtuous spiritual friends, they are like that merchant who, having encountered a bodhisattva, forever leaves birth and death behind to reach the other shore, just as a merchant leader attains great wealth and nobility.”
All conditioned dwellings in the world are like the Mare’s Mouth Ocean, which can consume all flowing waters.
So too it is with the renunciant bodhisattva, who carefully and discerningly observes the faults of the household life.

"You, son of good family, are unstained by the various pleasures of the five worldly desires; having grown weary of and renounced the suffering and hardship of birth and death within the triple world, you have entered the great city of cool serenity and peace."
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke again in verse:
“The renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his home As a mare at sea consumes all the flowing waters.”

For example, in the past, in the kingdom of Rādha, there was a bodhisattva named Prāptatīra (Attainer-of-the-Shore), who possessed great merit, wisdom, and skillful means. With unconditional compassion, he gathered in sentient beings;
having boarded a ship with this bodhisattva, the merchants obtained treasures and crossed to the other shore.
However, this Great Being was advanced in years and, taking no pleasure in benefiting others, was fond of meditative stillness.
A merchant leader invited the Bodhisattva, saying: "I wish to enter the great ocean to seek precious gems;
I pray only that the Great Being accept my invitation and cause me to be wealthy and free from want."
Thereupon the Bodhisattva, moved by great compassion, accepted the invitation and boarded a ship.
As they raised the great sails and encountered a favorable wind, they headed straight toward the southeast for the place of treasures.
Suddenly, a violent storm blew the ship, causing it to drift and fall into the South Sea, losing its way.
After seven days, the waters of the great ocean all turned into a golden hue;
the sea was filled with purple-golden sand, and the radiance of the jewels reflected a true golden color.
After several more days had passed, the waters of the great ocean turned white like jade or snow;
pearls and precious jewels filled the sea, which was why the seawater became white.
Furthermore, after several days, the waters of the great ocean transformed, becoming a deep azure like lapis lazuli;
blue beryl beads filled the great sea, which was why the water took on that deep azure hue.
Furthermore, after several days, the waters of the great ocean all turned into a deep crimson;
red crystal beads filled the sea, and thus the color of the water changed to match them.
After several more days, the waters of the great ocean turned black like ink;
thus, scorched by the celestial fire, the seawater became entirely the color of ink.
This sea is named Mare’s Mouth; it swallows the four oceans and all their tributary streams.
Whenever any ship passes through it, most people who reach this place perish.
The celestial fire blazed as intensely as a mountain of piled wood; its crackling sound was like the roar of thunder.

Seeing it from afar, the multitude were struck with terror and cried out, beating their breasts, as they addressed the Great Master: [They cried out, beating their breasts, and spoke to the Great Master.]
Thereupon the Bodhisattva gave rise to compassion; Not sparing his own body or life, he extended protection.
The violent winds soon ceased and favorable winds arose; They crossed over the perilous difficulties and reached the place of treasure.
Each obtained rare and precious jewels and reached the other shore, Forever leaving poverty behind to enjoy peace and happiness.
The renunciant bodhisattva is likewise: approaching the Buddhas like a caravan leader, forever leaving the burning house for true awakening, just as a merchant returns to his original home.
All the dwellings in the world are like the Mare’s Mouth Ocean;
those who have left the household life constantly weary of the household life, remaining unstained by the world and detached from the five desires.
Delighting in dwelling in seclusion with an unmoving mind, they have thoroughly mastered the profound, true, and wondrous principle;
whether staying amidst human villages and settlements, they are like bees gathering nectar from flowers without causing them harm.
Constantly benefiting sentient beings throughout the four modes of conduct, Without craving worldly pleasures or fame,
Always uttering gentle sounds from the mouth, Severing the continuity of coarse and vulgar speech;
Recognizing kindness and repaying it by cultivating wholesome deeds, So that both self and others may enter the true and eternal.
At that time, Jñānaprabha and ten thousand elders together addressed the Buddha with one voice, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!”
How rare, Sugata! It is so, it is so.
What the World-Honored One has spoken is most subtle and supreme, employing skillful means to benefit sentient beings.

As the Buddha has taught, I now fully understand that the dwellings of this world are like prisons; all unwholesome dharmas arise from such dwellings, whereas for those who have gone forth, there are truly immeasurable and boundless benefits.
"Therefore, we deeply delight in leaving the household life, so that in the present and the future we may constantly experience the joy of the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the elders:
"Excellent, excellent!"

You have resolved your minds with the aspiration to leave the household life. If a son of good family or a daughter of good family resolves their mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and leaves the household life to practice the Way for even one day and one night, they shall not fall into the evil realms for two million *kalpas*. They will always be born in favorable places and experience supreme, wondrous bliss; they will encounter spiritual friends and never regress, meet all Buddhas and receive the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), and sit upon the Vajra Seat to realize the path of perfect awakening.
"However, for one who has left the household life, maintaining the precepts is most difficult; those who can maintain the precepts are truly renunciants.
At that time, the elders addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

We uphold the precepts and cultivate all pure conducts; may we swiftly emerge from the ocean of suffering of birth and death; may we swiftly enter the precious palace of eternal bliss; may we extensively deliver all sentient beings; and may we quickly realize the wisdom of non-arising.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva and Mañjuśrī:
“In this manner, the elder entrusts you both; he exhorts you to cause him to leave the household life and receive and uphold the pure precepts.”
At that time, nine thousand people went forth from the household life before Maitreya to practice the Way and receive and uphold the Buddha’s precepts.
Seven thousand people together went forth from the household life before Mañjuśrī to practice the Way and receive the Buddha’s prohibitory precepts.
When such people as these have left the household life, they achieve the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*) and enter the secret realm of the Tathāgata, never again to regress.

Myriads of beings resolve upon Bodhicitta and reach the stage of non-retrogression; countless humans and devas become free from dust and defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye (*dharmanetra-viśuddhi*).
The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground in the Past Lives of the Buddha, Volume Four;
The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground in the Past Lives of the Buddha, Volume Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā of Kapiśī during the Great Tang Dynasty, by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Four: On Stainless Nature At that time, after Jñānaprabha and the other elders had gone forth into homelessness, they adjusted their Dharma robes, touched their five limbs to the ground, prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

"Having heard from the Buddha what we had never heard before regarding the various faults inherent in the household life, we have resolved to attain bodhicitta, become weary of and detached from the world, and have shaved our hair and beards to become bhikṣus."

We only pray that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha will, for our sake and for the sake of all sentient beings, expound upon the supreme merits of leaving the household life, so that those who hear it may give rise to a pure mind, delight in the practice of seclusion, and ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is never interrupted.
The World-Honored One’s great kindness and unconditioned compassion regard all sentient beings with pity as if they were Rāhula.
How should a renunciant bodhisattva abide?
How should they cultivate stainless karma?
"How does one subdue the mind that is subject to outflows?
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the bhikṣus such as Jñānaprabha:
"Excellent, excellent!"
You are a true son of the Buddha, for you are able to ask the Tathāgata about such a great matter for the sake of all sentient beings in the future.

It is so, it is so, just as you have said; the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for sentient beings, regards them with impartiality and without distinction, as if they were his only child.

Listen attentively now, and reflect upon it well; I shall analyze and expound for you how a bodhisattva who has gone forth should abide, how they should practice such stainless deeds, and how they should discipline the mind subject to outflows.
“Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣu Jñānaprabha:
“A renunciant bodhisattva, dwelling with such a mind, constantly reflects:
‘I have obtained a human body with all faculties complete; from where did I pass away to come to be born here?’”
Within the three realms, in which realm shall I be born?
Among the four great continents, in which place shall I be born?
Within the six destinies, in which destiny shall I receive birth?

By what causes and conditions can one leave behind parents, wife, children, and kinsmen to renounce the world and practice the Way, thereby escaping the bodies of those in the eight difficult circumstances?

Among the past thousand Buddhas of the *Ratnasaṃbhava* (Adorned) Kalpa, all have already entered *parinirvāṇa*. Among the future thousand Buddhas of the *Tārakopama* (Star-like) Kalpa, none have yet appeared in the world. As for the thousand Buddhas of the present *Bhadrakalpa* (Auspicious) Kalpa, how many Tathāgatas have appeared in the world, and whose work of transformation is now nearing its end as they enter *parinirvāṇa*?
How many Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, have not yet appeared in the world?

For these sentient beings, whose faculties and conditions have not yet matured and who have not heard the True Dharma, when will Maitreya come again, descending from Tuṣita Heaven to be born among humans and manifest the realization of the Buddha-way?
"What wholesome karma exists within my body?
What merit shall there be from the training in morality, concentration, and wisdom?
I have not encountered any of the Buddhas of the past; shall I be able to see the World-Honored One of the future?"
I am currently at the stage of an ordinary person; among the afflictions of my three karmas, which is the most heavy?
What sinful karma have I committed since birth?
Under which Buddha have I ever planted roots of goodness?
How long can this life and body of mine endure?

This day has already passed, and my life diminishes accordingly, just like a sheep being led to the slaughterhouse; gradually approaching death with no way to escape, where will I be reborn when this body perishes and my life ends?
How can one escape the sufferings of the three evil realms?
Yet this body of mine is cherished and nurtured with affection, yet it grows old moment by moment without a single pause; what wise person would cherish such a body?

Jñānaprabha, you should know! A renunciant bodhisattva constantly observes in this way throughout day and night: do not crave the worldly enjoyment of the five desires; practice with diligent effort without ever ceasing for a moment, as if removing a stone from atop one's head or extinguishing a fire on one's own hair. With a mind that constantly repents past transgressions, abide in these four kinds of stainless nature and single-mindedly practice the twelve dhūtas, subduing the mind like a caṇḍāla. Such a son of the Buddha is called a renunciant.
“Bhikṣu Jñānaprabha!
For what reason is it said that one who truly practices the conduct of a śramaṇa is like a caṇḍāla?

Whenever that caṇḍāla travels, he holds a mendicant’s staff (khakkhara) in his hand and does not dare to take the road; if someone approaches him closely, he rattles the staff so that they may hear it.”

In the midst of the great assembly, he conducts himself with humility and does not dare to be arrogant; when rebuked, his heart harbors no resentment and he never retaliates; he silently endures insults, abuse, and the lash.

Why is this? Because he knows his own inferior nature does not rank among the multitudes; for these reasons, he is without anger and without retaliation. Jñānaprabha, you should know that the renunciant bodhisattva is likewise:

having shaved off beard and hair, his appearance is like that of an infant; holding an alms-bowl, he depends on others for his livelihood; wearing the *kāṣāya* robe, it is as if he were clad in armor; walking with a mendicant’s staff, it is as if he were bearing a spear or lance; wielding the sword of wisdom, he destroys the thieves of affliction; and practicing the conduct of an infant, he benefits all beings.
Therefore, the sharp arrows of all three poisons do not penetrate the body of a true śramaṇa.
An ordained bodhisattva who cultivates the practice of patience through the gate of the three contemplations is called a true renunciant.
One contemplates all sentient beings as emanations of the Buddha, while contemplating oneself as a truly deluded person;
one contemplates all sentient beings with the thought of them being honorable and noble, while contemplating oneself with the thought of being a servant;
furthermore, one contemplates sentient beings as one's parents, while contemplating one's own body as their son or daughter.
A renunciant bodhisattva constantly maintains this contemplation: even when beaten or reviled, they never retaliate, skillfully employing expedient means to subdue their own mind.
"O Bhikṣu Jñānaprabha!
Listen attentively!
What are called the four types of stainless nature?

Regarding these four things—robes, bedding, food and drink, and medicinal decoations—to obtain whatever is available, whether coarse or fine, according to one's needs, and to remain free from greedy seeking: this is the stainless nature.
"O Bhikṣus! For what reason are these four practices called the 'Stainless Natures' (vimaladhātu)?

Jñānaprabha, you should know that from these arise all the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) of the Buddhas, Tathāgatas; thus the Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha are never interrupted. For this reason, they are named the Four Stainless Natures."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Bhikṣu Jñānaprabha, listen attentively! This is what a renunciant bodhisattva should do:
To embrace sentient beings with unconditional great compassion, Regarding them all as equal, like an only child.”
Having resolved to attain Bodhicitta and seek perfect enlightenment, one should practice the three kinds of dharmas for accomplishing Buddhahood:
the mind should always abide in the four stainless natures, one should cultivate the twelve dhūta practices,
and one’s heart should be humble like that of a caṇḍāla.
While engaged in the four modes of conduct, one should reflect thus:
"Countless Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions Advance toward the noble path moment by moment;
Since they have already practiced and realized it, so shall I. How could I continue to wander within the three realms?"
Constantly dwelling amidst the immeasurable sufferings of birth and death, in what realm does this body of mine now abide?
In which path of the six realms of saṃsāra do I dwell?
Through which mode of birth—womb, egg, moisture, or transformation—do I take rebirth?
In what should the actions of body, speech, and mind be cultivated?
Among the transgressions committed, which is the most grave?
Among the three natures of the mind, which is most prevalent?
Great compassion and great kindness flow in constant succession;
with great joy and great equanimity as the primary mind, he proclaims the wondrous Dharma for those with whom he has a karmic connection, cultivating his mind day and night without a moment’s pause.
Like one removing a stone from the crown of the head or extinguishing a fire on the head, one should never be apart from the three gates of contemplation:
Contemplating that all sentient beings are the Buddha-body, while I alone dwell among the ranks of ordinary beings;
That all sentient beings are equally noble and honorable, while I am a servant dwelling in lowliness.
All sentient beings of the world are my parents; I treat them as sons and daughters practicing filial piety.
When struck or reviled by others, I do not feel anger or resentment; I diligently cultivate patience, free from enmity and jealousy.
The mind does not cling even when making offerings through the four requisites; this is what is called the stainless nature (*vimala-dhātu*).

The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) and the Tathāgata’s body of retribution (*vipākakāya*)—such supreme, untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas as these have the four stainless natures as their foundation.
Those who constantly cultivate the practice of heedfulness are called true children of the Buddha who have left the home life;
the seeds of bodhi-wisdom increase moment by moment, and they fully accomplish the untainted noble path.
They swiftly transcend immeasurable kalpas and sit upright within the Flower King Dharma-realm.
The two adornments of merit and wisdom are both perfected; Throughout oceans of boundless eons, they benefit all living beings.
Through the accomplishment of their stainless nature, They realize and attain the fruit of the Tathāgata’s eternal abiding.
"Furthermore, Bhikṣu Jñānaprabha!

A renunciant bodhisattva should not harbor greedy attachment toward the robes he wears. Whether they be fine or coarse, he should accept whatever he obtains; he should simply regard the donor as a field of merit and must not disdain the quality of the clothing.
He must not preach the essentials of the Dharma extensively for the sake of robes, nor employ various skillful means that are associated with greed."

Ordinary worldlings, for the sake of clothing, engage in unrighteous greed and create unwholesome karma; they fall into the evil realms and pass through immeasurable kalpas, failing to encounter the Buddhas or hear the True Dharma. Once their suffering is exhausted, they are reborn among humans, yet remain impoverished and distressed, oppressed day and night by the suffering of not obtaining what they seek—clothing that does not cover their bodies and food that does not sustain their lives.
All such sufferings arise because, in previous lives, people killed many living beings for the sake of clothing and committed various kinds of transgressions.

A renunciant bodhisattva is not like this; they do not disdain what they receive, even if it is coarse or poor quality, but wear it as a Dharma robe out of a sense of shame and remorse. By doing so, they obtain ten benefits:
first, they can cover their bodies and remain free from shame, becoming fully endowed with a sense of shame and remorse as they practice wholesome dharmas.
Second, they remain far removed from cold and heat, as well as mosquitoes, gadflies, wild beasts, and venomous insects, practicing the Way in peace and security.
Third, they manifest the appearance of a renunciant śramaṇa, so that those who see them rejoice and abandon deviant thoughts.
Fourth, the *kāṣāya* is the sign of the precious banner of humans and devas; by honoring and prostrating to it, one may be reborn in the Brahma heavens.
Fifth, when donning the *kāṣāya*, one should conceive the thought that it is a jeweled stūpa; this can extinguish all transgressions and give rise to manifold merits.
Sixth, the original regulation is that the *kāṣāya* must be dyed to change its color, so as to distance one from thoughts of the five desires and prevent the arising of craving and attachment.
Seventh, the *kāṣāya* is the pure robe of the Buddha; because it eternally severs afflictions and serves as a fertile field for merit.
Eighth, by wearing the *kāṣāya*, one’s sinful karma is eliminated and the ten paths of wholesome action increase in every thought-moment.
Ninth, the *kāṣāya* is like a fertile field, for it can skillfully cause the bodhisattva path to grow.
Tenth, the *kāṣāya* is like armor, for the poisonous arrows of affliction cannot harm it.

Jñānaprabha, you should know that by these causes and conditions, the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas of the three periods of time all leave the household life in purity and wear the *kāṣāya*. These three types of sages sit together upon the precious bed of liberation; grasping the sword of wisdom, they shatter the demon of affliction and enter together into the single-flavor realm of all *nirvāṇa*.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"O Bhikṣu Jñānaprabha, listen well to the ten benefits of the great field of merit robe.
The clothing of the world increases desire and defilement; the Dharma robes of the Tathāgata are not like this."
The Dharma robes can shield one from worldly shame; With perfect modesty, they give rise to a field of merit.
They keep one far from cold, heat, and venomous insects; With a firm resolve for the Way, one attains the ultimate.
Manifesting renunciation to leave behind greed and desire, One cuts off the five views and practices correctly.
Beholding and paying homage to the precious banner of the *kāṣāya*, one generates the merit of Brahmā through such reverence;
when a Son of the Buddha dons the robe, they conceive of it as a reliquary stūpa, thereby generating merit, extinguishing transgressions, and moving the hearts of gods and humans.
With solemn countenance and reverent homage, he is a true śramaṇa; his conduct is untainted by any worldly dust.
Praised by all Buddhas as a fertile field of merit, he is the foremost in bringing benefit and happiness to all living beings.
The miraculous power of the *kāṣāya* is inconceivable; it enables one to cultivate and plant the practices for awakening.
The sprouts of the Path grow like seedlings in spring, and the wondrous fruit of awakening resembles the harvest in autumn.
It is a firm, adamantine, true armor, which the poisonous arrows of affliction cannot harm.
I have now briefly praised these ten benefits; were they to be explained extensively throughout kalpas, they would be boundless.
If a dragon wears even a single thread of this cloth, it shall escape being devoured by the King of the Garuḍas.
If a person crosses the sea while wearing this garment, they need not fear the perils of dragons, fish, or various spirits.
Though thunder and lightning strike with the wrath of heaven, those who wear the *kāṣāya* have no fear;
if one clad in white can personally uphold it, no malevolent spirits will be able to approach.
If one can resolve to leave the home life, Weary of and detached from the world to cultivate the Buddha-way, The palaces of Māras in the ten directions will all tremble;
Such a person shall swiftly realize the body of the Dharma King.
"Furthermore, Jñānaprabha Bodhisattva!
A renunciant son of the Buddha should constantly practice alms-gathering, and he should sacrifice his body and life rather than abandon this resolve. Why is this?
All sentient beings subsist upon food; therefore, the benefit of begging for alms is inexhaustible.
You should know that there are ten advantages for a renunciant bodhisattva who constantly practices begging for alms.
What are the ten?
First, one constantly subsists by begging for food, entering and leaving at will because one is not dependent on others.
Second, when begging for food, one first preaches the sublime Dharma to inspire virtuous thoughts, and only thereafter eats for oneself.

Third, one gives rise to great compassion for those who do not practice giving, and by preaching the True Dharma to them, causes them to develop a mind of renunciation so that they may generate supreme merit.
Fourth, by practicing according to the Buddha’s teachings, one increases the categories of ethical discipline, such that merit becomes perfect and wisdom becomes inexhaustible.
Fifth, by constantly practicing alms-gathering, the seven and nine types of pride will naturally be extinguished; one will be revered by all as a field of merit.
Sixth, while gathering alms, one shall attain the Tathāgata’s mark of the invisible crown of the head and be worthy of receiving vast offerings from the world.
Seventh, you, sons of the Buddha, should study this Dharma accordingly, upholding the Triple Gem and benefiting sentient beings.
Eighth, when begging for alms, you must not, for the sake of seeking food, give rise to a longing mind and praise any man or woman.
Ninth, when going on almsround, one must follow the proper sequence and should not discriminate between poor and wealthy households.
Tenth, constantly practicing almsround brings joy to all Buddhas and serves as the most excellent condition for attaining omniscience.
Bodhisattva Jñānaprabha!
I have briefly explained these ten kinds of benefits for you; if they were to be analyzed in detail, they would be immeasurable and boundless.
You bhikṣus and those in future ages who seek the Buddha-way should train yourselves in this manner.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Jñānaprabha Bodhisattva, listen attentively: A great being who has left the household life should abandon greed;
They should give rise to the mind of supramundane practice, Taking the dhūta practice of begging for food as their foundation.”
Ordinary beings dwell upon tainted nourishment, while noble ones rely entirely upon untainted nourishment;
whether noble or ordinary, tainted or untainted, there are none whatsoever who do not abide by means of nourishment.
For you, my sons of the Buddha, I shall expound the supramundane practices for the dual benefit of self and others;
praised by the Tathāgatas of the three times, there are ten benefits to the merit of begging for alms.
It is universally proclaimed that this practice is most supreme: entering and exiting with mastery and freedom from bondage;
first causing the donor to give rise to the initial resolve, and only then partaking of food so as to lead them toward Bodhi.
To eliminate stinginess and greed, he preached the sublime Dharma; He was able to give rise to the immeasurable mind of great equanimity.
Following the Great Teacher’s instruction, he practiced alms-gathering, Increasing his immeasurable pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
The seven and nine types of pride are naturally extinguished; He is revered by all humans and devas.
The Tathāgata’s uṣṇīṣa cannot be seen, As he turns the wondrous wheel of Dharma to transform the ten directions.
Transmit this Dharma throughout the limits of the future, so that the seeds of the Triple Gem shall never be severed.
If you give rise to deluded thoughts for the sake of food and drink, you should not praise men or women;
instead, arouse a mind of great compassion and equanimity, and do not harbor discrimination between the poor and the wealthy.
Pure alms-seeking is praised by the Buddha; from this, all-knowledge arises.
The Tathāgatas of the three times appear in the world and, for the sake of all sentient beings, teach the four kinds of nutriment:
edible food, contact, volition, and consciousness—these four are all tainted, worldly nutriments.
There is only the food of the joy of Dharma and the delight of dhyāna; this is indeed what the sages and saints consume.
You all should weary of and detach from worldly flavors, and seek instead the supramundane, untainted food.
"Furthermore, Jñānaprabha Bodhisattva!

A renunciant son of the Buddha should not be greedily attached to various medicines. If he falls ill, he should take those medicines discarded by others after they have been decocted—such as harītakī, vibhītaka, and āmalaka—and even throughout his entire life, he should consume only such discarded medicines. He should always maintain contentment regarding all medicines; one who acts thus is called a true śramaṇa."
A renunciant disciple of the Buddha who constantly wears discarded medicine attains ten kinds of benefits.
What are these ten?
First, because they do not approach others for the sake of seeking medicinal herbs, their craving and seeking are forever stilled, and they abide in right mindfulness.
Second, the gate of the contemplation of impurity is easily accomplished, and the mind that seeks transcendence can attain firm stability.
Third, one will never be greedily attached to various delicacies, quickly realizing true wisdom and partaking of the food of dhyāna-bliss.
Fourth, regarding all worldly wealth and possessions, one is always able to be content and attains liberation early.
Fifth, one does not associate with any ordinary worldlings, but instead draws near to supramundane, pure spiritual friends.
Sixth, by not loathing discarded medicines and the like, one attains liberation even through coarse food and drink.
Seventh, one never harbors expectations for esteemed medicines, for there is nothing in all the world that is not honored.
Eighth, one is swiftly able to subdue the diseases of all afflictions and realize the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding Dharma-body.
Ninth, one forever severs all afflictions within the three realms and is able to heal the grave physical and mental illnesses of sentient beings.
Tenth, by being able to follow the Buddha’s teachings and cultivate the bodhisattva practices, one will perfect merit and wisdom and attain great enlightenment.

Jñānaprabha, you should know! I have briefly explained these ten kinds of benefits of discarding medicine for your sake. Such sublime practices are cultivated and studied together by all bodhisattvas who have gone forth in the past, future, and present; you should expound and disseminate them for the sake of all sentient beings so that they shall not be interrupted. This constitutes a vast offering made to the Tathāgata, which cannot be equaled by any worldly offerings of wealth or honor. It ensures that one does not regress from the bodhisattva practices and swiftly realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Bhikṣu Jñānaprabha, listen well; this is the stainless medicine to be taken by those who have gone forth."

This is the foremost of the Bodhisattva’s sublime practices: regarding the illnesses of sentient beings as one's own, one rescues them from all sufferings through the grace of great compassion, and further bestows peace and happiness upon them with a mind of loving-kindness.
Giving the most supreme and wondrous medicine to others, taking for oneself what previous people have discarded—Bodhisattvas do not discriminate between noble and base medicines;
they simply treat all illnesses to bring peace and security.
Taking the leftover medicinal remains discarded by others, one drinks and takes them to cure their ailments;
there are ten benefits in taking the medicine discarded by others, which the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time all praise together.
Though seeking medicine, one does not rely on others; Forever ceasing all pursuit, one abides in right mindfulness.
The gateway of the contemplation of impurity easily reaches maturity, And is able to serve as a distant cause for Bodhi.
Not clinging to sweet flavors and free from all craving, one should seek the food of Dharma-joy and the delight of dhyāna;
being content with worldly wealth and treasures, one shall obtain the seven noble riches that are free from outflows.
Abandoning those foolish commoners, do not dwell with them; draw near to the noble and wise as your virtuous friends.
Thus, one does not disdain medicines that are cast aside by the multitude, nor does one harbor greedy craving for food and drink.

They do not long for rare delicacies or wondrous medicines; The reason they are universally revered in the world Is that they can heal the diseases of affliction in body and mind, And realize the Dharma-nature body of True Suchness.
Forever severing all habitual tendencies of the three realms, Realizing unsurpassed, true liberation,
Able to follow the Buddha’s teaching toward Bodhi, One fully accomplishes the fruit of the Sambhogakāya through merit and wisdom.
"You, sons of the Buddha, should all practice and study this; you shall sit upon the true adamantine site of enlightenment. Furthermore, Jñānaprabha!

A renunciant bodhisattva distances himself from clamor and dwells in an araṇya to cultivate and collect his mind. For immeasurable thousands of years he seeks the path of the Buddha. The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, having distanced themselves from all clamor, dwell in tranquil seclusion; they cultivate the myriad practices and realize the fruit of Bodhi. The Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and all noble sages who have realized the fruits of sainthood do likewise."
The forest hermitage (āraṇya) possesses ten kinds of virtues that enable one to realize the fruit of perfect enlightenment (sambodhi).
What are these ten superior virtues?
First, one dwells in the forest hermitage having attained mastery, because among the four modes of deportment (īryāpatha), one is not dependent on others.
Second, it is called an araṇya because it is free from the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self," for there is no attachment when staying beneath a tree.
Third, one has no craving or attachment toward bedding and other requisites; by virtue of this, one shall lie upon the bed of the four fearlessnesses.
Fourth, in an araṇya dwelling, the three poisons are attenuated, because one is free from the objective conditions that give rise to greed, hatred, and delusion.
Fifth, one delights in the araṇya and practices the conduct of seclusion, because one does not seek the five sensual pleasures of humans or devas.
Sixth, being able to renounce clamor and dwell in secluded places, practicing the Buddha-way without sparing one’s own body or life.
Seventh, delighting in tranquility and distancing oneself from worldly speech, abandoning the foolish and ordinary because of the absence of distraction.
Eighth, all mundane and supramundane undertakings are easily accomplished because they are free from obstacles.
Ninth, the forest hermitage (āraṇya) is the chamber for this samādhi, for it enables one to attain hundreds of thousands of great samādhis.
Tenth, they take purity as vast as space as their dwelling, for their minds are free from obstruction and have attained great wisdom.

Jñānaprabha, you should know that the forest hermitage possesses such immeasurable merits; for this reason, the sons of the Buddha who have left the household life vow to sacrifice their bodies and lives rather than depart from the mountain forests.
If one leaves the araṇya to enter a village for the sake of hearing the Dharma, or to provide for a sick person, a teacher, a preceptor, or one's parents, one should quickly return to the araṇya.
If there are causes and conditions such that one has not yet attained refuge, one should form this thought:
"This village is like a mountain forest; the wealth and possessions obtained here are as empty and false as a dream. Whatever one may obtain, one should not be greedily attached to it."
"Such a son of the Buddha is a mahāsattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"O Jñānaprabha and you others, listen well and attentively: This is the dwelling place of those who are free from afflictions."
Far removed from clamor and tranquil, this is the dwelling place of the ṛṣis.
Bodhisattvas of the three times seek awakening here; within the araṇya, they attain perfect enlightenment.
Pratyekabuddhas and the assembly of noble Śrāvakas likewise realize bodhi in this very place.
Dwelling in an araṇya brings ten benefits: it enables one to realize the fruits of the three vehicles;
one roams with sovereign ease like a lion, free from all fetters throughout the four modes of conduct.
The mountain forests and beneath the trees are what the Sages delight in; free from "self" and "what belongs to self," this is called araṇya.
With no attachment to robes or bedding, they sit upon the lion throne of the four fearlessnesses.
Free from all afflictions is called an araṇya;
with no attachment to any craving or love, one always dwells beyond material things, weary of worldly toil, and takes no pleasure in the five sensual desires of the world.
Those who dwell in solitude, far removed from clamor and noise, Renounce body and life to seek the path of the Buddha;
Able to abide in silence where no human sound is heard, They give rise to no distracted thoughts.
All virtuous deeds, mundane and supramundane, are accomplished without hindrance in the mind;
thus, the araṇya is the foundation from which hundreds of thousands of samādhis arise.
Taking great emptiness and stillness as a vacant chamber, the practitioner’s body and mind are free from obstruction;
possessing these ten benefits, for this reason the multitude of sages always dwell therein.
Jñānaprabha and all you sons of the Buddha, if you wish to swiftly accomplish all-knowledge,
do not abandon the path of enlightenment in forest retreats, even for a moment, even within your dreams.
Those who resolve their minds after my parinirvāṇa, and are able to dwell in forest hermitages (araṇya),
shall before long sit upon the King of Jewel Flowers and realize the fruit of the eternal bliss of the Dharmakāya.

At that time, when the World-Honored One was preaching this Dharma, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of those who had first resolved their minds attained non-retrogression from the unsurpassed path.

Then, the assembly of bodhisattvas, including Jñānaprabha and others, attained dhāraṇīs and were endowed with great supernormal powers; one million humans and devas gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment and realized the three gates of liberation.
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed the great assembly:

"If there are sons or daughters of good family with pure faith who hear this profound Dharma-gate of the four kinds of stainless nature, and who receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, and transcribe it—such persons as these shall encounter spiritual friends wherever they are born; they shall cultivate the Bodhisattva practices without ever regressing, and shall not be disturbed by any karmic actions or afflictions. In their present life, they shall attain great merit and wisdom, maintain the Three Jewels, and obtain the power of mastery; they shall succeed to the lineage of the Buddhas so that it remains unbroken. At the end of their lives, they will surely be reborn in the palace of the Tuṣita Heaven, where they shall attend upon Maitreya and realize the stage of non-retrogression. At the first assembly under the Dragon Flower Tree, they shall hear the True Dharma, receive the prediction of Bodhi, and swiftly attain the Way of the Buddha."

If one wishes to be born in the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, one shall attain rebirth there according to one's vow, see the Buddhas and hear the Dharma, and ultimately never regress from Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.

Chapter Five: The Aranya Chapter. At that time, there was a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva in the assembly named Constant Diligence (Sadāparihṛta). Empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, he rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, the forest retreat (āraṇyaka) is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa); those who resolve to seek enlightenment should not abandon the forest retreat.

In these forest hermitages (āraṇya) there are many sentient beings—tigers, leopards, jackals, wolves, venomous insects, and malevolent beasts, as well as birds and hunters—who do not recognize the Tathāgata, do not hear the True Dharma, and do not revere the Saṅgha. These sentient beings lack any roots of goodness and are far removed from liberation. For what reason does the Tathāgata cause those who practice and study to dwell in āraṇyas so that they may quickly attain Buddhahood?
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will,
for the sake of all sentient beings, analyze and explain [the Dharma] to resolve their doubts and bring them joy, causing them to give rise to the bodhicitta so that they do not regress.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Constant Diligence:
“Excellent, excellent, noble son!
By asking the Tathāgata about pure liberation out of great compassion, you bring benefit to all future practitioners; your merit is immeasurable.”
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall now, for your sake, analyze and expound the various merits of the araṇya dwelling.
"So be it, World-Honored One!"
"I wish to hear it with joy.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Constant Diligence:
"As you have said, one may become a sage in an araṇya; yet, since there are many sentient beings within the mountains and forests, by what causes and conditions do they fail to attain Buddhahood?"
This interpretation is not correct. Why is this so?

Because those sentient beings do not recognize the Three Jewels, do not know contentment, and do not distinguish between good and evil; thus, although there are various worldly treasures within the mountain forests, they cannot discover the location of hidden hoards. The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is not like this.
"Good son!

A bodhisattva is able to know that the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha is the supramundane treasure, while the seven precious hidden stores are mundane treasures. He can discern all their various characteristics and know where they are located, yet he does not greedily seek them, nor does he delight in seeing them, much less taking them with his own hands."

When a bodhisattva leaves the household life, they give rise to a firm resolve, not begrudging body or life, and having abandoned their parents and six kinds of kinsmen, they delight in dwelling in mountain forests, constantly reflecting:

"Even when the kalpa of this trichiliocosm comes to an end, and seven suns appear simultaneously, such that the conflagration blazes fiercely and consumes all things—including the sun, moon, stars, Sumeru, the king of mountains, the seven golden mountains, and the Iron Ring Mountains—all shall be dispersed when the time arrives."

The Peak of Existence, the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, is the summit of the three realms; yet when eighty thousand kalpas have ended, one returns to the lower planes. Though a Wheel-Turning Sage King may be surrounded by a thousand sons, with his seven treasures and retinue, and all four continents in submission, when the retribution of his lifespan is exhausted, it does not pause for even a moment.

I am just the same now; even if I were to live for a full hundred years, possessing all seven treasures and enjoying every pleasure, when the messengers of Yama arrive, I shall not escape impermanence.
He reflected thus:

"It would be better for me now to practice the bodhisattva path on behalf of my parents and all sentient beings; I shall attain an indestructible vajra body and return to the triple world to rescue and deliver my parents."
Having made this vow, he dwelt in an araṇya and made a great aspirational vow for the sake of all sentient beings.
A bodhisattva of superior capacity made this vow, saying:
"May it be that until I have attained Buddhahood, I shall always sit upright in the open air and never lie down."
The bodhisattvas of middling capacity made this vow, saying:
"May I, until I have attained Buddhahood, always sit upon the leaves of trees and never lie down.
The bodhisattvas of inferior capacity made this vow, saying:
"May I, until I have attained Buddhahood, always sit and never lie down within this stone chamber.
Thus, these three root bodhisattvas who had gone forth sat upon three kinds of seats, each forming this thought:
"The bodhisattvas of the past sat upon these very seats and were able to realize the gate of dhāraṇī and attain mastery over merit."
All Bodhisattvas of the past, present, and future have, at this very seat, attained the dhāraṇīs and achieved mastery through cultivation and realization;
I too shall likewise now sit here and surely accomplish the dhāraṇīs and attain mastery.
"If one has not yet attained mastery, one shall never abandon the forest hermitage (āraṇyaka).
"Furthermore, there may be bodhisattvas who, until they have fully perfected the four immeasurable minds (catur-apramāṇa), shall never abandon the forest hermitage."
There may be bodhisattvas who, until they have attained the perfection of the five supernormal powers, never abandon their dwelling in the araṇya.
There may be bodhisattvas who, until they have attained the perfection of the six pāramitās, never abandon their dwelling in the araṇya.
There may be bodhisattvas who, until they have attained perfect skillful means, never abandon the forest hermitage (āraṇya).
There may be bodhisattvas who, until they have been able to subdue all sentient beings, never abandon the forest hermitage.
There may be bodhisattvas who, until they have perfected the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), never abandon their dwelling in the forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*).
There may be bodhisattvas who, until they have been able to practice the dharma of the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), never abandon their dwelling in the forest hermitage.
There may be bodhisattvas who, though they have not yet perfected the wisdom of extensive learning, never abandon the forest hermitage (āraṇyaka).
There may be bodhisattvas who, though they have not yet perfected the power of firm faith, never abandon the forest hermitage.
There may be bodhisattvas who, though they have not yet been able to sever the sixty-two views, never abandon the aranya retreat.
There may be bodhisattvas who, though they have not yet been able to cultivate the eightfold noble path, never abandon the aranya retreat.
There may be bodhisattvas who, being unable to permanently sever the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the two obscurations, never abandon the forest hermitage (*araṇya*).
There may be bodhisattvas who, being unable to perfect the subtle wisdom that dispenses medicine according to the illness, never abandon the forest hermitage.
There may be bodhisattvas who, until they have perfected the great bodhicitta, will never abandon the aranya.
There may be bodhisattvas who, until they have perfected samādhis as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, will never abandon the aranya.
There may be bodhisattvas who, though not yet having perfected immeasurable supernormal powers, never abandon the forest hermitage (āraṇyaka).

There may be bodhisattvas who, through the power of meditative concentration and supernormal knowledge, perceive the eighteen kinds of emptiness without their minds being startled; until such great matters are accomplished, they never abandon the forest hermitage.
There may be bodhisattvas who, until they have perfected the knowledge of all modes, will never abandon the forest hermitage.
There may be bodhisattvas who, until they have attained the perfection of the knowledge of all aspects, will never abandon the forest hermitage.
There may be bodhisattvas who, as long as they have not yet practiced the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, never abandon the aranya hermitage.
There may be bodhisattvas who, as long as they have not yet perfected the myriad practices of the ten stages, never abandon the aranya hermitage.
There may be bodhisattvas who, throughout a hundred kalpas, have not yet been able to cultivate the karma for the primary and secondary marks, yet they never abandon the aranya.
There may be bodhisattvas who have not yet attained the four wisdoms of a Tathāgata in their full perfection, yet they never abandon the aranya.
There may be bodhisattvas who, until they have fully realized great parinirvāṇa, never forsake the aranya.
There may be bodhisattvas who, while seated upon the vajrāsana, do not rise until they have attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; this is called the aranya practice of a bodhisattva.
"Good son!

A renunciant bodhisattva, having resolved upon bodhicitta, enters the mountain forests and sits upon the three seats to refine body and mind. Having practiced the myriad deeds throughout three great eons, they realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
