"When the Tathāgatas of old were on the path of the stages, They dwelt in *araṇya* and secluded places free from dust,
Subduing and severing the afflictive and cognitive obstructions, Transcending the three realms and realizing *bodhi*."
In the past, the Bodhisattva cultivated his vows, taking the araṇya as his dwelling;
through countless asaṃkhyeya kalpas he cultivated merit and wisdom, reaching the culmination of the ten stages and realizing the three bodies.
Bodhisattvas of the future seeking the fruit of Buddhahood Enter deep mountains to cultivate sublime practices;
Severing the two obstacles, the causes of birth and death, They shall realize the true liberation of the three emptinesses.
The Bodhisattvas of the ten directions now, Cultivating myriad practices and dwelling in seclusion,
Spare neither body nor life in their quest for Bodhi, Moment by moment realizing the wisdom of non-arising.
If one wishes to swiftly realize profound samādhi, By cultivating wondrous concentration, supernatural powers arise;
In an araṇya dwelling with a mind free from strife, One can transform the great earth into the seven treasures.
If you wish to roam through the lands of the ten directions, Traveling to and fro with mastery of spiritual powers,
Making offerings to all Buddhas and benefiting all beings, Dwell in the forest hermitage, the place of fearlessness.
Desiring to realize the wisdom that existence and non-existence are like illusions, To thoroughly understand that all phenomena are primordially empty,
One dwells in an araṇya, the site of enlightenment, Causing all beings likewise to enter true liberation.
If you wish to swiftly attain the wisdom of suchness, Realize the suchness-nature of all phenomena,
And benefit sentient beings throughout an ocean of great eons, You should dwell in a forest hermitage, a place of empty stillness.
If a person desires to attain inconceivable wisdom, They shall enter the hermitage of supernatural powers,
Where Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, can contain a mustard seed, Yet neither the mountain-king nor the mustard seed lose their respective characteristics.
If one wishes to attain unimpeded wisdom, And preach the Dharma with a single sublime voice,
So that sentient beings, according to their kind, each gain understanding, One should dwell in an araṇya and cultivate sublime contemplation.
If you wish for neither arising nor ceasing, You should manifest in all lands throughout the ten directions;
Radiating light and preaching the Dharma to benefit all beings, Do not depart from the empty and tranquil hermitage.
If one presses the great earth with a toe, causing the worlds of the ten directions to tremble all over,
those who behold this sign and resolve their minds shall eliminate false views and dwell in an araṇya to contemplate their own minds.
If you wish for the Buddhas to appear, first offer sublime and exquisite offerings;
having brought the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) to full completion, dwell in an araṇya and cultivate wondrous conduct.
If a person, at the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, fulfills the meaning of dāna through their final offering,
they will forever sever poverty and the eight difficulties, and vow to dwell within an araṇya.
If you wish for both merit and wisdom to be perfected,
And to receive the Buddha’s entrustment to widely propagate the teachings When future Buddhas approach their parinirvāṇa, Dwell in an araṇya and cultivate the six recollections.
If, after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas, you compile their bequeathed Dharma to deliver sentient beings,
assist the Buddhas in praising the True Vehicle, and dwell in the empty and tranquil hermitages of the araṇya.
The Bhagavān, Great Teacher of humans and devas, is difficult to see and difficult to encounter, rarer even than the udumbara flower;
if you wish to behold him and practice offerings, you should dwell in an araṇya and propagate your compassionate vows.
Among all treasures, the Dharma is supreme; the attainment of Buddhahood and the transformation for the benefit of others all arise from it.
If one wishes to hear the Dharma constantly, one should dwell in an araṇya and cultivate the pure conduct.
From this present body until the attainment of the Buddha-body, may I always aspire to resolve my mind to propagate the True Teaching;
until I have attained Great Bodhi, may I never abandon the *āraṇya* in thought after thought.
If a person wishes to repay the kindness of their parents, They should act on behalf of their parents by making vows,
Entering an araṇya, the field of enlightenment, To constantly cultivate the wondrous Way day and night.
If one wishes to increase merit and wisdom in the present life, And not fall into the eight difficult states in the future,
Such sentient beings should give rise to a virtuous mind, Dwelling in an araṇya to cultivate compassionate vows.
Bodhisattvas of the three periods seek true awakening; they attain the Way and nirvana within the araṇya.
For this reason, it is called the Great Site of Enlightenment (Mahāmaṇḍala), where the noble assemblies of the Three Vehicles all dwell together.
The Bodhisattva, weary of suffering, enters the mountain forests;
seeking the Noble Path to deliver all living beings, he first delivers others before he himself attains Buddhahood, feeling compassion for all within the six realms and four modes of birth.
Bodhisattvas of superior capacity dwell in the open air; those of middling capacity dwell among the leaves;
and those of inferior capacity dwell in stone chambers. Until they have attained the Way of Buddhahood, they never lie down to sleep.
Bodhisattvas of the three periods dwell in araṇyas, Attaining the sovereign power of dhāraṇīs;
Now I vow to share the resolve of these bodhisattvas, And shall remain here constantly until I have attained total retention.
One attains great Bodhi in the forest hermitage; One enters Great Parinirvāṇa by virtue of the dwelling place.
The Bodhisattva gives rise to Vajra-wisdom, Severs delusions, realizes the Truth, and achieves Wondrous Enlightenment.
Extensively transforming sentient beings as they travel through villages, Seeking the bliss of nirvana, they dwell in mountain forests;
The causes of the ten thousand practices are fulfilled and the fruits are likewise perfected, Delivering all classes of beings until the end of future time.

At that time, as the World-Honored One expounded this practice of the *araṇā* (non-contention) for renunciant bodhisattvas, immeasurable bodhisattvas realized the Stage of Supreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*);
bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, free from the subtle afflictions of signs and functions, realized the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*);
and unspeakably unspeakable numbers of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas severed all obstacles and entered the Stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*sudurjayā-bhūmi*).
Boundless sentient beings gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), which is equal to the unequaled;
ninety-seven thousand living beings, far removed from dust and free from defilement, attained the pure Dharma-eye.

The Sutra on the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground of Past Lives, Volume Five, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā of Kapiśī during the Great Tang Dynasty by Imperial Decree. Chapter Six: Leaving the World At that time, there was a bodhisattva-mahāsattva in the assembly named Rativivekacaryā (Delighting in the Practice of Seclusion). Empowered by the Buddha’s majesty, he rose from his seat and, amidst the great assembly, spoke to the bodhisattvas concerning the practice of the araṇya (forest hermitage), addressing all the bodhisattvas universally:
“A bodhisattva who has left the household life and dwells in an araṇya should form this thought:
‘By what causes and conditions do I distance myself from the world to cultivate the pure and wondrous practices of an araṇya?’”
“Sons of the Buddha, listen with single-minded attention. Relying on the power of the Buddha, I shall now analyze and expound for you the practice of the araṇya.
The Bodhisattvas said, “Excellent, Great Being!”
"For the sake of those among us and those seeking enlightenment in future ages, we pray that you will speak of this; we delight in hearing it.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Delighting in Solitary Practice addressed the great assembly:

"The entire world is full of many terrors. To weary themselves of these various worldly terrors, bodhisattvas who have gone forth abandon their parents and all kinsmen to dwell in *āraṇyas* and cultivate the practice of solitude."
What are called the various forms of fear?
There may be a bodhisattva who thinks:
"I am the source of fear, for all afflictions arise from me."
Some bodhisattvas say that the sense of "mine" is a source of terror, for all afflictions arise from "mine.
Some bodhisattvas say that the seven types of pride are a source of terror, for the arising of various forms of pride leads one to fail to respect virtuous persons.
There may be bodhisattvas who regard those three poisons as a source of terror, because they create immeasurable sins and fall into the evil realms.
There may be bodhisattvas who regard those five desires as a source of terror, because they become addicted to worldly pleasures and fall into the eight difficult conditions.
For example, there is a seven-step snake in the world; when it harms a person, its venom is so potent that the victim dies immediately after taking seven steps.

If the venom of a single snake is already capable of harming a person, how much more so when five snakes act together to wound and kill? Their combined venom becomes even more intense, making it difficult for life to be preserved.

The five desires of the world are likewise thus: each individual sensual pleasure can give rise to eighty-four thousand subtle afflictions, deluding the foolish and causing them to fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, and other difficult states to undergo great suffering and distress; how much more so for those who are fully possessed of craving and attachment to these sensory objects?

Though countless Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges appear in the world to teach the Dharma and transform beings, one cannot see them even for a moment, as fleeting as a ray of light through a crack; yet one constantly dwells in the evil realms as if in one's own home, remaining amidst the lack of leisure as if in a pleasure garden.
In the past, there was a Buddha who, wishing to cause sentient beings to grow weary of and abandon the five desires,
spoke this verse: "Just as a moth beholding a flame, Competes to enter it out of love for the fire,
Failing to know the power of the burning wick, It surrenders its life within the flames, gladly consuming itself."
Ordinary worldlings are just like this: they crave and pursue beautiful forms, unaware that sensual desire defiles and clings to them;
thus, they are once again scorched by fire and brought to manifold sufferings.
For example, when a herd of deer dwells in the forest thickets, feeding on abundant grass to sustain themselves, a hunter feigns the sound of a doe;
hearing the sound, they follow it and all meet their death by the arrow.

Ordinary worldlings are just like this: they greedily cling to various pleasing sounds, unaware that sound can defile and bind them, so that they must once again undergo the various bitter retributions of the three miserable realms.
Just as a bee can fly far away, wandering through the spring forests to gather from various flowers,
yet for the sake of the fragrance on the temples of a rutting elephant, it is crushed to death by the elephant’s flapping ears.

Ordinary worldlings are just like this: they are attached to all fragrances of sensory enjoyment, unaware that such scents can defile the mind, and thus endure the suffering of the long night of saṃsāra.
Just as dragons and fish dwell in the water, swimming and diving at their own pleasure, yet for the sake of craving fragrant bait they swallow the hook;
forgetting their very lives in their love for flavor, they all meet with death.
Ordinary worldlings are just like this: their gustatory faculty craves flavors to sustain the body;
by killing others to live themselves, their minds are not impartial, and they thus experience the most grievous suffering of the three miserable realms.
For example, like a white elephant dwelling in the mountains and marshes, He is as sovereign as a lion king;
yet, his mind intoxicated by desire, he wanders in confusion, Pursuing a female elephant and giving rise to lustful attachment.
All ordinary beings are likewise; they rush toward those exquisite sensations like mad elephants.
Bound by the entanglements of affection without ceasing, they enter hell at death, where their suffering is immeasurable.
Men and women in the world greedily pursue one another, all because they delight in and are attached to various forms and desires;
by this, humans and devas are ensnared and bound, falling into the dark abyss of the three miserable realms.
If one can abandon the mind of craving and dwell in an araṇya to cultivate pure conduct,
one will surely transcend the suffering of birth and death and swiftly enter the palace of unconditioned, eternal bliss.
"Furthermore, there may be bodhisattvas who regard the craving for abundant wealth as a source of terror.
They constantly seek to amass their own treasures and do not enjoy them themselves; how much less could they possibly give them to impoverished sentient beings?"

Deeply conceiving attachment to one's own wealth and treasures, and desiring to diminish the wealth and treasures of others—due to these causes and conditions, after the end of life, one falls into the great hells and undergoes immeasurable suffering. Such retribution of suffering is called the first fruit of direct maturation (*vipāka-phala*).

Emerging from the hells, one receives the body of an animal; its form is constantly subjected to toil and hardship, with insufficient water and grass. Throughout a long period of time, it repays the damage caused by misappropriating the wealth of others. Such manifold sufferings are called the second fruit of direct retribution.

Having undergone these punishments, one is born among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), tormented by the sufferings of hunger and thirst. For immeasurable thousands of kalpas, one does not even hear the names of water, drink, or food; one's throat is like a needle and one's belly is like a mountain. Even if one obtains food or drink, it immediately transforms into fire. Such a body of suffering is called the third fruit of direct retribution.

Having exhausted these karmic offenses and been reborn among humans, one is poor, lowly, and subservient to others; whatever wealth or treasures one seeks is difficult to obtain, and at all times one lacks autonomy. Such residual retributions are called "resemblance fruits."

All bodhisattvas clearly perceive and understand such causes and effects; they constantly give rise to a sense of dread and desire liberation. Out of this dread, they distance themselves from their retinues and dwell in araṇyas.
There may be bodhisattvas who regard thirsting desire as a source of terror, because they pursue all manner of unobtained wealth and treasures day and night, giving rise to thirsting desire.
There may be bodhisattvas who experience fear due to the view of "I" and "mine," because such views serve as a basis for the various afflictions (*kleśa*).
There may be bodhisattvas who experience fear due to the view of phenomena (*dharma*), because such views serve as a basis for the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
There may be bodhisattvas for whom the sixty-two views constitute a terror, because they enter the forest of false views from which it is difficult to emerge.
There may be bodhisattvas for whom doubt constitutes a terror, because they give rise to uncertainty regarding the true and correct Dharma.

There may be some bodhisattvas who regard that view of annihilationism as a source of terror, for by clinging to the non-existence of future lives and repudiating cause and effect, they give rise to great false views and enter hell.

There may be bodhisattvas who regard the view of eternalism as a source of terror, for they hold that the bodies within the five destinies are permanent and fixed, remaining unchanging according to their wholesome or unwholesome karma.
There may be bodhisattvas who regard jealousy as a source of fear, because they cannot endure the prosperity of others and harbor ill will toward them.
There may be bodhisattvas who constantly regard restlessness as a source of fear, because their minds lack tranquility and give rise to distraction.

There may be bodhisattvas who, because they lack faith, experience terror; just as a person without hands will ultimately gain nothing even upon reaching a mountain of jewels, so too one without the hand of faith gains nothing even when encountering the Triple Gem.

There may be bodhisattvas who regard that lack of shame as a source of terror; for those who inwardly lack a sense of remorse and constantly commit various evils, the obstacles of karma and ignorance make it difficult for them to see the Buddha.

There may be bodhisattvas who take shamelessness as their terror, for through a lack of external modesty they abandon kindness and turn their backs on virtue, thereby falling into the three miserable realms within the cycle of birth and death.

There may be bodhisattvas who regard anger, resentment, and the like as terrors, for these can harm both oneself and others, creating mutual enmity and obstructing the path to Buddhahood throughout many kalpas.

There may be some bodhisattvas who regard such forgetfulness as a source of terror; they are unable to retain the teachings they have heard, for the loss of both the words and their meaning increases their ignorance.
There may be bodhisattvas who regard even all unwholesome and dark karmas as a source of terror. Why is this? All unwholesome acts are the cause of birth and death;

they lead to transmigration within the three realms, preventing one from attaining liberation. Thus, these immeasurable and boundless terrors are all capable of obstructing the supreme dharmas that transcend the world.
There may be bodhisattvas who regard the five hindrances as a source of terror, because these five afflictions shroud the bodhisattva’s bodhicitta.

There may be bodhisattvas who regard a mind of aversion as a source of terror, because they lack compassion for sentient beings and thus frequently regress from their cultivation of the practices of enlightenment.
There may be bodhisattvas who regard the defilement of breaking the precepts as a source of terror, for it pollutes the sublime Dharma and makes the attainment of its fruits difficult.
There may be bodhisattvas who regard those anxieties and afflictions as a source of terror, for when false conceptualizations blaze forth, one loses their wholesome karma.
There may be bodhisattvas who regard a mind of regret as a source of terror, because they give rise to remorse for the wholesome deeds they have cultivated.

There may be bodhisattvas who declare that madness and intoxication are sources of terror, because such states lead to a failure to distinguish between good and evil, and a lack of awareness of the distinction between the noble and the lowly.
There may be bodhisattvas who regard untimely death as a source of terror, because they fail to abide in right mindfulness and take refuge in impermanence.
There may be bodhisattvas who regard the karma of false speech as a source of terror, because whatever words they utter in life after life will not be trusted or accepted by any sentient beings.

There may be bodhisattvas who regard the four inversions as a source of terror; because of these four inversions, they transmigrate through birth and death, giving rise to afflictions and karma, and thus do not seek the Buddha.
There may be bodhisattvas who declare that evil friends are a source of terror, because by following unwholesome friends one commits evil deeds.

There may be bodhisattvas who regard the māra of the five aggregates as a source of terror; for this body of the five aggregates arises from afflictions, and once arisen, it immediately gives rise to immeasurable afflictions. Due to these various afflictions, one performs unwholesome karma, and by means of these delusions and karma, one falls into a great abyss. For these reasons, they give rise to terror.

There may be bodhisattvas who regard the māra of afflictions as a source of terror, for both great and small afflictions can perpetuate birth and death, causing them to retreat from the bodhicitta and fall into evil destinies.

There may be some bodhisattvas who, being weary of and afflicted by the Māra of death, experience fear; though they have resolved upon bodhicitta, they have not yet attained non-retrogression, because their bodies will perish at the end of life and they will be born into a state of regression.

There may be bodhisattvas who regard the various celestial māras as a source of terror; for the retinues of these celestial māras fill the desire realm, obstructing those who practice the Way and causing them to regress from bodhi.

There may be bodhisattvas who, out of a neutral state of mind, experience fear, whereby they are unable to progress in the cultivation of wholesome dharmas; thus, they let long periods pass in vain and regress from their virtuous deeds.

There may be bodhisattvas who regard those eight difficulties as a source of terror; for those who fall into the eight difficulties pass from darkness into darkness, as it is difficult to encounter light during the long night of birth and death.

There are some bodhisattvas who regard those hells as terrifying, because once one falls into hell, one undergoes great suffering and affliction for immeasurable eons, making liberation difficult to attain.

There may be bodhisattvas who perceive the realm of animals as terrifying, because within the animal kingdom one undergoes the retribution of ignorance and finds it difficult to escape for immeasurable kalpas.

There may be bodhisattvas who perceive the realm of hungry ghosts as terrifying, because for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges they must endure the sufferings of hunger and thirst, and because it is difficult to encounter the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.

There may be bodhisattvas who regard birth in the desire realm as a source of terror, because various afflictions arise there, leading them to commit evil deeds and fall into the three miserable realms.
There may be bodhisattvas who regard that form realm as a source of terror, because the obscured afflictions therein can obstruct meditative concentration.

There may be bodhisattvas who regard the formless realm as a source of terror; for although it is the most tranquil among the three realms, like nirvana, sentient beings falsely cling to it as the ultimate goal, only to fall into hell when their lives end at the conclusion of a kalpa.
There may be bodhisattvas who regard repeated birth and death as a source of terror, because they are born into families with wrong views from which it is difficult to escape.

There may be bodhisattvas who regard the wearying departure from birth and death as a source of terror, because they fear that dying here and being born there will lead to constant suffering and affliction, thereby obstructing their bodhisattva practice and pursuit of nirvana.
There may be bodhisattvas who regard worldly speech as a source of terror, because it constantly distracts the mind and obstructs wholesome karma.
There may be bodhisattvas who regard the mind, intellect, and consciousness as a source of terror, because their objects of focus and modes of activity are unknowable.
If one remains in a lay household due to such fears, the mind of goodness will be disturbed day and night in succession, and one will be unable to realize the state of fearlessness.
All past bodhisattvas dwelling in araṇya attained the dharma of fearlessness, which is precisely anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
all future bodhisattvas dwelling in araṇya shall likewise attain the dharma of fearlessness and anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Now, the great bodhisattvas of the ten directions dwell in araṇya, severing all obstacles and attaining the state of fearlessness in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"You all should know!

You must learn from and practice according to the Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time: by gathering mindfulness within body and mind and dwelling in an araṇya, subduing delusive thoughts so that there is forever no fear, you shall ultimately attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"Furthermore, when a renunciant bodhisattva dwells in an araṇya, what actions should they perform and what reflections should they maintain?
Day and night, they should constantly engage in such contemplation: "

"Whatever terrors exist in the world all arise from the self; for all terrors arise from attachment to the self, all terrors have the self as their root, all terrors arise from love of the self, all terrors arise from the notion of a self, and all terrors arise from the view of a self;

the self is the dwelling place of all terrors, for all terrors arise because of the self, all terrors arise from conceptual discrimination, all terrors arise from afflictions, and all afflictions arise from love of the self."
"If I dwell in an araṇya yet am unable to relinquish the grasping at 'I' and 'mine,' I should not remain in this araṇya; it would be better to return to dwelling in the houses of laypeople."
Why is this? If one possesses the notion of a self, one should not dwell in an araṇya.
If one possesses the notion of a person (pudgala), one should not dwell in an araṇya.
If a person possesses attachment to a self and what belongs to a self, they should not dwell in an araṇya.
If there is a view of dharmas, they should not dwell in an araṇya.
"If one possesses these four inverted attachments, one should not dwell in an araṇya.
Listen attentively!
If one practices while forming the conceptualization of nirvāṇa, one should not dwell in an araṇya; how much less so if one further gives rise to the conceptualizations of various afflictions?"
“Listen attentively!

If there are those who do not cling to the characteristics of any phenomena, they should dwell in an araṇya; this is called sitting at the bodhimaṇḍa of non-attachment, wherein all phenomena are unattainable.”
If the mind is pliant and free from contention, one should dwell in an araṇya.
If there is no attachment whatsoever to worldly conditions, one should dwell in an araṇya.
One who has no dependence upon dharmas such as forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects should dwell in an araṇya.
One who possesses the view of equality toward all dharmas should dwell in an araṇya.
One who is able to discipline one's own mind amidst the four modes of conduct should dwell in an araṇya.
One who is able to relinquish all fears should dwell in an araṇya.
O sons of the Buddha!
To state it in brief: those who seek liberation from all afflictions should dwell in forest hermitages (araṇya).
Those who wish to accomplish the causes for nirvāṇa should dwell in forest hermitages.
Those who are able to skillfully practice the four stainless natures should dwell in an araṇya.
Those who have few desires and are content with what they have should dwell in an araṇya.
Those who possess extensive learning and wisdom should dwell in an araṇya.
Those who are able to practice the three gates of liberation should dwell in an araṇya.
Those who wish to permanently sever the fetters of afflictions that bind them should dwell in an araṇya.
Those who wish to skillfully contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination should dwell in an araṇya.
One who has accomplished what was to be done should dwell in an araṇya.
One who has laid down the heavy burden should dwell in an araṇya.
Those who have realized the profound and subtle principle of *tathatā* (suchness) should dwell in an *araṇya* (hermitage).
You should know this!
In an *araṇya*, various medicinal herbs and trees, both large and small, grow; they have never experienced fear, nor do they engage in conceptual discrimination.

It is likewise for a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwelling in an araṇya: they contemplate their own body and mind as being no different from a withered tree, a wall, a brick, or a pebble, and they maintain no discrimination toward any phenomena.

I contemplate the body and mind as being like an illusion or a dream, devoid of any reality within. From moment to moment they age and decay; once the breath has gone out, it does not enter again. Due to the causes of good and evil, one receives retribution according to karma. This body is impermanent, arising and ceasing swiftly; this body is false and provisional, never remaining for long. Within such a body, there is no self and nothing belonging to a self; there is no sentient being, no life-principle, no nourisher, no person, no *pudgala*, no agent of action, and no infant.

Such characteristics as these are originally empty and quiescent, like space and like foam; one should constantly, moment by moment, practice such contemplation, whereby all terrors will be liberated, just as those trees have no fear.
At that time, the bodhisattvas attain a seat of great peace, bliss, and fearlessness; this is called a bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Furthermore, a renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya should continuously contemplate in this way day and night:
'This araṇya is a place of peace and happiness where one can skillfully cultivate the four stainless natures.'"
This araṇya is a place where one can skillfully cultivate contentment.
This araṇya is a place where one attains liberation from all afflictions.
This araṇya is a place where one is endowed with extensive learning and wisdom.
This araṇya is the place for subduing and severing the afflictive obscurations and the cognitive obscurations.
This araṇya is the place where one can enter the three gates of liberation.
This araṇya is the place where one can skillfully realize the eight liberations.
This araṇya is a place where one can skillfully contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination.
This araṇya is a place where one can effectively sever the obstacles of karma.
This araṇya is a place where one can attain the first fruit, that of the stream-enterer (srotāpanna).
This araṇya is the place where one can attain the second fruit, that of the Once-returner.
This araṇya is the place where one can attain the third fruit, that of the Non-returner.
This araṇya is the place where one attains the fourth fruit, that of the Arhat.
This araṇya is the place where the fruit of a pratyekabuddha is realized.
This araṇya is the place where what was to be done has been accomplished and mastery is attained.
This araṇya is the place where all heavy burdens are cast off and pliancy is gained.
This araṇya is the place for realizing the true suchness of the two kinds of emptiness.
This araṇya is the place where one can cultivate and realize immeasurable great loving-kindness.
This araṇya is the place where one cultivates and realizes immeasurable great compassion.
This araṇya is a place where one can skillfully cultivate the immeasurable state of joy (muditā).
This araṇya is a place where one can skillfully cultivate the immeasurable state of equanimity (upekṣā).
This araṇya is a place where one can give rise to the bodhicitta.
This is araṇya, where the bodhisattva practices until reaching the stage of the ten faiths.
This is araṇya, where one further advances in practice until reaching the stage of the ten abidings.
This is araṇya, where one progressively increases one's cultivation until reaching the stage of the ten practices.
This araṇya is the place for successively practicing the ten dedications.
This araṇya is the place for skillfully cultivating the four roots of goodness.
This araṇya is the place for practicing the six pāramitās.
This araṇya is the place for practicing from the first bhūmi to the tenth bhūmi.
This araṇya is the place for realizing the purification of the six sense faculties.
This araṇya is the place where one can skillfully realize the supernormal power of the divine eye.

This araṇya is a place where one attains the supernormal power of the divine ear, the knowledge of past lives, the knowledge of death and rebirth, the clarity of the supernatural faculties, and the knowledge of others' minds.
This araṇya is a place of shame and remorse.
This araṇya is a place of non-negligence.
This araṇya is a place for cultivating the five faculties.
This araṇya is a place for realizing immeasurable and boundless samādhis.
This araṇya is where one can attain the gateways of dhāraṇīs as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and realize the state of mastery.
This araṇya is where one awakens to the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
This araṇya is the place for forever transcending the triple world and severing birth and death.
This araṇya is where one attains non-retrogression;
this araṇya is where all demonic adversaries are subdued, karmic obstacles are eliminated, and one beholds the Buddha and hears the Dharma—such is this place.
This araṇya is where one attains the Buddha’s uncommon and supreme Dharma-gate.
This araṇya is the place for cultivating the purity of the aggregate of ethical discipline (śīlaskandha).
This araṇya is the place where untainted (anāsrava) samādhi arises.
This araṇya is the place where one can give rise to prajñā and realize liberation.
This araṇya is the place where one can give rise to the knowledge and vision of liberation.
In this araṇya, one attains the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
This araṇya is well-suited for the thorough cultivation and mastery of the twelve dhūtas.
This araṇya is a dwelling place where wisdom can discern the principles of the truths.
This araṇya is forever free from the birthplaces of the outflow-tainted five aggregates.
This araṇya is that which can bring about liberation from the twelve bases (āyatana).
This araṇya is that which is forever free from the eighteen realms (dhātu) of outflows (sāsrava).
This araṇya is that which subtly and profoundly contemplates the eighteen kinds of emptiness (śūnyatā).
This araṇya is the place that accommodates the emptiness of all dharmas.
This araṇya is the place where the ten wholesome dharmas increase and arise.
This araṇya is the place where the firm bodhicitta increases.
This araṇya is the place praised by all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
This araṇya is the place thus revered and praised by all bodhisattvas.
This is the araṇya where Vipaśyin Buddha attained enlightenment beneath a nyagrodha tree.
This is the araṇya where Śikhin Tathāgata attained enlightenment beneath a śirīṣa tree.
This is the araṇya where the Tathāgata Viśvabhū attained enlightenment beneath an aśvattha tree.
This is the araṇya where the Buddha Krakucchanda attained perfect enlightenment beneath an aśoka tree.
This is the araṇya where the Tathāgata Konāgamana attained equal and perfect enlightenment beneath an udumbara tree.
This is the araṇya where the Tathāgata Kāśyapa attained equal and perfect enlightenment beneath a pāṭala tree.
This is the araṇya, the place where Śākyamuni Tathāgata attained enlightenment beneath the Pippala tree.
You should know that in such araṇya locations,
there are immeasurable and boundless merits and benefits such as these.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Delighting in Solitary Practice spoke these verses for the great assembly:
"When a renunciant bodhisattva dwells in an araṇya, What thoughts and what deeds should they cultivate?"
All the terrors that exist in the world arise from the view of self and what belongs to self;
if one can sever this view of self and what belongs to self, all terrors will have no basis.
If there is a mind that clings to the view of self, the path to enlightenment will ultimately not be accomplished.
Nirvāṇa is eternally abiding and entirely without marks; how much more so are afflictions and non-dharmas?
Without clinging to any phenomena or sentient beings, with a mind free from contention, one cultivates right mindfulness.
Taming the mind within the four modes of deportment, one should dwell in an araṇya in constant tranquility.
Able to sever afflictions and possessing a mind of contentment, Dwelling in the empty and silent hermitage;
Entering the signless gate of the three liberations, Dwelling in the hermitage, free from dust and defilement.
Able to contemplate the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination, The Four Truths, and the two kinds of emptiness—
the wondrous and sublime principle— Unshaken by the eight worldly winds, Such a Great Being dwells in the araṇya.
One who can contemplate one's own body as being like withered wood, or like foam upon water or a magical illusion,
and who does not cling to the signs of the two extremes but dwells in equanimity— such a being resides in the araṇya.
The impermanent body is bound by sinful karma; from the outset it is false and fundamentally lacks reality.
The dualistic grasping at self and phenomena, as well as the characteristics of sin, cannot be found throughout the three periods of time.
One's own body and the bodies of others are non-dual; all phenomena are likewise so.
Contemplating the nature of phenomena as having neither coming nor going—in this way, the bodhisattva dwells in the araṇya.
Whether sandalwood is smeared upon his body or he is praised, or whether he is cut and sliced with a knife and reviled—
feeling neither love nor hatred toward these two types of people, such is the bodhisattva dwelling in the araṇya.
Having left the household life, one should dwell joyfully in an araṇya, contemplating thus day and night:
"The araṇya is the true site of enlightenment; it is there that all Tathāgatas attain perfect awakening."
The forest hermitage is the sublime emptiness of the True Dharma, the source from which the supramundane Right Dharma arises.
The forest hermitage is honored by the sages, for it is able to give birth to the noble paths of the Three Vehicles.
The araṇya is the dwelling place of the noble ones, for all sages and saints constantly abide therein.
The araṇya is the palace of the Tathāgatas, for it is that upon which the Buddhas of the ten directions rely.
The araṇya is the Vajrāsana, for it is where the Buddhas of the three times attain the Way.
The araṇya is the palace of nirvāṇa, for it is where the Tathāgatas of the three times enter parinirvāṇa.
The araṇya is a chamber of great compassion, for Bodhisattvas dwell here to cultivate loving-kindness;
The araṇya is a field of compassion, for the Buddhas of the three periods of time cultivated compassion therein.
The forest hermitage is a chamber of the six supernormal powers, for it is therein that Bodhisattvas sport.
The forest hermitage is great fearlessness, for it can sever all terrors.
The samādhi of the araṇya, because those seeking the Way attain concentration therein;
The dhāraṇī of the araṇya, because those who uphold mantras possess spiritual power therein.
The forest hermitage is a hall of wholesome dharmas, for it increases all wholesome dharmas.
The forest hermitage is the chamber of bodhi, for by practicing the path there, Bodhisattvas attain patience.
If you wish to forever transcend the suffering of the triple world, You should cultivate and realize bodhi and nirvāṇa;
To benefit all sentient beings throughout the entire dharma-realm, You should dwell in an araṇya, the chamber of bodhi.
The six perfections and four means of integration that have been cultivated, I dedicate and bestow upon the three realms of existence and the four debts of gratitude;
May self and others together enter the city of ambrosia, And together realize the true dharma-realm of suchness.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Delighting in Solitary Practice had preached this Dharma for the great assembly, the Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Good son!

For the sake of this great assembly and those seeking the Buddha-way in future ages, you shall analytically expound the supreme merits of the araṇya hermitage, thereby benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings of the present and future, so that they may advance toward the path of true and perfect enlightenment."
"The immeasurable merits you have accomplished cannot be fully exhausted even if a thousand Buddhas were to speak of them together.

At that time, within the assembly, the Bodhisattva Jñānaprabha and the great multitude of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya Bodhisattvas, having heard of the most supreme merits of the araṇya, immediately attained the dhāraṇī-door of hearing and retaining;
immeasurable sentient beings gave rise to the peerless, incomparable mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and attained the stage of non-retrogression.
One thousand billion sentient beings distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye.

Chapter Seven: On Disgust for the Body The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground in Previous Lives, Chapter Seven: On Disgust for the Body. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

Having realized this, we, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have gone forth from the household life, have become weary of and detached from the world; dwelling in araṇya, we subdue our minds and cultivate stainless conduct.
"However, when this bodhisattva dwells in a secluded place, what kind of contemplation should he apply to this very body?
At that time, the Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Good son!
Out of great compassion for sentient beings, you have questioned the Tathāgata regarding the Dharma-gate of the sublime practice of entering the contemplation of noble wisdom.
Listen attentively; I shall now explain it to you."
“Yes, World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it. “Good son!”

When a renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya seeks anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they minutely observe during the four modes of deportment that this out-flowing body consists of thirty-seven kinds of impure and foul things; it is unlovely and lacks solidity. One should contemplate this body as being like a clay vessel: though its exterior is skillfully adorned and decorated with various colors and the seven treasures of gold and silver, its interior is filled and packed to the brim with filth and all manner of impurities. Carried on two shoulders along the road, those who see it may feel love and delight, unaware that the vessel is filled with impurity. Within this vessel there are six black snakes; if even one snake moves, the vessel immediately breaks apart, becoming poisonous, harmful, and foul-smelling, ultimately beyond endurance.

People of the world adorn their bodies like those painted vessels filled with impurities. Greed, hatred, and delusion are called diseases of the mind; wind, bile, and phlegm are called diseases of the body. These six internal and external maladies can harm both body and mind, just as six snakes dwelling within a vessel: if each snake moves, the vessel is immediately destroyed; if each disease flares up, the body becomes impermanent.
"Good son!
When a renunciant bodhisattva dwells in seclusion and contemplates this body, it is called the first mark of the contemplation of impurity.
Furthermore, throughout the day and night, the renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his own body as foul, filthy, and impure, just like a dead dog."
Why is this? Because that body is also produced with the impurities of one's parents as its causal condition.
Furthermore, the renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his own body as being like an anthill inhabited by many ants.
At that time, a white elephant came to the side of the tower and touched it with its body; the tower immediately collapsed and shattered.
"Good son!

This tower represents the body of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). The white elephant is a messenger of Yamarāja; the body returning to the next world is like the elephant destroying the tower."
Furthermore, the renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his own body and reflects:
"This body of mine, from the crown of my head to my feet, is composed of skin, flesh, bone, and marrow joined together; it is like a plantain tree, for there is no core within."

Furthermore, the renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his own body as lacking any real strength: the skin and flesh thinly cover it like plaster on a wall; the hundreds of millions of hairs grow from it like grass sprouting from the earth; and the subtle wind-element enters and exits through the pores. What wise person would take pleasure in such a body?
Because it decays and transforms moment by moment,
the renunciant bodhisattva further contemplates his own body as being like raising a venomous snake only to suffer its harm.
Although I now nourish and sustain this body with food, drink, and clothing, it remains ungrateful and will ultimately cause me to fall into the evil realms.
Furthermore, the renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his own body as being like an enemy who feigns friendship, watching for an opportunity to administer poison and sever the life-faculty.
My body is likewise fundamentally not real, for it ultimately leads to impermanence and is not cherished by the noble ones.

Furthermore, the renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his own body as being like a bubble on the water; though it may possess the exquisite color of a lapis lazuli gem, it arises and ceases through momentary conditions and lacks constancy, for conditioned phenomena do not endure for even a single thought-moment.
Furthermore, the renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his own body as being like a city of gandharvas, which, though manifesting appearances, does not truly exist; my present body is likewise thus.
Furthermore, the renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his own body as being like a reflection; my body is likewise, existing yet not real.

The renunciant bodhisattva further contemplates his own body as being like a powerful foreign enemy; my body is now just like this, with the enemies of the afflictions plundering its roots of goodness.

Furthermore, the renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his own body as being like a dilapidated house which, despite being repaired and maintained, is destined to collapse; my body is likewise, for despite being cherished and cared for, it is inevitably impermanent.

Furthermore, the renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his own body as being like the people of a city-state near an enemy nation, who constantly harbor fear; likewise, my own body is now just so, fearing the enemy of impermanence in every moment of thought.

Furthermore, the renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his own body as being like immeasurable fuel being consumed by fire; yet that fierce fire is never satiated. His own body is likewise: with the fire of craving, he burns the fuel of the five desires, and the growth of his mind is just the same.

Furthermore, the renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his own body as being like a newborn child whom a compassionate mother constantly protects out of pity; my body is likewise, for if I do not protect this sickly body and mind, I will be unable to achieve any cultivation or realization.

Furthermore, the renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his own body as being impure by nature. It is like a person who, loathing the color of charcoal, employs various skillful means to wash it with water; yet after an immeasurable time, its blackness remains as before, and even until the charcoal is consumed, it yields no benefit. My body is likewise: it is tainted and impure, such that even if one were to wash it with the waters of the ocean until the end of the future, it would be of no avail, just as in that case.

Furthermore, the renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his own body as being like firewood drenched in oil and set ablaze by flames; moreover, it encounters a great wind that cannot be stopped. This body is likewise so: it is called the fuel of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), drenched with the oil of craving and attachment, set ablaze by the fire of hatred, and buffeted by the force of the wind of ignorance without respite.
The renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his own body as being like a malignant disease, for it is the dwelling place of the four hundred and four ailments;
and it is also like the large intestine, for it is the dwelling place of eighty-four thousand worms.
This is a realm of impermanence, for the exhaled breath does not return and is thus impermanent.
It is also like insentient matter, for the conscious spirit is easily detached from it, becoming like a tile or a stone.
Furthermore, it is like a river, for it does not abide for even a moment from one instant to the next.
Furthermore, it is like pressing oil, for one undergoes toil and suffering in all matters.
To have no support is like an infant who has lost its parents.
To have no protection is like a frog being swallowed by a snake.
It is like a bottomless pit, for the mind and mental factors cannot be known;
it is constantly insatiable, for the mind never tires of the pleasures of the five desires;
and it is perpetually lacking in autonomy, for it is bound by the two views of annihilationism and eternalism.
They lack a sense of shame and remorse because, despite having been nurtured and raised, they abandon their benefactor.
They are like corpses, for during the day and night they draw near to destruction.
They experience only various sufferings, as there is no true happiness in any state.
It is the basis for suffering, because all manner of suffering dwells within this body.
It is like an empty village, for within this body there is no sovereign master.
It is ultimately empty and quiescent, being merely the false fabrications of pervasive conceptualization.
It is like an echo in a valley, for it is manifested through that which is entirely false and illusory.
It is also like a ship; if there is no helmsman, it will drift and sink.
It is also like a great carriage transporting wealth and treasures.
Why is this? Because one rides upon the Mahāyāna to reach bodhi. Good son!

The renunciant bodhisattva observes day and night; it is not that they do not cherish such a body, but rather because they desire to cause sentient beings to emerge from the ocean of birth and death and reach the other shore.
At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished speaking this Dharma, he addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya, saying:
“Good son! To practice such conduct as this is what is called the essential Dharma to be contemplated by a child of the Buddha who has left the household life.”

If there are sons of the Buddha who resolve upon the bodhicitta and, seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, dwell in an araṇya to cultivate these thirty-seven contemplations, and furthermore teach others to practice these essential dharmas—explaining, copying, receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting them; if they remain far removed from all attachment to "self" and "mine," forever severing craving for the worldly pleasures of the five desires, and are swiftly able to accomplish indestructible faith, seeking great bodhi without sparing even their own bodies or lives, let alone any worldly treasures.

In this very life, one will certainly attain the ultimate fulfillment of the vajra-jñāna-mudrā of all Tathāgatas; one shall never regress from the unsurpassed path, swiftly perfect the six pāramitās and the myriad practices, and rapidly achieve anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At that time, eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas who had newly resolved their minds toward awakening within the assembly deeply grew weary of the world and attained the power of great forbearance, never again to regress from the unsurpassed path.
One hundred thousand brahmins gave rise to the bodhicitta, matured their faculty of faith, and attained the stage of non-retrogression.
Thirty-six thousand sons and daughters of good family were distanced from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.

The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground in Past Lives, Volume Six, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajña of Kaśmīra by Imperial Decree. Chapter Eight: The Perfections (Pāramitā). At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason do you so earnestly praise dwelling in an araṇya to practice the bodhisattva path, yet do not praise dwelling in other places to practice the bodhisattva path?
Once, the Tathāgata was on Vulture Peak Mountain, where he extensively expounded the essential Dharma for the sake of the bodhisattvas, saying:

"A bodhisattva may at times stay in the house of a courtesan or associate with a butcher, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them through countless skillful means to bring benefit to sentient beings, preaching the sublime Dharma so that they may enter the Buddha-way."

"The sublime Dharma taught today by the World-Honored One for those who have newly resolved their minds is not like that; yet we, being of such a kind, have personally heard the profound Dharma before the Buddha and are free from doubt."
We only pray that the Tathāgata will,
for the sake of those seeking the Buddha-way in future ages, expound the profound and subtle True Dharma, so that the bodhisattva practice may never again regress.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya: “Good son!
Among those who resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and seek the path to enlightenment, there are two kinds of bodhisattvas:”
The first is the householder, and the second is the renunciant.
A householder bodhisattva, desiring to transform and guide those in brothels and butcher shops, may approach them all; a renunciant bodhisattva does not do so.
However, these bodhisattvas each have nine grades. Those of the three superior grades of faculties all dwell in araṇyas, practicing uninterrupted diligence to benefit sentient beings.

As for the bodhisattvas of the middle and lower grades of faculties, their places of residence are not fixed according to their needs; they may dwell in araṇyas or reside in villages, benefiting and bringing peace to sentient beings in accordance with conditions. You should observe such gateways of practice.
"Furthermore, noble son!

A bodhisattva who has left the household life cultivates the path of the Buddha; having already attained the untainted and true Dharma, he brings benefit and happiness to all sentient beings according to their conditions."

If there is a son of the Buddha who has not yet attained true wisdom but dwells in an araṇya, he must certainly draw near to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; if he encounters a true spiritual friend, he will surely never retreat from the bodhisattva practices.
For these reasons, sons of the Buddha, you should with a sincere heart seek to behold a single Buddha and a single Bodhisattva. Good sons!
This is called the essential dharma for transcending the world; you should all cultivate and study it with a single mind.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

A renunciant bodhisattva who, weary of and detached from the world, dwells in an araṇya, will—with little exertion—perfect eighty-four thousand practices of the pāramitās and swiftly realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

Why is this? If one abandons fame and profit to dwell in mountain forests, one will certainly have no stinginess regarding body, life, or wealth, and will never be bound by attachments; thus, the three types of *pāramitās* will naturally be easily fulfilled.
Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
A bodhisattva who dwells in an araṇya and has left the household life does not accumulate wealth or treasures; by what causes and conditions is he able to bring the dānapāramitā to fulfillment?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya: “Good son!

When a bodhisattva who has renounced the world and dwells in an araṇya enters a village to beg for food, he first gives a small portion of it to sentient beings and then gives another portion to those who desire it; this is what is called the pāramitā of dāna.”

To offer one’s own life as an offering to the Triple Gem, and to give away one’s head, eyes, marrow, and brain to those who come seeking them, is what is called the perfection of intimacy (*upaniṣad-pāramitā*).
To preach the supramundane Dharma for the sake of those seeking the Dharma, so that they may resolve to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, is what is called the perfection of reality (*bhūta-pāramitā*).
“Good son! This is called a renunciant bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the perfection of giving.
Furthermore, good son!”

When a renunciant bodhisattva dwells in an araṇya and practices the twelve dhūta ascetic virtues, if while walking they look only two cubits ahead of them so as not to harm living beings, this is called the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).
To steadfastly uphold the prohibitions and precepts without sparing one’s own body or life is what is called the "proximate pāramitā.
To seek the transcendence of the world by preaching the Dharma and teaching others, causing them to resolve upon unexcelled bodhicitta, is what is called the "true pāramitā."
"Noble son!
This is called the accomplishment of the perfection of ethical discipline by a renunciant bodhisattva.
Furthermore, noble son!"

When a renunciant bodhisattva dwells in an araṇya, they are able to extinguish anger and attain the samādhi of loving-kindness; furthermore, by not disparaging or insulting any sentient beings, this is termed the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
If one were to preach a single phrase of Dharma for the sake of a single person, causing them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, this may be called the true *pāramitā*.
"Good son! This is called the renunciant bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the perfection of patience.
Furthermore, good son!"

The renunciant bodhisattva, for the sake of enabling sentient beings to attain Buddhahood, cultivates the practice of diligence. Although they have not yet attained Buddhahood and their merit and wisdom are still weak, they do not crave ease and pleasure, nor do they commit various transgressions. They give rise to deep joy regarding the ascetic practices performed by bodhisattvas in the past, honoring and looking up to them with constant, uninterrupted devotion. By these causes and conditions, this is termed the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā).
To cast away body and life as one discards mucus or saliva, and to never be indolent at any time, is what is called the perfection of intimacy (*upaniṣad-pāramitā*).

To encounter those with the necessary conditions and teach them the supreme path, causing them to advance toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, is what is called the perfection of reality (*tattva-pāramitā*).
Through the mind of diligence, these ten practices will not regress in the past, will be steadfast in the present, and will be swiftly fulfilled in the future.
Son of good family!
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva who has gone forth accomplishing the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā).

"Furthermore, noble son! A renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya cultivates samādhi in order to gather wholesome dharmas so they are not lost; he enters various liberations to forever sever extreme views; he manifests supernatural powers to transform sentient beings and cause them to attain right knowledge; he cuts off the root of afflictions and enters the true dharma-realm; and he awakens to the path of reality as he should proceed toward bodhi. By these causes and conditions, he is named the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā)."

Wishing to cause all sentient beings to be no different from oneself and to attain complete fulfillment, one tames sentient beings without abandoning samādhi; practicing this samādhi without sparing even body or life is what is called the perfection of intimacy (upaniṣad-pāramitā).
To preach the profound and wondrous Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, causing them all to incline toward unsurpassed bodhi, is what is called the "true pāramitā. Good son!
This is called the renunciant bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the dhyāna-pāramitā. "Furthermore, son of good family!

A renunciant bodhisattva dwells in seclusion, drawing near to and making offerings to all Buddhas and bodhisattvas who possess omniscience; they constantly delight in hearing the profound and wondrous Dharma, their hearts filled with yearning and never weary of it; they are well able to discern the truth of the two truths, sever the two obstacles, and master the five sciences; by expounding the essentials of all dharmas, they can resolve the doubts of the multitude. Through these causes and conditions, they are named as having attained the prajñā-pāramitā."
To seek even half a verse, one discards body and life, undaunted by manifold sufferings and resolute in the pursuit of Bodhi; this is the perfection of intimacy (*upāya-pāramitā*).

To preach the Dharma for others within the great assembly, without withholding any profound or subtle meanings, and to enable them to give rise to the mind of great Bodhi and attain non-retrogression in the bodhisattva practices; to constantly observe that one’s own body, the forest hermitage (*araṇya*), the mind of Bodhi, and the true *dharmakāya*—these four—are without distinction; because one contemplates this wondrous principle in such a manner, it is called the perfection of truth (*satya-pāramitā*).
"Noble son!
This is called a renunciant bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the perfection of wisdom.
Furthermore, noble son!"

A renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in a secluded place is constantly able to cultivate the supreme perfection of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya-pāramitā*). By means of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), they can discern the differences in the inclinations, afflictions, and mental activities of sentient beings, administering medicine according to their ailments so that all may be cured. They sport with mastery in supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and samādhis, give rise to great compassionate vows to mature sentient beings, and attain thorough penetration of all the teachings of the Buddhas. For these reasons, they are named as having attained the perfection of skillful means.
For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, one does not cling at all to body, life, or wealth; this is termed the "perfection of intimacy" (*upāya-pāramitā*).

Regarding all sentient beings with equanimity toward both enemies and kin, one teaches the subtle and wondrous Dharma to lead them into the Buddha’s wisdom; this is termed the "perfection of reality" (*tattva-pāramitā*).
“Good son! This is called the bodhisattva who has gone forth accomplishing the perfection of skillful means.
Furthermore, good son!”

When a renunciant bodhisattva enters the mountain forests, they are able to constantly practice the perfection of aspiration for the sake of all sentient beings. Their minds perpetually contemplate the true nature of all phenomena—the wondrous principle of the Middle Way, which is neither existent nor empty. They are fully capable of discerning all worldly affairs and constantly cultivate loving-kindness and compassion to transform sentient beings. By virtue of these causes and conditions, this is named the perfection of aspiration.

To embrace sentient beings through the four great vows, even to the point of sacrificing one’s own body without violating the vow of compassion, is called the perfection of intimacy (*upaniṣad-pāramitā*).
To preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma with unimpeded eloquence, such that those who hear it never ultimately regress, is called the perfection of reality (*tattva-pāramitā*).
“Good son! This is called the bodhisattva who has gone forth accomplishing the perfection of aspiration (praṇidhāna-pāramitā).
Furthermore, good son!”

When a renunciant bodhisattva dwells in an araṇya, through the power of correct wisdom, they thoroughly understand the black and white mental activities of sentient beings. Being able to preach the appropriate Dharma for those beings, they cause them to enter the profound and wondrous meaning of the Mahāyāna, whereby they can abide in ultimate nirvāṇa. For these reasons, this is termed the *bala-pāramitā* (perfection of power).

By perceiving with the eye of right wisdom the principle that the five aggregates are empty and quiescent, one is able to relinquish body and life to benefit sentient beings; therefore, this is called the perfection of intimacy (*upaniṣad-pāramitā*).

By employing the power of wondrous wisdom to transform those with false views, causing them to sever the evil karma of saṃsāric birth and death and to advance toward the ultimate nirvāṇa of eternal bliss, this is what is called the "true pāramitā."
“Noble son!
This is called the bodhisattva who has gone forth accomplishing the perfection of power (balapāramitā).
Furthermore, noble son!”

When an ordained bodhisattva dwells in an araṇya, thoroughly understands good and evil regarding all phenomena, remains far removed from false views while embracing the true Dharma, and neither loathes saṃsāra nor delights in nirvāṇa, this is called the perfection of wisdom (jñāna-pāramitā).

Not cherishing one's own self but feeling compassion for sentient beings, constantly practicing great renunciation of body, life, and wealth—this is called the *upāya-pāramitā* (perfection of skillful means).

Using subtle and wondrous wisdom to preach the Dharma of the One Vehicle for all sentient beings, causing them to enter *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—by these causes and conditions, it is called the *tattva-pāramitā* (perfection of reality).
"Noble son!
This is called the bodhisattva who has gone forth achieving the perfection of wisdom. Noble son!"
For what reason are these pāramitās said to have eighty-four thousand distinct varieties?
You should know this:
for those with excessive desire, two thousand one hundred pāramitās were analytically expounded.
For those with a predominance of hatred, he analytically expounds two thousand one hundred pāramitās;
for those with a predominance of delusion, he analytically expounds two thousand one hundred pāramitās;
and for those with equal proportions of the three poisons, he analytically expounds two thousand one hundred pāramitās.
"Noble son!
Taking these two thousand one hundred pāramitās as the foundation, they increase tenfold to become eighty-four thousand pāramitās; such dharmas as these are all practices for the benefit of others."
"Good son!

If there are sentient beings whose natures are difficult to tame, and whose minds have not yet been subdued even after hearing this Dharma, one should then proclaim for them the eighty-four thousand gates of samādhi; such wondrous teachings are all practices for self-benefit."

If there are sentient beings whose natures are difficult to tame, and whose minds remain unsubdued even after hearing this Dharma, one shall immediately proclaim for them the eighty-four thousand dharani-gates; such wondrous teachings are all practices for the benefit of others.
"Good son!
For the sake of taming all sentient beings, I have taught such dharmas as well as countless skillful means, manifesting various forms to transform and guide living beings."
"Good son!
For this reason, all humans and devas universally acclaim the Tathāgata, calling him the 'Teacher.
Good son!"

All the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the future and the present, have all practiced eighty-four thousand gates of *pāramitā*, eighty-four thousand gates of *samādhi*, and eighty-four thousand gates of *dhāraṇī*. Having forever severed the eighty-four thousand subtle affliction-obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the eighty-four thousand subtle cognitive-obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), they all proceed to the king of *bodhi*-trees in the *araṇya*, sit upon the diamond throne (*vajrāsana*), and enter the diamond concentration (*vajrasamādhi*). Having subdued all the celestial Māra-enemies, they realize *anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Great Dharma King who transcends the three realms, Appears in the world to transform all classes of beings;
Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges Enter the gate of the Buddha’s ambrosial wisdom."
The Honored One Maitreya, who attained the Way through kalpas past, Inquires with a heart of great compassion:
“Excellent, stainless Prince of Dharma! Your wisdom is able to inquire about the true Buddha-vehicle.”
With the fearless eloquence of a lion, I shall expound the path leading to awakening within the Mahāyāna;
you all should listen with single-minded attention and carefully, so that it may be transmitted to those who are to receive it in the future.
The worlds of the ten directions may be made empty, But let not the supramundane path be severed or exhausted.
Those seeking liberation via the supramundane path Do not exceed the three faculties and nine grades.
Those of superior capacity of the three grades dwell in forest hermitages; those of middling and inferior capacities transform the world according to conditions.
The fruits of the Way they seek are equal and without distinction, as they together realize the ocean of True Suchness and Buddha-nature.
Having already attained the untainted state, these true Mahāsattvas manifest according to what is appropriate to deliver all sentient beings;
they reveal the gate of the non-duality of existence and emptiness, benefiting themselves and others without interruption.
O sons of the Buddhas who have not yet attained the outflow-free state, you should diligently cultivate the three trainings;
dedicate your roots of goodness for the sake of all sentient beings, and with single-minded devotion, focus your mindfulness on the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
May I always behold the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, Whose bodies are adorned with boundless merit;
May I constantly hear the sound of the rain of Dharma, So that all may be universally moistened and their minds never regress.
Though my body constantly dwells in hell, it is not that I do not draw near the Great Compassionate Honored One;
though my body constantly dwells in saṃsāra, it is not that I do not personally hear the subtle and wondrous Dharma.
For these reasons, O sons of the Buddha, bind your minds and constantly keep the Teacher of Gods and Humans in mind;
if there are sons of the Buddha who cultivate the Noble Path, they shall give rise to the unsurpassed Bodhicitta.
Disenchanted with the world, one dwells in an araṇya; this too is called practicing the three perfections:
first giving one's own food daily, and further bestowing the treasure of the Dharma upon sentient beings.
Generosity is the purity of the three spheres; by cultivating this cause, one’s virtue becomes perfected.
Know that the realization of the pāramitā arises solely from the purity of mind, not from material wealth.
If one gives precious wealth with a defiled mind, it is not as good as giving even a small portion with a pure mind;
such a gift of material wealth is called the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), and this pāramitā is neither two nor three.
One who can give away their own body, life, wife, and children is thus called "approaching deliverance.
If there is a son of good family seeking the Dharma,
for whom one expounds all Mahāyāna sūtras and causes them to resolve upon unsurpassed bodhicitta— this alone is named the "true pāramitā."
Endowed with compassion, pure faith, and a sense of shame and dread of blame, they gather in sentient beings and cause them to leave greed behind.
May they fulfill the unsurpassed wisdom of the Tathāgata; this twofold giving of wealth and Dharma is called the first crossing.
Firmly upholding the Bodhisattva’s three clusters of precepts, Awakening to bodhi and departing from birth and death,
Protecting the Buddha-dharma so it may abide in the world— To be able to repent of transgressions is true observance of the precepts.
Subduing the mind of anger through the contemplation of compassion, one should reflect upon past causes when confronted by enmity and harm;
sparing neither body nor life to rescue sentient beings—this is called the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
Capable of performing what is difficult to do without ever forsaking it, constantly advancing throughout three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas;
with an unshared lack of defilement, they perpetually refine the mind, seeking liberation for the sake of delivering sentient beings.
Attaining mastery over entering and emerging from samādhi, They manifest transformations and supernatural powers while wandering through the ten directions;
To sever the causes of sentient beings' afflictions, They seek liberation through the gates of samādhi.
If you wish to accomplish true wisdom, Draw near to Bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas;
Delight in hearing the sublime gates of supramundane principles, Cultivate the attainment of the three insights and sever the two obstacles.
Able to discern the differences in the minds of sentient beings, He administers medicine according to their ailments for them to take and practice;
With compassion and skillful means suited to their faculties, He benefits living beings through expedient methods and delivers the multitudes from existence.
Contemplating the true meaning of all phenomena, Neither clinging to the middle nor the extremes, and free from existence and non-existence;
Pure wisdom, uninterrupted, realizes suchness, Equally fulfilling the two benefits throughout the entire dharma-realm.
With the power of wisdom, he understands the natures of sentient beings, And for them, he preaches various teachings that accord with their needs;
With the power of wisdom, he enters the minds of sentient beings, Causing them to sever the root of saṃsāric birth and death;
With the power of wisdom, he can distinguish between black and white dharmas, Fully understanding what to adopt and what to abandon according to circumstances.
Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are fundamentally equal; To bring sentient beings to fulfillment, they transcend discrimination.
These ten kinds of sublime practices Are subsumed within the eighty-four thousand [teachings].
According to their respective categories, these supreme dharma-gates Are called the Bodhisattva pāramitās.
The eighty-four thousand samādhis can extinguish the distracted minds of sentient beings;
The eighty-four thousand dhāraṇī-doors can eliminate the obstacles of delusion and dissolve the hosts of Māras.
Through the power of skillful means, the Great Sage, the Dharma King, transforms sentient beings with three essential teachings;
casting his net of instruction across the ocean of birth and death, he establishes them in the place of peace and bliss for humans and devas.
At that time, when the World-Honored One was preaching this Dharma, eighty-four thousand devaputras of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven severed the obstacles of the three realms and realized the Stage of Joy;
countless hundreds of thousands of devaputras of the six heavens of desire awakened to the patience of the non-arising of dharmas and attained dhāraṇīs;
and sixteen great kings attained the dhāraṇī of hearing and retaining.

The immeasurable fourfold assembly, having heard of the bodhisattva practices, some attained the stage of non-retrogression, some attained gates of samādhi, some attained dhāraṇīs, and some attained great supernormal powers;
some bodhisattvas realized the second, third, or even up to the tenth stage, leaping for joy;
and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of humans and devas resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and never again regressed.
Eight thousand devas and humans distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye.

Chapter Nine: Adornment of Merit The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground in Previous Lives, Chapter Nine: Adornment of Merit At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, one who achieves the merit of dwelling in an araṇya shall attain Buddhahood.
How does a bodhisattva cultivate various merits so that they are able to dwell within such an araṇya?
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for me!
At that time, the Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, saying:
“O son of good family!
When you practice and study, if you possess but one virtue, that person should dwell in an araṇya to seek the unsurpassed path.
What is this one?
This means that one contemplates that the very source of all afflictions is one's own mind; having thoroughly realized this principle, one is capable of dwelling in an araṇya. Why is this so?
For example, it is like a rabid dog that, when driven and beaten by a person, pursues only the shards and stones and not the person.

Those who have newly resolved to attain enlightenment and dwell in an araṇya in future ages will be just like this: if they see forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects and their minds become stained with attachment, these people do not know the root of afflictions, nor do they know that the five sense objects arise from one's own mind. This is precisely what is called being unable to dwell well in an araṇya; for this reason, they delight in dwelling in tranquility while seeking the unsurpassed path.
All Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, when the objects of the five desires appear before them, should observe their own minds and think thus:

"From beginningless time until this day, I have transmigrated through the six realms of existence with no prospect of escape; all this has arisen from the delusions of my own false mind, which has greedily craved and become attached to the objects of the five desires."
"A bodhisattva such as this is said to be capable of dwelling in an araṇya.
Suppose someone were to ask:
'Which sentient beings will attain Buddhahood in future ages?'"

One should point out that such a person, in a future age, shall emerge from the suffering of the triple world, shatter the armies of the four Māras, swiftly attain Bodhi, and enter the wisdom of the Buddha; all the world, including the devas, nāgas, the eight classes of beings, asuras, and others, should offer them worship.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, with a pure mind, makes offerings to such a true and virtuous disciple of the Buddha dwelling in an araṇya, the merit they obtain will be immeasurable and boundless.
Furthermore, if there should be another person who makes offerings of various precious jewels to their compassionate mother, the merit obtained would likewise be without distinction. Why is this?

Because such a person shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, turn the wheel of the true Dharma to deliver the multitudes of devas and humans, continue the lineage of the Triple Gem so that it is never severed, and act as a refuge for all sentient beings.
